sections.walkthrough: Expected output: burn 20.0x page true recovered false missing true. Both window samples are explicit input data; they are not collected automatically from a real monitoring system. Use tolerances when asserting floating-point rates.

sections.body: A long window captures significant consumption, while a short window confirms the problem is still active. Windows, thresholds and minimum event volume depend on the service and response time; a low-traffic service may need additional signals and careful sampling. Write down who receives the alert, the symptom, evidence links and a first safe action. Separate an urgent user-impacting page from a capacity-planning ticket.
sections.title: Combine time windows with a response contract

sections.body: For a Go HTTP service, count eligible outcomes and record latency with stable operation labels. Avoid user IDs, raw URLs, request bodies, secrets and unbounded error strings as metric labels. Correlate structured logs and traces without treating either as a substitute for an aggregate SLI. A per-instance health probe answers a routing/process question; it is not automatically the service-level user outcome.
sections.title: Keep telemetry bounded and useful

sections.body: Feed a sustained high-error sample, a brief spike, a recovered short window, zero observations and impossible counters into the model. Verify that missing evidence is visibly unavailable. Explain why each scenario pages or does not. Add a small load test in a disposable native service, observe the real route and compare client timeouts with server outcomes. Preserve the incident timeline and tune the policy from those observations, rather than muting unexplained alerts.
sections.title: Rehearse one page and one recovery

reading.takeaway: Define eligible events, compute error-budget burn and require both recent and sustained evidence before paging.

lessons.title: Use an SLO to decide when an incident needs attention

lessons.explanation: An incident begins with user impact and uncertainty. A useful responder establishes scope, a current owner and an evidence timeline before trying unrelated commands. Recovery must preserve work the service already acknowledged, including writes accepted after a backup or a server move.
lessons.objective: Use a bounded runbook to gather evidence, choose a reversible mitigation and distinguish binary rollback from restoring persistent data.

cautions: Rehearse restoration in isolation and preserve/reconcile later accepted writes. Binary compatibility, persistent-data recovery and route verification are separate obligations.
designGuide.cost: Automation needs explicit ownership, bounded privileges, tests and recovery evidence; a shorter command is not sufficient.
strengths: Use a bounded runbook to gather evidence, choose a reversible mitigation and distinguish binary rollback from restoring persistent data.
Make changes reviewable and verify the result against the original contract.

alternatives: Overwrite the live volume and assume the writes can be retried
Treat an image rollback as a complete database recovery
quiz.correct: Preserve accepted writes before restoring state
quiz.explanation: Rehearse restoration in isolation and preserve/reconcile later accepted writes. Binary compatibility, persistent-data recovery and route verification are separate obligations.
quiz.hint: Track the writer boundary and where later acknowledged work lives.
quiz.question: An old backup predates accepted writes. What makes a restore plan reviewable?

review.answer: Preserve accepted writes before restoring state

sections.body: Confirm the environment, service, affected operation and time window. Inspect the actual serving image, route, process health, recent release and user-outcome telemetry. For Kubernetes, verify context/namespace before logs or rollout inspection; for a Linux service, verify the named unit and journal window. Record facts separately from hypotheses. Keep access credentials and customer payloads out of shared incident notes.
sections.title: Start with read-only evidence and an explicit target

sections.body: A mitigation may reduce traffic, disable a failing optional feature or restore a compatible binary. Name the person controlling the change, the exact target and version, the expected result, a deadline and the point at which to stop or reverse. Preserve original evidence while limiting ongoing impact. Communicate the observed effect rather than declaring recovery because a command exited zero. Concurrent responders should avoid silently changing the same resource.
sections.title: Select a mitigation with an owner and stop condition

sections.body: The program returns a reviewable recommendation and performs no rollback or restore. An old binary is a candidate only when its declared reader range includes the current schema. If a restore would erase later acknowledged writes, recovering into a separate environment and reconciling those writes must be considered. The model intentionally has no “overwrite live data now” action.
sections.title: A recovery decision model
sections.walkthrough: Expected lines: candidate: roll back binary; verify route and outcomes; roll forward or restore separately and reconcile accepted writes; rehearse isolated restore; do not overwrite the live writer. Compatibility metadata itself needs tests against real schemas, not optimistic labels.

sections.body: A completed backup job does not prove a usable restore. In an isolated environment, restore a known snapshot, verify integrity and application reads, document required configuration/key references and measure recovery time. State the accepted data-loss window and the source of truth for later writes. A container image rollback does not restore a database, and copying files while a writer is active is not automatically a consistent backup. Use the storage engine’s documented recovery method.
sections.title: Rehearse backup restoration before an emergency

sections.body: Verify the user operation through the real route and observe the recovery window. Record the impact, detection gap, sequence of actions, contributing conditions and evidence for recovery. Add an independently testable action with an owner and due criterion: a missing compatibility test, a clearer runbook or a safer rollout gate. Keep the record focused on system behavior and learning. The goal is to reduce the chance and cost of repetition, not to identify a person to blame.
sections.title: Close the loop with a blameless improvement

reading.takeaway: Use a bounded runbook to gather evidence, choose a reversible mitigation and distinguish binary rollback from restoring persistent data.

lessons.title: Respond to an incident without destroying the accepted writes

lessons.explanation: A green build does not authorize a deployment. Each job needs an identity, a target and a bounded permission set. Keep production credentials out of source, course exports and lab files.
lessons.objective: Separate authentication, authorization and credential lifetime in a delivery workflow.

cautions: An identity can authenticate successfully and still be denied a resource action. Test that denial deliberately.
designGuide.cost: Real provider and network evidence requires an owned disposable environment; local files describe a contract without performing the integration.
strengths: Separate authentication, authorization and credential lifetime in a delivery workflow.
Keep an explicit contract and retain both successful and denied observations.

alternatives: Only the friendly name of the deployment role.
A shared administrator key committed with the pipeline.
quiz.correct: Issuer, audience, workload claims
quiz.explanation: An identity can authenticate successfully and still be denied a resource action. Test that denial deliberately.
quiz.hint: Separate who may assume the role from what the role may do.
quiz.question: What should constrain a workload identity exchange?

review.answer: Issuer, audience, workload claims

sections.body: Record the CI job identity, environment and intended action before choosing permissions. A pull request from a fork should not receive deployment rights. Separate artifact-read, staging-deploy and production-promote roles. Restrict both the allowed actions and resource scope; a role name alone does not establish the boundary.
sections.title: Identify the principal and target

sections.body: A workload identity can exchange an identity token for a short-lived role session. Bind trust to the expected issuer, audience, repository and protected environment. Inspect the trust policy as well as the permission policy. Avoid storing a long-lived administrator key in a workflow variable. Rotation and expiration reduce exposure but do not replace authorization.
sections.title: Prefer a short-lived exchange

sections.body: In an owned disposable account, verify that the staging role can inspect its own target and is denied production changes. Record the principal, resource, attempted action and redacted audit event. Never paste tokens into logs. The local shell deliberately has no cloud authentication or egress; write the expected access matrix here, then perform the integration test in your own isolated environment.
sections.code:
principal          staging/read  staging/deploy  production/deploy
ci-verify          allow         deny            deny
ci-staging         allow         allow           deny
ci-production      allow         deny            allow after approval
sections.title: Prove denial as well as success
sections.walkthrough: Read each row as a distinct principal, not as one shared token. Verification has no deployment rights. Staging can change only staging. The production row still requires a separately approved job and a matching trust policy; this matrix is a design artifact, not evidence that a cloud policy was installed.

reading.takeaway: An operational identity is a narrow authorization contract with a lifetime, not a reusable administrator secret.

lessons.title: IAM: give a job one narrow, short-lived identity

lessons.explanation: Declarative infrastructure tools compare configuration, recorded state and an observed provider view. A plan is a proposal at an observation boundary; it is not a guarantee that the world stays unchanged until apply.
lessons.objective: Explain state ownership, review a proposed change and recover from a failed apply without discarding evidence.

cautions: Locking coordinates cooperating writers; it does not prove that an apply is safe or that external drift cannot happen.
designGuide.cost: Real provider and network evidence requires an owned disposable environment; local files describe a contract without performing the integration.
strengths: Explain state ownership, review a proposed change and recover from a failed apply without discarding evidence.
Keep an explicit contract and retain both successful and denied observations.

alternatives: Delete the state file and recreate every object.
Force-unlock immediately without checking the current writer.
quiz.correct: Inspect state and resources; re-plan
quiz.explanation: Locking coordinates cooperating writers; it does not prove that an apply is safe or that external drift cannot happen.
quiz.hint: Retain the record that connects intent to real objects.
quiz.question: What should follow a partial apply failure?

review.answer: Inspect state and resources; re-plan

sections.body: Configuration describes intent; state binds configured resources to provider objects; a refresh observes the current remote system. Drift is an out-of-band change, not necessarily permission to overwrite it. Before an apply, identify the workspace, backend, account and region. A correct plan against the wrong account is still a dangerous change.
sections.title: Separate the three views

sections.body: Use a backend with appropriate state locking and access control, keep state and plan files out of public repositories, and serialize writers. State can contain sensitive values. Do not remove a lock simply because another job is slow: establish ownership and whether the operation is still running. A forced unlock or manual state edit requires a recovery procedure and evidence.
sections.title: Preserve state ownership

sections.body: Review create/update/destroy actions and blast radius before an explicit apply in a disposable environment. After a partial failure, inspect both provider reality and state, re-plan and resolve the cause. Do not delete state to make a red error disappear. Restore and import are operations with identity and backup requirements, not generic undo commands. The app provides no provider executables or remote backend; the exercise here is a reviewable plan and access checklist, followed by a real rehearsal in your own environment.
sections.code:
configuration: desired replicas = 3
state:         service id = svc-42, last replicas = 2
provider:      svc-42 currently has 1 replica
plan:          update svc-42 to 3, destroy 0
apply:         requires owned lock and explicit approval
sections.title: Verify outcomes and recovery
sections.walkthrough: The service identity binds state to one real resource. Refresh discovers a count of one; configuration still requests three. Review the update against that observation and the selected account before applying. If an apply fails, preserve both the state and provider evidence, then make a fresh plan instead of assuming every action was rolled back.

reading.takeaway: Treat infrastructure state as sensitive operational evidence with one accountable writer.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code: plan, lock and inspect drift

lessons.explanation: A request can fail before an HTTP handler runs. Start from the exact caller, hostname, port and scheme, then locate the first failing boundary: name resolution, connection, TLS identity or application contract.
lessons.objective: Collect evidence at the failing boundary without disabling peer verification.

cautions: Repeatedly testing from a different environment can hide the original failure. Preserve the caller and verify the failing boundary.
designGuide.cost: Real provider and network evidence requires an owned disposable environment; local files describe a contract without performing the integration.
strengths: Collect evidence at the failing boundary without disabling peer verification.
Keep an explicit contract and retain both successful and denied observations.

alternatives: That the TLS peer identity is trusted and matches the hostname.
That the application route is healthy and returns the intended version.
quiz.correct: Name resolution for that caller
quiz.explanation: Repeatedly testing from a different environment can hide the original failure. Preserve the caller and verify the failing boundary.
quiz.hint: Separate name resolution from the connection and application contract.
quiz.question: What does a successful DNS lookup prove?

review.answer: Name resolution for that caller

sections.body: DNS results and routing depend on the actual environment. A successful lookup on a laptop does not establish what a pod resolves. Identify the namespace, search domains, service name, endpoint addresses and caller network policy. Record timestamps and the failing request before changing configuration.
sections.title: Keep the caller in the experiment

sections.body: An address resolving is not proof that the port accepts connections. A connected socket is not proof of the TLS peer name or trusted chain. A TLS handshake is not proof that a route returns the expected version. Use explicit deadlines and correlate a request ID with server evidence. Disabling certificate validation hides the trust failure instead of diagnosing it.
sections.title: Separate layers and preserve identity

sections.body: Write down the expected name, scheme, port, peer identity and HTTP status/body. Change one boundary at a time in an owned disposable environment, re-run the same request, and retain negative cases. Local shell files can model a contract and log analysis, but do not generate DNS, TLS or cluster evidence. The app has no guest sockets, curl, SSH or kubectl; use an isolated native environment for those integration checks.
sections.code:
caller: orders-pod, namespace shop
name:   payments.shop.svc.cluster.local
DNS:    returned 10.0.0.12
TCP:    port 443 accepted
TLS:    peer hostname mismatch
HTTP:   not reached
sections.title: Turn the finding into a regression check
sections.walkthrough: The DNS and TCP observations establish only their own boundaries from the named caller. A TLS hostname mismatch prevents a trusted HTTP request, so no HTTP health conclusion follows. Keep verification enabled, inspect the requested hostname and certificate identity, correct the contract, and repeat the request from the same caller.

reading.takeaway: A useful incident note identifies the first failed boundary and proves recovery from the same caller.

lessons.title: Diagnose a service boundary: DNS, transport, TLS and HTTP

summary: Operational CLIs, reconciliation, verified delivery, SLOs, incidents and data-safe recovery.
title: Around Go: DevOps and reliability
translationNote: Begin with command line, containers and Kubernetes. Go models run locally; real infrastructure, process and monitoring exercises need your own disposable native environment.

lessons.explanation: MongoDB stores BSON documents and the Go driver manages discovery and pools for the deployment. A collection handle is not a new physical connection. Reuse a client across requests, model the fields the application owns, and keep network setup outside request-time package initialization.
lessons.objective: Connect with the Go v2 driver and separate construction, readiness, request work and cleanup.

cautions: Connect configures a client; a bounded Ping separately tests current server readiness. Neither promises that future network operations cannot fail or time out.
designGuide.cost: One shared client owns pools and topology monitoring; each additional service instance multiplies that connection demand.
strengths: Connect with the Go v2 driver and separate construction, readiness, request work and cleanup.

alternatives: Every future operation will complete within its deadline
A new client must be created for each collection operation
quiz.correct: Does not alone prove server readiness
quiz.explanation: Connect configures a client; a bounded Ping separately tests current server readiness. Neither promises that future network operations cannot fail or time out.
quiz.hint: Construction and a bounded server operation are separate events.
quiz.question: What does a successful mongo.Connect call establish?

review.answer: Does not alone prove server readiness

sections.body: The example uses go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2, with v2.3.1 as a reproducible example pin. Connect constructs the client; a successful Ping is separate evidence that a server is reachable. In a native development checkout, obtain the URI from configuration and use the deployment’s required authentication and TLS.
sections.code:
client, err := mongo.Connect(options.Client().ApplyURI(uri).SetMaxPoolSize(16))
if err != nil { return err }
probe, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
err = client.Ping(probe, readpref.Primary())
cancel()
if err != nil {
    cleanup, stop := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
    defer stop()
    _ = client.Disconnect(cleanup)
    return err
}
sections.title: Construct the client and probe readiness
sections.walkthrough: The fragment belongs to a startup function returning error and imports context, time, mongo, mongo/options and mongo/readpref from the v2 driver. The pool size is illustrative, not a production sizing recommendation.

sections.body: Use BSON tags and explicit field types instead of letting every layer pass an unstructured map. Validate external input before constructing a query. ErrNoDocuments is an expected absence case when the contract allows it; it is different from a timeout, authorization failure or decode error.
sections.title: Decode into a deliberate schema
sections.walkthrough: notes is a collection from the shared client; tenant and id come from validated application inputs. The application defines ErrNotFound. An omitted tenant predicate could become a data-isolation bug even if the database query is fast.

sections.body: Every request operation should inherit a bounded caller context. Startup probes and final Disconnect need their own lifetimes; do not reuse an already canceled request context for cleanup. These native service snippets are reading material: GopherForge does not add remote MongoDB sockets to its WASI execution sandbox.
sections.title: Use separate lifetimes

reading.takeaway: Reuse a configured v2 client, prove readiness separately, decode explicit BSON models and distinguish absence from infrastructure failures.

lessons.title: MongoDB: one client, explicit deadlines and typed documents

lessons.explanation: A query that is fast with ten documents may scan a large collection after real traffic arrives. Shape the filter, sort and returned fields around an actual use case, then inspect the execution plan and the documents examined. Indexes improve selected reads while adding write, memory and maintenance cost.
lessons.objective: Use explain evidence, tenant predicates and stable pagination rather than adding indexes blindly.

cautions: The useful plan depends on filter, sort, selectivity and index shape. Explain measures examined work; a client pool setting does not guarantee index use.
designGuide.cost: Each index consumes storage, memory and write maintenance; keep it only when the measured access pattern earns that cost.
strengths: Use explain evidence, tenant predicates and stable pagination rather than adding indexes blindly.

alternatives: Any index guarantees constant-time queries
Pool size determines whether every query uses its index
quiz.correct: Trades selected read work for storage and write cost
quiz.explanation: The useful plan depends on filter, sort, selectivity and index shape. Explain measures examined work; a client pool setting does not guarantee index use.
quiz.hint: Compare work examined with useful rows returned.
quiz.question: Which trade-off should be evaluated when adding a MongoDB index?

review.answer: Trades selected read work for storage and write cost

sections.body: In an isolated development database, consider a tenant’s newest notes. A compound index starts with tenant equality and then the chosen sort keys. Keep the tie-breaker consistent with pagination so equal timestamps do not create unstable page boundaries.
sections.code:
db.notes.createIndex({tenant: 1, createdAt: -1, _id: -1})
db.notes.find({tenant: "demo"}, {body: 1, createdAt: 1})
  .sort({createdAt: -1, _id: -1}).limit(20).explain("executionStats")
sections.title: Create an index for one access pattern
sections.walkthrough: These mongosh commands assume demo documents in a development database. Compare nReturned, totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined and inspect the winning plan; explain executionStats runs the query and can itself add load.

sections.body: For descending pagination, continue before the last (createdAt, _id) pair instead of repeatedly skipping an ever-growing number of earlier results. Match the sort and predicate with the index, and define what happens when documents change between pages.
sections.title: Use a stable continuation predicate
sections.walkthrough: The timestamp and ObjectId are example continuation values, not an offset. New writes may change a live listing; a stable ordering is not automatically a snapshot of the collection across multiple requests.

sections.body: A large limit, broad regex, missing tenant condition or incompatible sort can overwhelm a previously adequate pool. Index order, multikey behavior and collation affect usable plans. Measure representative data distribution and write latency before retaining another index; hints can hide a modeling error.
sections.title: Verify selectivity and write cost

reading.takeaway: Design filter, sort, projection and continuation together, verify examined work with explain, and account for index maintenance on every write.

lessons.title: MongoDB: design the query and its compound index together

lessons.explanation: Reading a document, changing a field in Go and writing it back leaves a window for another request to change the same value. Memory race detection cannot find that distributed lost update. Express the allowed transition in the database predicate and inspect whether the write actually matched.
lessons.objective: Prevent lost updates with atomic operators and optimistic version checks.

cautions: No driver error does not mean the predicate matched. Check MatchedCount and handle an absent or stale-version document; one-document atomicity does not cover every business invariant.
designGuide.cost: Version conflicts become visible application outcomes; the caller needs retry, merge or user-facing conflict behavior.
strengths: Prevent lost updates with atomic operators and optimistic version checks.

alternatives: Only whether the preceding read found a document
Whether the Go race detector reported shared memory
quiz.correct: Is an outcome to handle, not automatic success
quiz.explanation: No driver error does not mean the predicate matched. Check MatchedCount and handle an absent or stale-version document; one-document atomicity does not cover every business invariant.
quiz.hint: No driver error does not imply that the predicate matched.
quiz.question: How should a version-checked MongoDB update that matches no document be treated?

review.answer: Is an outcome to handle, not automatic success

sections.body: Use an atomic field operator when it expresses the intended operation. A client-side read followed by replacement can lose a concurrent edit or erase fields the caller never loaded. Include ownership predicates such as the tenant in the write, not only in the earlier read.
sections.title: Update fields without replacing unrelated state
sections.walkthrough: This fragment assumes the shared v2 driver collection and application variables. A zero match can mean stale version or absence; map that to the application contract rather than reporting an unconditional successful save.

sections.body: A preliminary find cannot guarantee that another request will not insert the same business key. Define a unique index for that invariant and handle duplicate-key errors deliberately. In multi-tenant systems, decide whether uniqueness is global or scoped to a tenant.
sections.title: Enforce uniqueness where concurrent writers meet
sections.walkthrough: The example is a development upsert keyed by a stable external identifier. Review existing duplicate data before adding the unique index; deployment of an invariant is itself a migration that can fail.

sections.body: One atomic update does not make a two-document business operation atomic. Prefer a document model that contains the invariant when practical, or use a transaction with a clear cost and retry policy. Avoid promising exactly-once business effects just because the driver can retry an eligible write.
sections.title: Single-document atomicity has a boundary

reading.takeaway: Use conditional atomic writes and database-enforced uniqueness for concurrent invariants. Treat unmatched writes and duplicate keys as meaningful outcomes.

lessons.title: MongoDB: put the invariant in the write predicate

lessons.explanation: A transaction can protect a multi-document invariant, but it adds coordination and can retry work. A callback that charges a card or sends email while updating documents can repeat an external effect. Keep the database transition inside the transaction and move external delivery behind an explicit durable boundary.
lessons.objective: Choose transaction boundaries, concerns and idempotency for ambiguous failures.

cautions: The driver can rerun the transaction callback. MongoDB cannot roll back an external payment or email, so make database work repeatable and deliver external effects through an idempotent boundary.
designGuide.cost: Transactions add coordination and contention; the outbox adds durable records, delivery workers and duplicate handling.
strengths: Choose transaction boundaries, concerns and idempotency for ambiguous failures.

alternatives: MongoDB automatically rolls back every remote HTTP service
A shared session makes all goroutines globally sequential
quiz.correct: Can repeat its application-side code
quiz.explanation: The driver can rerun the transaction callback. MongoDB cannot roll back an external payment or email, so make database work repeatable and deliver external effects through an idempotent boundary.
quiz.hint: The database cannot undo an effect in another system.
quiz.question: What can an automatic WithTransaction retry do to the application callback?

review.answer: Can repeat its application-side code

sections.body: The Go v2 driver’s WithTransaction callback receives the context that operations in the transaction must use. Do not share a session concurrently across goroutines or start parallel operations inside one transaction. A replica-set or supported sharded deployment is required; a standalone local server is not equivalent.
sections.title: Keep session work sequential and owned
sections.walkthrough: The application constructs order and event with stable operation identifiers and uses collections from the same shared client. The callback contains database work only; the outbox consumer sends the external notification after commit.

sections.body: Read concern, write concern and read preference affect visibility and acknowledgment. A timeout or lost response can leave the caller unsure whether a commit happened. Reconcile using the durable operation ID rather than assuming every error means nothing changed.
sections.code:
db.orders.createIndex({operationID: 1}, {unique: true})
db.outbox.createIndex({eventID: 1}, {unique: true})
db.orders.findOne({operationID: "checkout-demo-42"})
sections.title: Define what committed means for this operation
sections.walkthrough: These development commands illustrate the durable keys used for reconciliation. Unique identifiers do not on their own deliver an external effect exactly once; the receiver and delivery process also need idempotency.

sections.body: Inject a transient transaction failure, an ambiguous commit response and a consumer crash after sending but before marking delivery. Verify the resulting invariant and duplicate handling. Short transactions reduce contention; do not perform slow HTTP calls or user interaction while holding a transaction open.
sections.title: Test the failure windows

reading.takeaway: A retryable transaction callback should contain repeatable database work. Use durable operation IDs and an outbox when the business action crosses systems.

lessons.title: MongoDB transactions: retry database work, not external effects

lessons.explanation: A cursor lets an application consume a result in batches; it is not permission to read the entire database without a budget. The query, projection, batch size, total limit and request deadline jointly determine network work and application memory. Check errors after iteration, not only when opening the cursor.
lessons.objective: Avoid loading an unbounded collection into application memory.

cautions: Streaming only stays memory-bounded when the query and downstream consumer both have explicit limits.
designGuide.cost: Bounded iteration reduces retained memory but requires cursor ownership, cancellation and downstream backpressure.
strengths: Avoid loading an unbounded collection into application memory.

alternatives: It makes the server ignore all query predicates
It automatically discards every decoded document
quiz.correct: Controls batches, not the total result limit
quiz.explanation: Streaming only stays memory-bounded when the query and downstream consumer both have explicit limits.
quiz.hint: The consumer may still retain every batch.
quiz.question: Why is a small batch size insufficient protection against memory growth?

review.answer: Controls batches, not the total result limit

sections.body: The v2 cursor’s Next can fail after some documents have already been decoded. Close the cursor on every path and propagate decode and cursor errors. A batch size controls transfer grouping; a total limit controls how much useful work the request is willing to perform.
sections.title: Iterate with a deadline and a total limit
sections.walkthrough: The fragment assumes a bounded ctx, the application’s Note model and a consumer that does not retain every document. Cleanup gets a fresh bounded context so a canceled request does not prevent the cursor-close attempt.

sections.body: For a list view, return a small subset rather than large embedded payloads. Calling All on an unbounded cursor can materialize the whole result and exhaust memory. BatchSize does not impose a total row limit or protect you if consume appends every document to a slice.
sections.code:
db.notes.find({tenant: "demo"}, {body: 1, createdAt: 1})
  .sort({createdAt: -1, _id: -1}).limit(100).batchSize(25)
sections.title: Project only what this path needs
sections.walkthrough: The development shell query caps the result independently of the batch size. Keep a supporting index for the actual filter and sort and measure response bytes as well as document count.

sections.body: If documents are sent to worker goroutines, use a bounded channel and cancellation path. Otherwise a streaming query can simply move the unbounded queue into Go memory. Do not concurrently use one cursor from multiple goroutines; give iteration one owner and distribute decoded values deliberately.
sections.title: Own downstream backpressure

reading.takeaway: Bound total work separately from batch grouping, inspect cursor.Err, close on every path, and keep downstream buffering bounded.

lessons.title: MongoDB cursors: bound the result and close the stream

lessons.explanation: When every operation slows down, a larger pool can multiply pressure on the same database. Investigate where the deadline is spent: waiting in the application, selecting a server, checking out a connection, creating a socket or executing a query. Count all application instances and topology servers in the capacity model.
lessons.objective: Separate server selection, pool checkout, query time and application queueing.

cautions: Client pool capacity, waiting goroutines and total deployment connections are different quantities.
designGuide.cost: Admission limits trade immediate overload rejection for bounded waiting; tuning requires client and server telemetry together.
strengths: Separate server selection, pool checkout, query time and application queueing.

alternatives: Adding an unbounded goroutine for every queued operation
Retrying every failed write forever
quiz.correct: Can increase pressure without reducing the bottleneck
quiz.explanation: Client pool capacity, waiting goroutines and total deployment connections are different quantities.
quiz.hint: Find the stage that consumes the operation deadline.
quiz.question: What risk does a larger connection pool carry when the database is already the bottleneck?

review.answer: Can increase pressure without reducing the bottleneck

sections.body: A pool is associated with a server in the topology; monitoring connections add to the total. MaxPoolSize limits active pool capacity, not the number of goroutines allowed to wait. Give operations a deadline and bound application admission so overload does not become an invisible growing queue.
sections.code:
opts := options.Client().ApplyURI(uri).
    SetMaxPoolSize(16).SetMaxConnecting(2).
    SetMaxConnIdleTime(60*time.Second).SetTimeout(2*time.Second)
client, err := mongo.Connect(opts)
if err != nil { return err }
sections.title: Reuse a bounded shared client
sections.walkthrough: These are illustrative v2 settings for a small service, not universal recommendations. Estimate total connections across all instances and topology members and compare checkout wait with query duration before changing the cap.

sections.body: In a development environment, inspect operation behavior with an explain plan and server metrics. Add client-side pool and command monitoring at the application boundary; avoid logging credentials, raw documents or sensitive filter values in telemetry.
sections.code:
db.notes.find({tenant: "demo"}).limit(20).explain("executionStats")
db.serverStatus().connections
db.serverStatus().opcounters
sections.title: Use evidence from both client and database
sections.walkthrough: Availability of server metrics depends on deployment permissions and product. Correlate a time window of pool checkout wait, request errors and examined documents; a lifetime counter alone cannot explain current tail latency.

sections.body: One overall deadline should cover queueing and attempts. Restrict retryable work and test server failover, pool saturation and slow-query recovery. Separate a deliberately slow bulk operation from latency-sensitive traffic when their budgets differ, and prefer fixing an inefficient query to adding thousands of waiting goroutines.
sections.title: Recover without a retry storm

reading.takeaway: Bound admission and waiting as well as sockets, then tune using correlated request, pool and query evidence. More connections do not repair an overloaded database.

lessons.title: MongoDB under load: budget waiting before enlarging the pool

lessons.explanation: Redis is often used as a low-latency data-structure service, but the network, client pool and command cost still exist. Create a shared client, keep a bounded operation context and distinguish redis.Nil from transport failures. A missing optional cache entry and an unavailable required store have different application contracts.
lessons.objective: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.

cautions: redis.Nil from GET means this key is absent. A transport failure is a different result; unlimited fallback work during an outage can overwhelm the origin.
designGuide.cost: Shared pools save connection setup; their total size, retries and waiting must fit the deployment’s capacity budget.
strengths: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.

alternatives: Treat both as evidence that Redis lost every key
Assume both guarantee an origin database request will be cheap
quiz.correct: Means the key is absent, not a connection outage
quiz.explanation: redis.Nil from GET means this key is absent. A transport failure is a different result; unlimited fallback work during an outage can overwhelm the origin.
quiz.hint: Choose behavior for each error class.
quiz.question: How should a GET cache miss differ from a transport error?

review.answer: Means the key is absent, not a connection outage

sections.body: This lesson uses github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 with v9.16.0 as an example pin. PoolSize and MaxActiveConns are distinct knobs; do not assume a pool’s preferred retained size is a universal hard ceiling. Confirm options against the pinned version rather than copying future-version defaults.
sections.title: Construct one client with explicit example budgets
sections.walkthrough: The values illustrate a bounded small-client configuration, with automatic retries disabled so policy is visible. Production TLS, authentication and addresses come from configuration; re-enable suitable retries only with an overall operation budget and duplicate-effect analysis.

sections.body: redis.Nil represents a missing key for a GET, not a dead server. Preserve other errors so a caller can apply the intended fallback or failure policy. A fallback that recomputes expensive data on every transport failure can overwhelm the primary database during a Redis outage.
sections.title: Handle absence explicitly
sections.walkthrough: This is a helper returning string and error. The application supplies a bounded ctx and loadFromOrigin; the example deliberately surfaces infrastructure failure instead of silently starting unlimited origin requests.

sections.body: Later client versions can change pooling and pipeline behavior. Pin and test the version used by the service, including cancellation and saturation. These native network examples are not executable Redis access inside the app’s WASI sandbox; they teach the surrounding Go service environment.
sections.title: Keep version and workload assumptions visible

reading.takeaway: Reuse the client, configure bounded waiting and handle value, miss and outage separately. Fallback and retry behavior are application decisions, not invisible conveniences.

lessons.title: Redis: share the client and distinguish a miss from an outage

lessons.explanation: A cache duplicates another source of truth, so freshness and ownership must be explicit. Cache-aside reads can miss together, all query the origin and then repopulate the same key. TTL bounds one kind of staleness; it does not prevent a stampede or make a read-modify-write sequence correct.
lessons.objective: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.

cautions: In-process coalescing does not coordinate other replicas or make invalidation races disappear.
designGuide.cost: Caching adds duplicate state, invalidation and miss coordination; measure saved origin work against stale-data risk.
strengths: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.

alternatives: Only a longer TTL on keys that have not been created yet
One unlimited goroutine for every origin request
quiz.correct: Does not prevent misses from flooding the origin
quiz.explanation: In-process coalescing does not coordinate other replicas or make invalidation races disappear.
quiz.hint: Consider the empty-cache path, including all replicas.
quiz.question: Why is cache-aside alone insufficient protection during a burst of misses?

review.answer: Does not prevent misses from flooding the origin

sections.body: Use one SET operation with expiry when creating an expiring value. A separate SET followed by EXPIRE leaves a failure window where the key can survive without the intended lifetime. An ordinary later SET can also change existing TTL behavior, so decide the overwrite policy.
sections.code:
redis-cli SET demo:product:42 '{"name":"tea"}' EX 60
redis-cli GET demo:product:42
redis-cli TTL demo:product:42
sections.title: Set value and expiration together
sections.walkthrough: Run against an isolated development Redis using the demo namespace. TTL reports remaining expiry state, not freshness relative to a database update that happened after the value was cached.

sections.body: Coalesce identical in-process fills and independently bound the total number of origin calls. A per-key singleflight group only coordinates callers in this process; many service replicas can still miss together. Optional TTL jitter spreads expirations but does not guarantee a global rate limit.
sections.title: Bound concurrent misses
sections.walkthrough: The fragment shows the atomic value-plus-expiry client operation after an origin load. It does not implement coalescing or cross-process coordination; those policies belong to the loader boundary and must be tested separately.

sections.body: Negative caching can reduce repeated absent-item lookups, but use a short deliberate lifetime and a representation distinct from a real value. A database update followed by cache deletion can race with an older in-flight fill. Use versioned keys or another coherent invalidation design when that stale-write window is unacceptable.
sections.title: Handle stale and missing data as distinct cases

reading.takeaway: Set TTL atomically, bound origin fills and define the acceptable stale window. TTL, coalescing and invalidation address different failure modes.

lessons.title: Redis cache-aside: TTLs do not solve concurrent fills

lessons.explanation: Pipelining lets a client send multiple commands without waiting for every individual round trip. It can improve throughput for independent work, but it does not make the group indivisible. Large batches also retain commands and replies in memory and can worsen latency for other work.
lessons.objective: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.

cautions: MULTI/EXEC does not roll back already executed commands after a runtime command error.
designGuide.cost: Batches reduce network round trips while retaining command/reply memory and increasing ambiguous partial-outcome work.
strengths: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.

alternatives: Every earlier write rolls back if a later command errors
No other client can execute a command between its commands
quiz.correct: Batches round trips without making the group atomic
quiz.explanation: MULTI/EXEC does not roll back already executed commands after a runtime command error.
quiz.hint: Transport batching and a transactional boundary are different.
quiz.question: What does pipelining guarantee about the whole batch?

review.answer: Batches round trips without making the group atomic

sections.body: Queue a small known batch and inspect the returned command objects. An error from Exec needs interpretation alongside each command result. A connection failure can leave the caller uncertain which writes the server executed; a batch is not an automatic rollback boundary.
sections.title: Batch independent work
sections.walkthrough: This fragment batches two independent reads and tolerates missing keys explicitly. A write pipeline needs its own partial-outcome and retry policy; replaying all writes after an ambiguous error can duplicate effects.

sections.body: MULTI/EXEC groups commands atomically with respect to interleaving, but runtime command errors do not provide relational-database rollback. WATCH adds optimistic checks and can require a whole retry. A Lua script can perform a short conditional transition, but expensive scripts block other work on the server execution path.
sections.code:
redis-cli <<'REDIS'
MULTI
SET demo:a 1
INCR demo:count
EXEC
REDIS
sections.title: Choose atomicity separately
sections.walkthrough: The heredoc sends all commands through one redis-cli connection against an isolated development instance. Starting separate redis-cli processes for MULTI and EXEC would not create one transaction; connection ownership is part of the protocol.

sections.body: Cap commands and total encoded bytes, not only the number of business items. Measure batch duration, reply sizes and tail latency while other clients work. Client versions may use separate pipeline pools, so inspect the pinned version when calculating deployment-wide connection limits.
sections.title: Set a memory and latency budget for batches

reading.takeaway: Batch bounded independent work to reduce round trips, and choose atomicity and retry semantics explicitly. Inspect partial outcomes rather than assuming Exec implies rollback.

lessons.title: Redis pipelines save round trips; they are not transactions

lessons.explanation: A counter with a timeout and a temporary ownership key look small, but concurrent requests and pauses expose their failure windows. Put dependent steps in one short atomic transition and distinguish an expired lease from a durable guarantee that only one worker can ever act.
lessons.objective: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.

cautions: Expiry changes the Redis key, not the execution state of an old process. A paused former owner can resume after a new owner starts; the protected resource may need fencing.
designGuide.cost: Atomic scripts add protocol and recovery complexity; a lease is weaker than a durable resource-side ownership guarantee.
strengths: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.

alternatives: Redis pauses every process that previously held the key
A unique token prevents all network failures
quiz.correct: Does not stop a paused former owner from continuing
quiz.explanation: Expiry changes the Redis key, not the execution state of an old process. A paused former owner can resume after a new owner starts; the protected resource may need fencing.
quiz.hint: A key’s lifetime and a process’s execution lifetime differ.
quiz.question: Why can a resource still need fencing after a lease expires?

review.answer: Does not stop a paused former owner from continuing

sections.body: INCR followed by EXPIRE in separate operations can leave a counter without expiry if the client fails between them. A short script can attach expiry only when the counter is first created. This is an anchored fixed-window example, not a smooth sliding-window limiter.
sections.code:
counter := redis.NewScript(`
local n = redis.call("INCR", KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
return n
`)
n, err := counter.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{"demo:rate"}, 1000).Int64()
if err != nil { return err }
if n > 100 { return ErrLimited }
sections.title: Make a fixed-window counter transition atomic
sections.walkthrough: The go-redis script API passes one explicitly named development key and a positive window in milliseconds. This example permits 100 events in a window anchored at the first increment; ErrLimited is an application error. Define unavailable-store behavior separately.

sections.body: SET key token NX PX can create a temporary lease. Release by checking the stored token and deleting in the same atomic operation, not by a GET and later DEL. Generate a unique token for each acquisition; a stale owner must not remove a new owner’s lease.
sections.code:
release := redis.NewScript(`
local current = redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])
if current == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
end
return 0
`)
// token is unique to this successful SET key token NX PX acquisition.
deleted, err := release.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{key}, token).Int64()
if err != nil { return err }
_ = deleted // 0 means the lease no longer belongs to this acquisition.
sections.title: A lease must be released only by its owner
sections.walkthrough: The script compares the acquisition token inside the server before deletion. It solves that release race, but a paused worker may still continue after its lease expires; a protected resource may need fencing or another stronger ownership mechanism.

sections.body: An acknowledgment can be lost, a lease can expire during a pause and failover can change which writes survive. A Redis key alone is not a proof of exclusive business execution across failures. Use resource-side idempotency, version checks or fencing when duplicate work could violate an invariant.
sections.title: Explain the failure model before calling it a lock

reading.takeaway: Make dependent counter steps atomic and release leases by token. Design the downstream invariant for pauses, ambiguity and expired ownership.

lessons.title: Redis counters and leases need atomic transitions and ownership

lessons.explanation: A consumer group tracks delivery and acknowledgment, not automatic exactly-once application effects. A worker may crash after updating another database but before XACK. Redelivery is useful recovery, so the handler must recognize an operation it has already applied.
lessons.objective: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.

cautions: The effect may commit before a worker crashes without acknowledging. Redelivery can then repeat it; pending-entry recovery needs destination-side idempotency.
designGuide.cost: Consumer groups need retention, pending-work recovery, idempotent effects and explicit storage durability.
strengths: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.

alternatives: Consumer groups roll back all external databases on failure
Reading with > guarantees an entry is delivered only once forever
quiz.correct: Can cause redelivery after an effect already happened
quiz.explanation: The effect may commit before a worker crashes without acknowledging. Redelivery can then repeat it; pending-entry recovery needs destination-side idempotency.
quiz.hint: The worker can fail between the effect and acknowledgment.
quiz.question: A consumer performed its external effect but crashed before acknowledging. What can later recovery cause?

review.answer: Can cause redelivery after an effect already happened

sections.body: In an isolated development instance, create a stream and group and append a demonstration event. XREADGROUP with > asks for new entries for this group. Acknowledge only after the application’s durable effect succeeds.
sections.code:
redis-cli XGROUP CREATE demo:events workers 0 MKSTREAM
redis-cli XADD demo:events '*' operationID order-42 kind created
redis-cli XREADGROUP GROUP workers worker-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS demo:events '>'
sections.title: Read new entries with one group
sections.walkthrough: Replace worker names per process and retain the stream entry ID returned by the read. The demonstration group starts from 0 intentionally; starting at $ instead changes whether existing history is delivered.

sections.body: A delivered but unacknowledged entry remains pending for the group. Inspect pending work and use a supported reclaim mechanism after an appropriate idle threshold. A slow healthy worker and a dead worker can look alike, so claiming work must not assume the old consumer has physically stopped.
sections.code:
redis-cli XPENDING demo:events workers
redis-cli XAUTOCLAIM demo:events workers worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
# After the effect succeeds, acknowledge its actual returned entry ID:
# redis-cli XACK demo:events workers 1710000000000-0
sections.title: Inspect and reclaim pending entries
sections.walkthrough: XAUTOCLAIM requires a compatible server version and returns a continuation cursor as well as claimed entries. Iterate with explicit work bounds; the sample acknowledgment ID is a placeholder, not a success shortcut.

sections.body: Deduplicate the operation at the durable destination and treat replay as a normal path. Configure stream trimming so it does not discard work that still matters to consumers. Acknowledgment does not itself specify Redis persistence, replication acknowledgment or recovery guarantees; test those separately for the deployment.
sections.title: Keep delivery, retention and durability distinct

reading.takeaway: Acknowledge after a durable idempotent effect, recover pending work deliberately, and budget retention and storage independently of consumer-group delivery.

lessons.title: Redis Streams: acknowledge after the durable effect

lessons.explanation: Redis command latency can rise because of expensive commands, a hot key, big values, persistence work, network delay or waiting in the client. A low average hides queues and timeout bursts. Correlate request errors with server and client evidence before increasing goroutines or connection limits.
lessons.objective: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.

cautions: SLOWLOG measures server execution. Callers can still wait for a client connection or network response; retries can then amplify load or repeat an ambiguous write.
designGuide.cost: Latency and eviction policies trade memory, availability and persistence work; client concurrency cannot remove a hot-key bottleneck.
strengths: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.

alternatives: Redis always measures the full HTTP request path
SCAN COUNT imposes an exact global rate limit
quiz.correct: Does not exclude client-pool or network latency
quiz.explanation: SLOWLOG measures server execution. Callers can still wait for a client connection or network response; retries can then amplify load or repeat an ambiguous write.
quiz.hint: Locate waiting before and after server command execution.
quiz.question: Why can callers time out while SLOWLOG shows no slow commands?

review.answer: Does not exclude client-pool or network latency

sections.body: In an authorized development environment, inspect memory, command statistics and recent slow commands. SLOWLOG measures server command execution, not every network or client-pool delay. Keep raw keys and command arguments out of broadly shared diagnostics when they may contain user data.
sections.code:
redis-cli INFO memory
redis-cli INFO stats
redis-cli INFO commandstats
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10
redis-cli LATENCY LATEST
sections.title: Use focused observation commands
sections.walkthrough: Metrics and latency monitoring availability depend on server configuration and permissions. Compare the same time window with client pool wait and request p99; a quiet SLOWLOG does not prove that callers were fast.

sections.body: KEYS can block while traversing a large keyspace. SCAN divides that work into cursor-driven steps, but it is not a snapshot, COUNT is a hint and keys may appear more than once. Keep downstream handling idempotent and avoid moving all returned keys into one giant slice.
sections.code:
redis-cli SCAN 0 MATCH 'demo:*' COUNT 100
# Continue with the returned cursor until it is 0.
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE demo:product:42
sections.title: Scan incrementally and cap batch work
sections.walkthrough: A single SCAN call is not a complete inventory. Even incremental maintenance needs rate and time budgets; do not run an unbounded sweep simply because each individual command looks small.

sections.body: Eviction policy and persistence determine whether a value can disappear and what survives failure. Replication is not automatically synchronous durability. Retrying INCR after a lost response may apply the effect twice; use an operation identifier and a suitable atomic protocol when duplicate effects are unacceptable. Bound retries within one deadline and measure recovery after overload.
sections.title: Define storage and retry guarantees

reading.takeaway: Separate client wait from server execution, keep maintenance incremental and design for eviction, persistence and ambiguous write outcomes. More concurrency is not a repair for a hot bottleneck.

lessons.title: Redis under load: hot keys, memory pressure and ambiguous retries

summary: Clients, queries, atomic writes, caching, streams and behavior under load.
title: Around Go: MongoDB and Redis
translationNote: Read worked native-service examples here. Run them against an isolated development database on your own machine; these lessons do not add network sockets to the app sandbox.

lessons.explanation: sql.DB is a concurrency-safe pool handle, not a single database connection. Reuse it across the application and close it after its users drain. These lessons describe native Go services using a real driver; the app’s bounded WASI programs cannot open remote database sockets.
lessons.objective: Configure database/sql as a shared pool and measure its actual pressure.

cautions: A larger connection cap can move waiting into an overloaded database. Admission and query efficiency still need their own policies.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL: one pool, explicit capacity and observable waiting
strengths: Configure database/sql as a shared pool and measure its actual pressure.
Own one shared pool, bound operation lifetimes and admission, and measure pool waits across all replicas before changing connection limits.

alternatives: One dedicated connection reserved for each handler
One global pool automatically shared by every service replica
quiz.correct: A shared pool, not one connection
quiz.explanation: A larger connection cap can move waiting into an overloaded database. Admission and query efficiency still need their own policies.
quiz.hint: Multiply per-process settings by every active pool owner.
quiz.question: What does one shared *sql.DB represent inside a Go service?

review.answer: A shared pool, not one connection

sections.body: sql.Open generally constructs a handle rather than proving connectivity. Use a bounded PingContext for startup evidence, then handle every operation error separately. Configure a reviewed driver version in the native service module; pgx/v5/stdlib is one PostgreSQL driver option.
sections.title: Construct once and verify readiness
sections.walkthrough: This startup-function fragment imports database/sql, context, fmt, time and the chosen PostgreSQL driver registration. The DSN comes from configuration. The numeric settings are examples, not sizing advice; a returned shared pool needs one application lifetime owner.

sections.body: A limit of twelve per replica means something different with two replicas than with fifty. Reserve database capacity for migrations, administration and other applications. SetMaxOpenConns bounds this pool’s open connections; it is not a global request limiter or a cap on goroutines waiting to acquire one.
sections.title: Budget across the deployment

sections.body: DB.Stats exposes OpenConnections, InUse, Idle, WaitCount and WaitDuration. Wait counters accumulate, so compare their changes over the same measurement interval. A high wait rate can reflect slow transactions, leaked rows or too much admission rather than a pool that should simply be enlarged.
sections.code:
stats := db.Stats()
fmt.Println(stats.OpenConnections, stats.InUse, stats.Idle)
fmt.Println(stats.WaitCount, stats.WaitDuration)
// Record deltas over a defined interval alongside request latency.
sections.title: Read counters as changes over an interval
sections.walkthrough: The fragment observes a shared sql.DB and imports fmt. Lifetime counters do not identify the present bottleneck by themselves. Correlate a pool-wait interval with query latency, queue length, errors and the database’s own evidence.

sections.body: A native pgxpool.Pool is another pool abstraction with its own settings and metrics. Do not wrap one pool in another or assume database/sql option names apply unchanged. Choose the API the service uses, then test saturation and shutdown for that actual combination.
sections.title: Distinguish other pool APIs

reading.takeaway: Own one shared pool, bound operation lifetimes and admission, and measure pool waits across all replicas before changing connection limits.

lessons.title: SQL: one pool, explicit capacity and observable waiting

lessons.explanation: A successful QueryContext does not mean every row will decode successfully. Network and server errors can occur during iteration, and Scan can fail on a type or null mismatch. Decide whether partial results are meaningful; do not silently return a successful incomplete list.
lessons.objective: Write a cancellation-aware query loop without losing iteration failures.

cautions: A parameterized tenant value still requires authorization, and LIMIT is not a universal bound on query execution cost.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL rows: close, check errors and bound the result
strengths: Write a cancellation-aware query loop without losing iteration failures.
Check Query, Scan and final iteration errors as separate phases. Close owned rows, authorize scope and cap returned work before reporting a successful result.

alternatives: Return three records with no error
Ignore the final iteration status
quiz.correct: Rows.Err after the loop
quiz.explanation: A parameterized tenant value still requires authorization, and LIMIT is not a universal bound on query execution cost.
quiz.hint: Next returning false can mean end of rows or an error.
quiz.question: What must be checked after Rows.Next stops before claiming that the complete query succeeded?

review.answer: Rows.Err after the loop

sections.body: This PostgreSQL helper returns at most one hundred identifiers, uses a parameter for the tenant value and returns no successful partial result on failure. A real endpoint must derive tenant from authorization, not merely trust a request parameter.
sections.title: Bound a tenant-scoped query
sections.walkthrough: The helper imports context and database/sql and assumes a PostgreSQL-compatible driver and a notes table with an integer id. Close releases resources on early return; Err checks failure after Next becomes false. For a query whose close result affects correctness, handle that result explicitly too.

sections.body: QueryRowContext defers its error until Scan. Distinguish sql.ErrNoRows from an infrastructure or conversion failure. Use nullable types or pointers when the schema permits null; a zero int is not automatically a missing value. Keep parameter placeholders consistent with the chosen driver.
sections.title: Handle one row and null deliberately

sections.body: The $1 parameter protects a value position. It does not let a caller supply an arbitrary table name or ORDER BY expression safely. Choose identifiers and sort directions from a fixed application allowlist, and bind all untrusted values separately.
sections.title: Parameters bind values, not SQL grammar

sections.body: A LIMIT bounds this helper’s row count, not the byte size of arbitrary columns or total work examined by the plan. For exports, stream bounded records and carry cancellation to the cursor. Test a failure after several rows and define the response protocol once output has started.
sections.title: Separate buffering from streaming

reading.takeaway: Check Query, Scan and final iteration errors as separate phases. Close owned rows, authorize scope and cap returned work before reporting a successful result.

lessons.title: SQL rows: close, check errors and bound the result

lessons.explanation: Beginning a transaction does not attach later calls on sql.DB to it. The transaction handle owns a particular transactional connection. A helper that accidentally queries db instead of tx may see another state, escape rollback or wait for a second connection while holding the first.
lessons.objective: Place an atomic business transition inside one explicit transaction owner.

cautions: A transaction does not automatically include pool calls or an external provider. Check commit outcomes and idempotency at the actual boundary.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL transactions: every participating call uses the transaction
strengths: Place an atomic business transition inside one explicit transaction owner.
One owner starts the transaction, passes its handle to every participating call and finishes it. Database atomicity does not include remote side effects.

alternatives: Any *sql.DB that receives the same context
Any query executed inside the same Go function
quiz.correct: The same transaction handle
quiz.explanation: A transaction does not automatically include pool calls or an external provider. Check commit outcomes and idempotency at the actual boundary.
quiz.hint: Context propagation and transaction membership are different contracts.
quiz.question: What must a helper use for its write to participate in the caller’s open SQL transaction?

review.answer: The same transaction handle

sections.body: This abbreviated PostgreSQL transfer updates both accounts through tx. Reject nonpositive amounts before starting, use an exact integer minor-unit representation and treat account currency and authorization as additional domain constraints.
sections.title: Make the atomic boundary visible
sections.walkthrough: This function-body fragment assumes validated amount/from/to and application errors. Every write uses tx. The deferred Rollback is harmless after a successful Commit. A complete transfer also scopes ownership, checks currency and overflow bounds, and defines retry/idempotency semantics.

sections.body: A helper can accept the ExecContext or QueryContext capability it needs instead of a hidden global db. That makes accidental pool calls easier to see. The runtime guarantee still comes from passing the same transaction handle to every participating operation, not from an interface name alone.
sections.title: Pass a narrow transaction capability

sections.body: An email, HTTP payment or message publish is not rolled back by the SQL transaction. Persist a durable outbox or intent with the state change, then deliver through an idempotent protocol. Do not keep a transaction open while waiting for a user or a slow remote service.
sections.title: Keep external effects outside the callback

sections.body: A lost reply can make a durable outcome uncertain. Distinguish documented serialization/deadlock failures from transport ambiguity. Use a stable operation ID to reconcile the latter. Test abort-before-write, error-after-write and commit-then-disconnect separately.
sections.title: Do not interpret every commit error as an abort

reading.takeaway: One owner starts the transaction, passes its handle to every participating call and finishes it. Database atomicity does not include remote side effects.

lessons.title: SQL transactions: every participating call uses the transaction

lessons.explanation: A transaction can be atomic without providing the isolation an invariant needs. Two transactions may both read a condition as true and each make a different write that breaks the combined rule. Exact behavior depends on the database and isolation level; this lesson uses PostgreSQL terminology explicitly.
lessons.objective: Explain why atomic statements alone may not preserve a multi-row invariant.

cautions: Isolation levels and lock details are database-specific. Do not promise one engine’s exact behavior for every SQL driver.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL isolation and deadlocks: test the business invariant
strengths: Explain why atomic statements alone may not preserve a multi-row invariant.
Choose isolation and locking from the invariant, understand the database-specific failures and prove the protocol with concurrent transactions on the actual engine.

alternatives: More goroutines in the unit-test fake
A larger client-side connection pool
quiz.correct: Database races need database tests
quiz.explanation: Isolation levels and lock details are database-specific. Do not promise one engine’s exact behavior for every SQL driver.
quiz.hint: The authoritative state is in another concurrency system.
quiz.question: Two replicas pass Go race tests but violate a multi-row invariant. What evidence is missing?

review.answer: Database races need database tests

sections.body: Imagine two on-call doctors, each allowed to leave only while another remains. Both transactions read two active doctors and each removes its own row. The final state violates the rule even though every individual write is valid. This is a business-level concurrency problem, not an unsynchronized Go map access.
sections.title: Name the anomaly

sections.body: A suitable constraint, conditional update, lock protocol or serializable transaction can protect an invariant, depending on how it is represented. PostgreSQL serializable isolation may reject a transaction that would create an incompatible history. Applications must handle that failure rather than treating serializable as a promise that no request ever retries.
sections.title: Choose a database-enforced protocol
sections.walkthrough: This native transaction skeleton imports database/sql and assumes a driver supporting the requested isolation. It deliberately omits application SQL: the correct statements depend on the invariant. Test the protocol against the actual database rather than a fake that always accepts commits.

sections.body: Two transfers can lock accounts in opposite orders and deadlock. Acquire relevant locks in a consistent order where possible, keep transactions short and avoid holding locks across remote calls. Deadlock detection prevents one kind of permanent wait by aborting work; it does not make the application transition automatically succeed.
sections.title: Use consistent lock order

sections.body: Use synchronization barriers to place both transactions after their initial reads, then release their writes. Assert the final invariant and the expected failure/retry behavior. A process-local mutex cannot establish the same guarantee across every service replica, and the race detector does not observe database interleavings.
sections.title: Reproduce with two independent connections

reading.takeaway: Choose isolation and locking from the invariant, understand the database-specific failures and prove the protocol with concurrent transactions on the actual engine.

lessons.title: SQL isolation and deadlocks: test the business invariant

lessons.explanation: Retrying the last failed SQL statement can be wrong when an earlier statement read stale state or the transaction is already aborted. A safe retry policy names the driver error, restarts the complete business unit when appropriate, stays within a total deadline and prevents repeated external effects.
lessons.objective: Separate retryable transaction aborts from an ambiguous committed operation.

cautions: Retry classification is driver-specific. Preserve one total deadline and use durable deduplication for ambiguous side effects.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL retries: restart a safe transaction, reconcile an unknown result
strengths: Separate retryable transaction aborts from an ambiguous committed operation.
Retry a documented safe unit within one budget. Reconcile uncertain commit outcomes through durable operation identity rather than assuming an error proves no effect occurred.

alternatives: The charge definitely failed and needs a fresh payment identity
Any non-nil error proves that the server rolled back
quiz.correct: The durable outcome may be unknown
quiz.explanation: Retry classification is driver-specific. Preserve one total deadline and use durable deduplication for ambiguous side effects.
quiz.hint: Distinguish an explicit abort from a missing acknowledgment.
quiz.question: A network error arrives after a charge may have committed. What can be concluded about the durable effect?

review.answer: The durable outcome may be unknown
review.prompt: A commit reply is lost. Assume?

sections.body: For PostgreSQL, serialization_failure is SQLSTATE 40001 and deadlock_detected is 40P01. Inspect structured driver errors rather than parsing an English error message. Those codes are not interchangeable with a lost network response, which can leave an outcome unknown.
sections.title: Classify with the real driver
sections.walkthrough: The native fragment imports errors and github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn. It only classifies two PostgreSQL conditions; it is not a complete retry loop and does not claim every network or database error is retryable.

sections.body: Use a small reviewed attempt cap, bounded jittered delay and the remaining overall deadline. Recreate the transaction and re-read necessary state on each attempt. Do not let HTTP, application and driver retries multiply independently into a storm while every request retains a connection or body.
sections.title: Give one layer the retry budget

sections.body: If a payment-like command committed but its reply was lost, retrying without an operation identity can duplicate the transition. Store a scoped idempotency key and request fingerprint under a uniqueness rule. Return the prior result or reconcile provider state; a transaction cannot un-send a remote charge.
sections.title: Reconcile transport ambiguity

sections.body: Inject a known abort before commit, an exhausted deadline, concurrent duplicate commands and commit-then-disconnect. Assert one durable business effect and a useful response classification. Include isolation and schema compatibility in a release rollback plan; reverting a binary does not erase committed data.
sections.title: Test the windows, not only the loop count

reading.takeaway: Retry a documented safe unit within one budget. Reconcile uncertain commit outcomes through durable operation identity rather than assuming an error proves no effect occurred.

lessons.title: SQL retries: restart a safe transaction, reconcile an unknown result

summary: Shared pools, rows, transactions, isolation, deadlocks and retry-safe commands.
title: Around Go: SQL services
translationNote: Worked native Go and PostgreSQL examples. Use an isolated database in your own development environment; the app does not open database sockets.

lessons.explanation: Gin is a router, a request context and a middleware chain built on top of net/http. A *gin.Engine is an ordinary http.Handler, so everything you know about http.Server, httptest and timeouts still applies. Start with a function that returns a configured engine: main can serve it, and a test can call it directly.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin engine, register routes with a path parameter and exercise them without opening a port.

cautions: r.Run starts a server with no timeouts; prefer an explicit http.Server.
Set gin.TestMode before building the engine to keep test output clean.
designGuide.cost: One constructor function and a test table; nothing beyond what a single-route service already needs.
strengths: Routing is testable in milliseconds without sockets.
The middleware chain is explicit from the first line.

alternatives: gin.Default disables networking in test mode
Gin ships its own server that replaces http.Server
quiz.correct: An http.Handler you can host or test directly
quiz.explanation: The engine implements ServeHTTP, so httptest.NewRecorder can capture its response exactly as http.Server would deliver it to a client.
quiz.hint: Look at which method the test loop calls on the router.
quiz.question: Why can a Gin router be tested without opening a network port?

review.answer: An http.Handler you can host or test directly

sections.body: The standard library already parses requests, writes responses and runs servers. Gin adds a fast radix-tree router with named parameters, a *gin.Context that carries the request, the response writer and per-request values through a chain of handlers, plus helpers for binding input and rendering JSON. It does not replace http.Server: the engine is the Handler you give to one. Keeping that split in mind answers most questions about timeouts, TLS and shutdown later in the course.
sections.title: What Gin adds to net/http

sections.body: A Gin service is an ordinary Go module. Create it with go mod init, add Gin at an explicit version with go get, and commit both go.mod and go.sum: the checksum file is what lets every later build prove that it downloaded the same Gin you reviewed. Pin the version deliberately and upgrade it on purpose after reading the release notes, rather than taking whatever happens to be newest on the day someone clones the repository.
sections.code:
mkdir notes-api && cd notes-api
go mod init example.com/notes-api
go get github.com/gin-gonic/gin@v1.12.0
# write main.go, then:
go run .
curl -i http://localhost:8080/health
sections.title: Create the module and add Gin
sections.walkthrough: go get records gin v1.12.0 in go.mod and the hashes of Gin and its dependencies in go.sum. go run . builds and starts the package in the current directory. The curl line answers only once main hosts the engine in an http.Server, as shown later in this lesson.
