The trade-offs are honest ones: no jumping to page 37 and no cheap total count. Offset remains acceptable for small, rarely changing admin tables.
sections.title: Offset pages drift; key-based pages do not

sections.body: parseList is the gate: it rejects malformed query strings and unknown parameters, bounds the limit, checks the sort against the allow-list and decodes the cursor. The store sorts by the chosen key with the ID as tie-breaker, skips everything up to the cursor, and fetches one extra row to learn whether another page exists. The program first shows offset drift on the same data, then walks the cursor pages while a new note arrives, and finally sends invalid queries.
sections.title: List, filter and sort the notes
sections.walkthrough: The offset line returns n5 and n4, then n4 again after n6 is inserted, the classic duplicate. The cursor walk returns n5 n4, then n3 n2, then n1 with more=false; the new n6 does not disturb later pages because it sorts before the cursor and will appear on a fresh first page. n2 and n3 share a timestamp, and the ID breaks the tie deterministically. The decoded cursor is just JSON with the sort, the last key and the last ID. pinned=true with sort=title returns n1 n4, limit=500 is clamped to 100 and echoed back, and the three bad queries each get a 400 naming the problem. The last one matters: URL.Query, and therefore c.Query, silently drops pairs containing a semicolon, while url.ParseQuery reports the error so the API can reject it.

sections.body: If two rows compare equal on the sort key, neither SQL nor slices.SortFunc promises their relative order, and it can differ between two executions of the same query. A page that ends between tied rows then gives the next request no exact place to resume, so a row is skipped or repeated. Appending a unique column, the ID, to every sort order makes the order total, and the cursor must carry both values. Support it with a composite index such as (created_at, id). Watch the key format too. The in-memory model compares keys as strings, so timestamps are formatted at fixed width in UTC. PostgreSQL stores timestamps with microsecond precision while Go keeps nanoseconds, so truncate to microseconds before writing; otherwise the key in the cursor never equals the stored value and the boundary comparison is subtly wrong.
sections.title: A total order needs a tie-breaker

sections.body: Calling the cursor opaque is a contract with clients: they must pass it back unchanged and never build one, so you can change its format later. It is not a security property. base64url is an encoding, and the program decodes the cursor in one line. Treat a cursor like any other input: decode it, validate every field, reject it if it was issued for a different sort, and never place in it anything the caller could not already see. If tampering matters, append an HMAC computed with a server key and verify it before use. Authorization must not depend on the cursor; the owner filter comes from the authenticated request on every page, so a forged cursor can at most move the starting point within the caller's own notes. For the limit, pick a default, clamp at a maximum, echo the effective value and reject zero or non-numeric input with 400.
sections.title: Opaque cursors are encoded, not secret

sections.body: Reject unknown query parameters: a client that types pined=true and silently receives every note has a bug that nobody will notice. For sorting, the allow-list is not just validation; it is the only bridge between user input and SQL text. A placeholder binds a value, never an identifier, so ORDER BY $1 sorts every row by the same constant and no error appears. Interpolating the column name instead is SQL injection. Map each public sort name to a constant clause and build the query from those constants plus placeholders.
sections.title: Allow-lists for filters and sorts, constants for SQL
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the PostgreSQL side of the same API; run it against a database in your own environment. orderBy and afterCursor are the allow-list expressed as SQL constants, and parseList has already guaranteed that q.sort is one of their keys. Only placeholder numbers are formatted into the string; every client-supplied value, including the cursor key and ID, travels in args. The row comparison (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) matches the ORDER BY direction and can use the composite index. Text keys such as title compare with the column collation in SQL, which may differ from the byte order the in-memory model uses.

reading.takeaway: Page by the last (sort key, id) in a validated opaque cursor, cap the limit, reject unknown parameters, and map allow-listed sort names to constant SQL instead of interpolating them.

lessons.title: Paginate with opaque cursors, a bounded limit and a total order; filter only through allow-lists

lessons.explanation: By now each notes handler writes its own gin.H{"error": ...}. Clients parse several shapes, someone eventually returns err.Error() and leaks a database host, and nobody can list which statuses an endpoint produces. RFC 9457 supplies a standard envelope. A taxonomy in the domain and one mapping function supply the discipline. The errors-testing lesson established one response owner; this lesson gives that owner a contract.
lessons.objective: Return application/problem+json for every failure by mapping a small domain error taxonomy to HTTP statuses in a single Gin middleware.

cautions: An unmapped new error kind silently becomes a 500 unless a test checks coverage.
A handler that writes before failing leaves the middleware able only to log.
designGuide.cost: A small taxonomy, one mapping function and a middleware; existing handlers change from writing JSON to returning after c.Error.
strengths: Clients parse one documented error shape and branch on a stable type URI.
Internal error text stays in logs by construction.
Adding a route cannot add a new, undocumented error format.

alternatives: In each handler, so every route chooses its own status
In the notes service, which returns the HTTP status code
quiz.correct: One error middleware, using errors.Is and errors.As
quiz.explanation: One mapping middleware means one table to review, one envelope for clients and no handler that can forget to hide an internal error's text.
quiz.hint: The domain package does not import net/http.
quiz.question: In the notes API, where should a wrapped notes.ErrConflict become a 409 application/problem+json response?

review.answer: One error middleware, using errors.Is and errors.As
review.prompt: Who turns domain errors into HTTP?

sections.body: The notes package defines what can go wrong in business terms: ErrNotFound, ErrConflict and ErrForbidden as sentinel values, and *ValidationError as a type that carries field-level reasons. Services wrap them with fmt.Errorf and %w to add context such as the note ID, and the wrapped chain still matches. The domain does not import net/http and does not know that 404 exists; a CLI or a queue worker can use the same errors. Malformed JSON is different: the domain never sees request bytes, so that error belongs to httpapi. Keep the taxonomy small. Four or five kinds cover most APIs, and each new kind is a decision about how clients should react, not a new spelling of "something failed".
sections.title: Name failures in the domain, not in HTTP

sections.body: Every handler now ends a failure with c.Error(err) and returns; none of them chooses a status. The problems middleware calls c.Next, looks at the last recorded error and asks problemFor, the only mapping table in the service, for a Problem. It logs the cause of server errors, skips writing if a handler already committed a response, and renders application/problem+json. NoRoute records ErrNotFound, so unknown paths get the same envelope.
sections.title: Handlers record, the middleware responds
sections.walkthrough: problemFor checks the typed error first with errors.AsType, the generic counterpart of errors.As in the Go 1.27 standard library, then the sentinels with errors.Is; both see through the %w wrapping, so "load note n9: notes: not found" still maps to 404. The 400 for truncated JSON never repeats the decoder message. The 422 carries the field list from ValidationError, the one error type written for clients. The 500 shows the split: the log line has the full driver message, including user and host, while the body says only Internal Server Error. The last line is an unregistered path, which Gin routes through global middleware and the NoRoute handler, so it is a problem document rather than Gin's plain-text default.

sections.body: RFC 9457, which obsoletes RFC 7807, defines a JSON object served as application/problem+json. type is a URI reference that identifies the problem type and is what clients should branch on; when it is absent it means about:blank, and then title should be the standard phrase for the status code. title is a short summary of the type that should not change between occurrences except for localization. status is advisory and must match the real response status. detail explains this occurrence and should help the client correct the request, not debug the server. instance identifies the occurrence. Extension members such as errors are allowed, and clients must ignore extensions they do not understand.
sections.title: The problem document, member by member
sections.walkthrough: This is the 422 body from the program, pretty-printed. The type URI is a stable identifier under your control and can resolve to human documentation; example.com is a placeholder. title stays the same for every validation failure, while detail and the errors extension describe this request. instance here is the request path; a request ID or a urn:uuid value is also acceptable if support tooling needs to find the matching log line.

sections.body: The text of an arbitrary error is written for developers: it contains SQL fragments, hostnames, user names, file paths and library versions. Public text therefore comes only from the mapping table or from error types designed to be public, such as ValidationError; an unrecognized error becomes a 500 with about:blank and no detail. Log the cause with a request ID and return that ID as an extension member if support needs to correlate. Choose between 403 and 404 deliberately: when the caller may not even know a note exists, answer 404 so the status does not confirm it; use 403 when the caller can see the note but may not perform this action. Two Gin details make the middleware work. Setting Content-Type before c.JSON is preserved, because Gin's JSON renderer only sets the header when it is absent. And when a handler has already written, the middleware must only log, because a second write cannot change a status that is already on the wire.
sections.title: What must never reach the body

sections.body: For each member of the taxonomy and for one unknown error, send a request through ServeHTTP and assert the status, the Content-Type and the decoded body; the API-tests lesson builds this table. Add one test that fails when an exported sentinel has no mapping, so a new error kind cannot silently become a 500. Assert that 500 bodies contain no detail at all, since that is the regression that leaks credentials. Clients should branch on type, so changing a type URI is a breaking change; changing title wording is not.
sections.title: Test the envelope as a contract

reading.takeaway: Let handlers call c.Error with domain errors, map them in one middleware with errors.Is and errors.AsType to application/problem+json, and never copy an unrecognized error's text into the body.

lessons.title: One error envelope: RFC 9457 problem details mapped from domain errors in one middleware

lessons.explanation: A mobile client sends POST /notes, the connection drops before the 201 arrives, and the client retries. Without help the server creates a second note. HTTP defines PUT and DELETE as idempotent; POST is not, so the client supplies a unique key and the server promises that one key yields at most one effect and one stored response. This lesson adds that promise to the notes API.
lessons.objective: Add Idempotency-Key handling to POST /notes so retries replay the original response, conflicting reuse is rejected and in-flight duplicates wait.

cautions: A separate idempotency store leaves a crash window; prefer one transaction with the effect.
Unscoped keys can replay one tenant's response to another.
designGuide.cost: One record per write request for the retention period, a lease for pending entries and an extra read and write on every POST.
strengths: Clients can retry ambiguous POSTs without creating duplicates.
Changed payloads and concurrent duplicates are rejected explicitly.
Replays return the identical status, headers and body.

alternatives: Replay the first response, because the key matches
Run the new request and overwrite the stored response
quiz.correct: 422: the key is bound to the first request's fingerprint
quiz.explanation: Replaying would hand back a note the client did not ask for and hide its bug; running it would allow a second effect. Rejecting with 422 keeps one key bound to one request.
quiz.hint: The key promises one effect for one request; ask whether this is still the same request.
quiz.question: A client reuses Idempotency-Key k1 with a different JSON body after the first request succeeded. What should the server do?

review.answer: 422: the key is bound to the first request's fingerprint

sections.body: A timeout is ambiguous: the request may have failed before the handler ran, or succeeded with only the response lost. The client cannot tell, so a safe retry needs the server to remember. The client generates a random key, typically a UUID, for each logical operation and reuses it only when retrying that operation. The server keeps one record per caller and key with a fingerprint of the request, its state and, once finished, the response. Each arrival then has exactly one outcome: a new key runs the handler; a finished identical request is replayed; an identical request still running gets 409; the same key with a different request gets 422; a missing key gets 400. These choices follow the IETF HTTPAPI working group's Idempotency-Key header draft, which is still a draft, so document them in your API contract.
sections.title: Why a retry duplicates, and what the key promises

sections.body: Idempotent runs before the create handler. It reads and restores the body, fingerprints the request, and calls Begin, which checks and reserves the key in one critical section. On a fresh reservation it swaps c.Writer for a captureWriter that copies everything written, runs the handler with c.Next, and stores the status, Location and body. A deferred function releases the reservation when the handler ends in a 5xx or panics. The program holds one request open with channels so the in-progress case is deterministic.
sections.title: A middleware that reserves, captures and replays
sections.walkthrough: The first k1 creates n1. The retry with the same body never reaches the handler: it gets the stored 201, the same Location and Idempotent-Replayed=true. Reusing k1 with a different title is 422, and a request without a key is 400. For k2, a goroutine starts the slow request, and main waits on entered until the handler is inside Create, so the reservation certainly exists; the second k2 then gets 409 with Retry-After. Closing release lets the first k2 finish with 201 for n2. Finally the fake clock moves 25 hours forward, past the 24-hour retention, and the old k1 creates n3: an expired key is a new request. Three notes exist, not five.

sections.body: The fingerprint is SHA-256 over the method, the route pattern from c.FullPath and the raw body bytes. Byte equality is strict: a client that re-serializes the same JSON with different key order or spacing gets 422. Most APIs accept that and tell clients to resend the identical bytes; canonicalizing JSON before hashing is possible but easy to get subtly wrong. Scope every key by the authenticated principal. Without scope, two tenants that happen to choose the same key would see each other's responses, a data leak rather than a duplicate. Bound the key length and the body size before reading; the binding-limits lesson covers MaxBytesReader. Store whatever the client needs to treat a replay as the original, here status, Location and body. The Idempotent-Replayed header is a convention some APIs use, not a standard, but it makes replays visible in logs and client debugging.
sections.title: Fingerprints, scope and what gets stored

sections.body: Begin must check and reserve atomically or two concurrent first attempts both run. The mutex does it here; in PostgreSQL use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and check the affected row count, and in Redis use SET with NX and an expiry. A pending record also needs a lease: if the process dies mid-request, nothing releases it, and every retry gets 409 until the record expires. Give pending records a short lock expiry separate from the retention TTL, and make the retention longer than any client's retry window. The deeper gap is that the note and the idempotency record live in different stores. A crash after the note is committed but before Finish loses the stored response, and a retry after the lease runs out creates a duplicate; releasing on a 5xx has the same hole if the effect committed before the error. The robust design writes the idempotency record in the same database transaction as the note, so the effect and the response commit together.
sections.title: In progress, expiry and the crash window

sections.body: Cover each branch through ServeHTTP: a fresh key, an identical replay that leaves exactly one note in the store, a changed body that returns 422, a missing key, an in-progress duplicate held open with channels as the program does, expiry driven by an injected clock and a 5xx that releases the key so the retry runs again. Add a test that fires many identical requests from goroutines and asserts that the handler ran once, and run the suite with -race. Assert the replayed body byte for byte, because the promise is the same response, not a similar one.
sections.title: Test every outcome, including the concurrent one

reading.takeaway: Reserve each principal-scoped key atomically with a request fingerprint, replay the stored response for identical retries, answer 422 for a changed payload and 409 while in progress, and retain records longer than clients retry.

lessons.title: Make POST safe to retry with Idempotency-Key: fingerprint, reserve, replay and expire

lessons.explanation: Two people open the same note. One adds a line; the other fixes the title from the copy loaded earlier, and that second save quietly erases the first edit. Each request was valid on its own. The bug is that the server never asked which version the client was editing. HTTP already has the vocabulary for that question: ETag, If-Match, 412 Precondition Failed and 428 Precondition Required.
lessons.objective: Version the notes resource, expose the version as an ETag and require If-Match on writes so a stale client cannot overwrite a newer edit.

cautions: A check in the handler followed by an unconditional write still races.
Weak ETags never satisfy If-Match, so writes need strong validators.
designGuide.cost: A version column, a conditional UPDATE and client code that handles 412 by re-reading and merging.
strengths: Concurrent edits are detected instead of silently overwritten.
No locks are held while clients read or think.
Uses standard HTTP headers and statuses that clients and proxies understand.

alternatives: 412 Precondition Failed, because no version matched
200 OK, applying the write as last-write-wins
quiz.correct: 428 Precondition Required
quiz.explanation: 412 reports a precondition that was present and false. RFC 6585 defines 428 for a server that requires a precondition the request did not include.
quiz.hint: One status means a condition was evaluated and failed; another means no condition was sent.
quiz.question: The notes API requires conditional writes. A client sends PUT /notes/n1 without an If-Match header. Which response is correct?

review.answer: 428 Precondition Required

sections.body: The store's mutex from the CRUD lesson makes each write atomic, but the dangerous gap is not inside a request. It is between one client's GET and its later PUT, while another client writes. A lock cannot cover that gap without holding it across user think time, and abandoned locks are worse than the original bug. Optimistic concurrency accepts that conflicts are rare and detects them at write time instead: every note carries a version, every successful write increments it, and a write names the version it was based on. If the stored version has moved, the write is refused and the client decides what to do. Nothing is locked while people read.
sections.title: A lost update spans two requests

sections.body: GET returns the version as a strong ETag such as "1". The guarded PUT requires If-Match, compares it with the current version and asks the store to replace the note only if the version is still the one it checked. The naive route with no checks runs first to reproduce the bug, then the guarded route replays the same two edits.
sections.title: ETag out, If-Match in, compare-and-swap in the store
sections.walkthrough: On the naive route both writes succeed and the final body is "flights": client A's hotel is gone and nobody was told. On the guarded route both clients read ETag "1". A writes with If-Match "1" and gets 200 with ETag "2". B writes from the stale copy with If-Match "1" and gets 412. Without If-Match B gets 428, so skipping the header is not a way around the check. W/"2" names the current version but is weak, and If-Match uses strong comparison, so it fails too. B re-reads, gets "2", reapplies the title change onto the current body and receives ETag "3"; the final note keeps both edits. Replace re-checks the version under its own lock because another writer can win between the handler's Get and the write.

sections.body: RFC 9110 defines an entity tag as a quoted string, optionally prefixed with W/ to mark it weak. If-Match is evaluated with strong comparison, so a weak tag can never satisfy it, and the asterisk matches any current representation, which is useful to say "update only if it exists". When the condition is false the server must not perform the method; the usual answer is 412, and RFC 9110 also permits a 2xx when the server can verify that the requested change is already reflected in the current state. RFC 6585 adds 428 for a server that requires conditional requests and receives one without a condition. Send the new ETag with every successful write so the client does not need an extra GET. PATCH needs exactly the same guard as PUT: a partial update made from stale assumptions is still a lost update. In the full service, 412 and 428 go through the problems middleware as two more problem types.
sections.title: The rules HTTP already defines

sections.body: The version check and the increment must be one operation in the store. A handler that reads the version, compares it and then issues an unconditional write has a race between the compare and the write. In SQL the condition goes into the UPDATE itself, and a statement that matched no rows tells you the condition failed. Do not use updated_at as the version: clock resolution and skew make two writes look simultaneous. Increment the version on every change that alters the representation, and if the representation includes data from elsewhere, such as an author name from another table, either include that in the version or derive the ETag from a hash of the representation.
sections.title: Make the check atomic where the data lives
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the PostgreSQL adapter for the same Replace contract; run it against your own database. The WHERE clause checks ID, owner and version in the same statement that increments the version, so two writers holding version 5 cannot both succeed; the second matches zero rows. RETURNING gives the new version for the ETag. On sql.ErrNoRows a second query distinguishes a deleted note, which maps to 404, from a version that moved on, which maps to 412.

sections.body: On 412 a client re-reads, merges or shows the conflict to the person, and retries with the fresh ETag. Automatically resending the same body with the new ETag is just last-write-wins with extra steps. Conditional writes also interact with retries: if a PUT succeeded but the response was lost, the retry with the old If-Match gets 412 from this implementation, and the client should re-read and notice its change is already there. Test the contract through ServeHTTP: missing header is 428, a stale tag is 412, a weak tag is 412, a fresh tag is 200 with the next ETag, and two goroutines writing with the same tag produce exactly one 200.
sections.title: What clients and tests must do

reading.takeaway: Expose a version as a strong ETag, require If-Match on PUT and PATCH with 428 when it is absent, and let the store compare and increment the version atomically, answering 412 on mismatch.

lessons.title: Stop lost updates with versions, ETag and If-Match: 428 when missing, 412 when stale

lessons.explanation: Tests that call a handler function directly miss the bugs that live between handlers: middleware order, error mapping, headers and the exact JSON a client parses. Sending requests through the router production uses, with a fake store behind it, tests the API contract in milliseconds. A table turns the next case into a few lines, and asserting whole bodies is what catches the regression that a status check waves through.
lessons.objective: Write table-driven tests that send requests through the real Gin router with fakes and assert status, contract headers and semantically compared JSON bodies.

cautions: float64 decoding loses precision for integers above 2^53.
Fakes do not prove the real store works; keep separate integration tests.
designGuide.cost: A fake per dependency, a test helper and the discipline to inject time and IDs everywhere.
strengths: Tests the real middleware chain and error mapping in milliseconds.
Whole-body comparison catches leaks and accidental fields.
New cases are one table row, so regressions get reproduced cheaply.

alternatives: httptest cannot expose the body until it is decoded
It ignores extra members, so tests survive new fields
quiz.correct: Key order and whitespace are not part of the contract
quiz.explanation: Two encodings of one object can differ in key order and spacing. Decoding compares values, and because DeepEqual still sees every member, an unexpected detail field fails the test.
quiz.hint: Consider what changes in the bytes when the same object is encoded twice.
quiz.question: Why does assertJSONEqual decode both the expected and the actual body into any before comparing them?

review.answer: Key order and whitespace are not part of the contract

sections.body: In these tests everything a request touches in production is real except the outermost dependencies. The engine, the problems middleware, the handlers and the notes service are the production code, built through the same constructors main uses. The store, the clock and the ID source are fakes injected as the dependencies lesson showed, which makes every body deterministic. Each case builds its own fake and router, so cases share nothing and can run in parallel. Assert three things per response: the status, every header that is part of the contract such as Location, Content-Type, ETag or Retry-After, and the entire body as a JSON value. A storage adapter gets its own integration tests against a real database; mixing the two makes API tests slow and flaky.
sections.title: Test the router, fake only the edges

sections.body: The test file lives next to the handlers but uses the external package httpapi_test, so it can only call what main can call: NewRouter, NewHandler and the notes constructors. That keeps the tests honest about the public wiring. TestMain sets Gin's mode once, because SetMode writes a process-wide variable and parallel subtests must not race on it.
sections.title: handler_test.go: the table and the assertions
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs in internal/httpapi of the module from the layout lesson and runs there with go test -race ./internal/httpapi. Each table row names the request and the expected contract. t.Run gives every case its own name in the output, and t.Parallel is safe because the router and fake are per case; since Go 1.22 the loop variable tc is a fresh variable on each iteration, so the closure needs no copy. newTestRouter uses t.Helper and t.Fatal for wiring errors. assertJSONEqual decodes both sides into any and compares them with reflect.DeepEqual, reporting the full actual body on mismatch. fakeStore, with a mutex and an err field, lives in fake_test.go in the same package.

sections.body: The runnable model condenses the notes and httpapi packages into one file and runs the same four cases three times: against the current build, against a regressed build with status-only checks, and against the regressed build with full checks. The regression is a plausible "debugging aid": the problems middleware copies err.Error() into detail for unexpected errors.
sections.title: The same table, runnable, against a regression
sections.walkthrough: check sends one request and collects failures instead of calling t.Errorf, so main can print a PASS or FAIL line per case. Header names are checked in sorted order to keep output stable. The current build passes everything; note that the expected create body lists keys in a different order and with spaces, and still matches. On the regressed build, status-only checks pass all four cases, because a leaking 500 is still a 500. Full checks fail the store-failure case and print the body that would have reached clients, with the database address in detail.

sections.body: Byte comparison breaks for reasons that are not part of the contract: key order in maps, field order after a struct refactor, whitespace, and HTML escaping, since encoding/json escapes <, > and & by default and Gin's c.PureJSON does not. Decoding both sides into any and comparing with reflect.DeepEqual compares values instead. It is still strict in the useful direction: an extra member, a missing member and a null where a string was expected all fail, which is exactly how the leaked detail was caught. Two caveats remain. Numbers decode to float64, so integers above 2^53 lose precision; decode with json.Decoder.UseNumber when IDs or amounts are large. And volatile fields should be made deterministic by injecting the clock and ID source rather than deleted before comparing, because deleted fields are untested fields.
sections.title: Compare JSON by meaning, and know the limits

sections.body: For each route, include the success path with its headers, every error kind the problems middleware maps and one failing store that must produce a bare 500. Add middleware-level rows: an unknown route, an oversized body, a missing Idempotency-Key, a missing or stale If-Match. Where a request has side effects, inspect the fake afterwards; a replayed idempotent POST must leave exactly one note. Run with -race and -count=1, and occasionally with -shuffle=on to surface hidden ordering between cases. When a bug escapes, its reproduction becomes a new row before the fix.
sections.title: What the table should cover

reading.takeaway: Drive tests through the production router with fakes for the store, clock and IDs, and assert status, contract headers and the whole JSON body compared semantically, so a leaked detail fails the build.

lessons.title: Table-driven API tests through the real router: status, headers and JSON compared by meaning

lessons.explanation: The last piece of the notes API is the code that runs first. A typo in an environment variable should stop a deploy with a clear message, not start a server with a default timeout, a debug-mode router or a proxy list that trusts the whole internet. This lesson builds the configuration loader, then assembles every package from the earlier lessons in cmd/api/main.go.
lessons.objective: Load and validate configuration from the environment, fail fast with every problem listed, and wire store, service, handlers, engine and http.Server with signal-driven shutdown.

cautions: URL.Redacted masks only the password; tokens in query strings still leak.
Using the signal context as BaseContext cancels draining requests.
designGuide.cost: A config package with a test table and a slightly longer main; both are cheaper than one misconfigured production start.
strengths: Bad deployments fail before serving, with every problem listed.
All wiring is in one short function that names every dependency.
Shutdown has one owner and one budget taken from configuration.

alternatives: Shutdown would then wait forever for that context
BaseContext applies only to HTTP/2 connections
quiz.correct: No: SIGTERM would cancel requests that are draining
quiz.explanation: Every request context derives from BaseContext, so cancelling it on SIGTERM aborts the in-flight requests that a graceful Shutdown is meant to let finish.
quiz.hint: Follow the signal context down to each request's r.Context().
quiz.question: Why should run not set http.Server.BaseContext to return the signal.NotifyContext context?

review.answer: No: SIGTERM would cancel requests that are draining

sections.body: Environment variables are untyped strings set by people and deployment templates, so they fail in predictable ways. A duration written as 5 without a unit does not parse. A misspelled name is silently ignored and the default applies. A value can parse correctly and still be dangerous, such as a shutdown budget longer than the platform waits before killing the process, or a trusted-proxy range of 0.0.0.0/0. And a database URL printed at startup leaks its password into logs. The loader answers each one: typed fields, explicit ranges, an error for unknown names under the application prefix, defaults that are safe in production, and a String method that redacts secrets. It also collects every problem before returning, so one failed deploy shows the whole list instead of one error per attempt.
sections.title: Configuration is input: parse it, bound it, reject it

sections.body: Load takes the environment as a slice of KEY=value strings, the shape os.Environ returns, rather than calling os.Getenv itself. That keeps it a pure function: tests pass literal slices, and main passes the real environment. Small closures parse each kind of value and append to a shared error list, cross-field rules run at the end, and errors.Join combines everything into one error whose message has one line per problem.
sections.title: Load, validate and print the effective settings
sections.walkthrough: The first configuration is valid: the database URL prints with its password replaced by xxxxx, because URL.Redacted masks only the password component, and the single proxy address becomes a /32 prefix. HOME is ignored because only the NOTES_ prefix is checked. With no variables at all the defaults are complete and conservative: release mode, bounded timeouts and no trusted proxies; the memory store default suits development, and a production deploy sets NOTES_STORE=postgres. The bad configuration reports six problems at once: a misspelled name, a duration without a unit, a shutdown budget above the 25-second ceiling, an address without a colon, a proxy range that would trust every client and a missing database URL that the postgres store requires.

sections.body: main does nothing but call run and translate its error into an exit status. run loads configuration, creates the signal context, builds the graph from the inside out, binds the listener, serves, and on a signal drains with a budget. Every constructor from the earlier lessons appears exactly once here, and no other package names a concrete type from another package.
sections.title: The composition root
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment; it opens a real socket. Because run returns errors instead of exiting, its deferred calls always execute before os.Exit. gin.SetMode runs before NewRouter calls gin.New, and NewRouter returns the error from SetTrustedProxies, so a bad list stops startup. net.Listen binds before the serving goroutine starts, so a busy port is an immediate error rather than a log line from a goroutine. On SIGTERM the context is cancelled and context.Cause reports "terminated signal received". stop restores default signal handling, Shutdown drains within cfg.ShutdownTimeout using a fresh context, Close drops whatever remains if the budget runs out, and ErrServerClosed from Serve is the normal result.

sections.body: Do not pass the signal context to http.Server.BaseContext. Every request context derives from it, so the first SIGTERM would cancel the very requests Shutdown is trying to let finish. Gin reads GIN_MODE once, in its package init, and the fragment then overrides it with SetMode; pick one source of truth, here the validated config, so two settings cannot disagree. The 25-second ceiling on the shutdown budget exists to fit under a platform grace period such as the Kubernetes default of 30 seconds, leaving time for the remaining teardown. Readiness withdrawal, header and idle timeouts, and joining background workers are covered in the server-lifecycle lesson; this root only has to give them one owner and one budget. If a Postgres adapter replaces the memory store, open it before the listener and close it after Shutdown returns, so no request runs against a closed pool.
sections.title: Startup and shutdown details that bite

sections.body: Load is a pure function of a slice, so a table test covers every rule: each default, each range edge, each unknown name, the redacted String output and the combined error text. The composition root is harder to unit test, which is why it should stay thin. A useful refactor is run(ctx, environ) with the signal context created in main: an integration test can then start the service on 127.0.0.1:0, send one request, cancel the context and assert a clean return within the budget, without sending real signals. Log the effective configuration once at startup; when an incident starts with "which timeout was this pod running with?", that line answers it.
sections.title: Test startup like any other code

reading.takeaway: Parse configuration into a typed, bounded struct that reports every error at once and redacts secrets, then wire store, service, handlers, engine and server in main, with signal.NotifyContext starting a budgeted Shutdown.

lessons.title: Start from validated configuration and wire the whole service in one composition root

summary: Layout, dependencies, CRUD, pagination, problem details, idempotency keys, optimistic concurrency, API tests and startup.
title: Gin project: a complete REST API
translationNote: One service grows lesson by lesson. The models run in memory; a deployment adds a database, TLS and observability in your own environment.

lessons.explanation: store.Query(c) compiles because *gin.Context implements context.Context, and in a default Gin engine it quietly throws away cancellation, deadlines and tracing values. The context passed to data access decides whether a query stops when its client leaves and whether background work outlives the response. Gin hands you two candidates, and only one of them is a real request context.
lessons.objective: Predict what *gin.Context returns as a context.Context under each ContextWithFallback setting and give stores and background work a context that is actually canceled, or deliberately not.

cautions: Never use c or c.Writer after the handler returns; the pool hands it to the next request.
context.WithoutCancel also drops the deadline, so add your own timeout and shutdown hook.
designGuide.cost: Threading ctx through every service signature and typing c.Request.Context() at each call site; detached work needs its own lifetime management.
strengths: Cancellation, deadlines and trace values reach every store call regardless of engine flags.
Background work has an explicit owner, budget and shutdown path.

alternatives: context.Canceled, because c wraps the request context
context.DeadlineExceeded once WriteTimeout expires
quiz.correct: Never canceled: Done is nil and Err stays nil
quiz.explanation: Deadline, Done and Err delegate to c.Request.Context() only when engine.ContextWithFallback is true, and gin.New leaves it false, so the store never learns the client left. Passing c.Request.Context() works under either setting.
quiz.hint: Look at what Done and Err check before they delegate to c.Request.
quiz.question: In Gin v1.12.0 with gin.New() defaults, a handler calls store.Query(c) and the client disconnects mid-query. What does the store see through that context?

review.answer: Never canceled: Done is nil and Err stays nil
review.prompt: c as a context under gin.New()?

sections.body: c.Request.Context() belongs to net/http. The server cancels it when the client's connection closes, when an HTTP/2 stream is reset, or when ServeHTTP returns, and middleware derives deadlines and values from it with WithTimeout and WithValue. *gin.Context is something else: a mutable struct that the engine takes from a sync.Pool for each request, fills with the request, route params and keys, and puts back when the chain returns. It implements Deadline, Done, Err and Value so that it can be passed where a context.Context is expected, but those four methods are an adapter whose behavior depends on an engine flag. The request-deadlines lesson showed what happens when a hung store is given c. This lesson takes the adapter apart, follows c back into the pool and works out what c.Copy is actually for.
sections.title: Two contexts travel with every Gin request

sections.body: In context.go, Deadline, Done and Err first call hasRequestContext, which is true only when engine.ContextWithFallback is set and c.Request has a context. Otherwise Deadline reports ok=false, Done returns nil and Err returns nil. A nil channel is never ready, so a select on c.Done() waits forever, and a driver that checks ctx.Err() before each round trip never finds a reason to stop. Value has a fixed lookup order. The key gin.ContextRequestKey, the constant 0 of type gin.ContextKeyType, returns c.Request. The string gin.ContextKey returns c itself. Any other string key is looked up in c.Keys. Only after that, and only with fallback on, does the lookup reach c.Request.Context(). Typed keys, which context.WithValue users and tracing libraries rely on, therefore return nil by default. A typed key stored with c.Set is never found through Value at all, because only string keys consult c.Keys; the middleware-basics lesson met the same gap from the other side. Both gin.New() and gin.Default() leave ContextWithFallback false.
sections.title: Read the adapter in the v1.12.0 source

sections.body: The program models a driver that refuses work for a finished context and reads a trace ID the way an instrumented client would. A middleware stores the trace ID in the request context and a tenant in c.Keys. The same routes run on two engines, fallback off and on, with a request whose context carries a deadline and whose client has already gone. The last request starts work that runs after the handler has returned and the request context has been canceled, which is what net/http does when ServeHTTP returns.
sections.title: Hand the same store both contexts
sections.walkthrough: With fallback off, c reports no deadline, a nil Done channel and a nil Err for a request whose context is both deadlined and canceled. Only the string key tenant survives, because Value finds it in c.Keys, while the typed trace key comes back nil. store(c) therefore runs a query for a client that left and loses the trace ID, and store(c.Request.Context()) sees context.Canceled on either engine. With fallback on, c delegates and behaves like the request context. In the /after handler, c.Copy shares the *http.Request, so the copy's request context is canceled as soon as the request ends, while its Keys are a snapshot: the c.Set after Copy does not reach it. context.WithoutCancel keeps the trace value and drops the cancellation. The deferred closures capture req, cp and detached, never c.

sections.body: engine.ServeHTTP takes a *gin.Context from engine.pool, points it at the new writer and request, resets its params, keys, errors and query cache, runs the chain and puts it back. Identity therefore belongs to a pool slot, not to a request. A goroutine that kept c after the handler returned holds a pointer that the next request will fill: c.Param returns another caller's ID, c.Keys holds another principal or nothing, c.Request is a stranger's request, and with fallback on c.Done becomes the stranger's cancellation, so your background work stops when someone else disconnects. Every one of those reads is a data race with the reset in the next ServeHTTP. ContextWithFallback fixes none of it, and even c.Request.Context(), captured honestly before returning, is canceled right after ServeHTTP returns. The race detector reports the bug only when a test actually reuses the context while the goroutine still reads it, so drive handlers that start goroutines with a burst of requests under go test -race.
sections.title: The handler returns and the pool takes c back

sections.body: Copy builds a new Context that shares the same *http.Request, clones Keys with maps.Clone, copies Params and keeps the full path and the engine. It detaches the writer: the copy's underlying ResponseWriter is nil, so a write through cp.Writer panics instead of corrupting a recycled response, and its handler index is set to the abort value, so cp.Next does nothing. maps.Clone is shallow, so a pointer or slice stored in Keys is still shared with the handler. Errors and Accepted are not copied, and no lifetime is extended. Use Copy when a goroutine needs request data such as params, keys or c.FullPath() after the handler returns. Use neither c nor the copy as the goroutine's context: with fallback off it is never canceled, and with fallback on it is canceled the moment the response is done. Build the work's input as a value and give it a context you own.
sections.title: What c.Copy hands a goroutine, and what it does not
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs to a real service and runs in your own environment; Handlers, AuditEvent and tenantFrom are your types. The event is a plain value built before the goroutine starts, so the goroutine never touches c. WithoutCancel also drops the deadline, so the goroutine sets its own five-second budget, and context.AfterFunc cancels it when the service's shutdown context ends; shutdown then waits on h.wg. The log call still carries the trace values from the request. Work that must survive a crash belongs in a durable queue instead, as the context-workers lesson explains.

sections.body: Make one rule for the codebase: functions below the HTTP layer take ctx context.Context as their first parameter, and handlers pass c.Request.Context(). The rule works with any engine and is obvious in review. Turning ContextWithFallback on is still a reasonable safety net, because helpers that accept a context.Context then receive cancellation and tracing values when someone passes c by mistake. Set it once while building the engine; it is a plain field read on every call, so changing it while serving is a data race. Expect behavior to change when you flip it: code that was silently never canceled starts returning context.Canceled, which usually exposes a goroutine that kept c. Neither setting rescues retention, and typed keys stored with c.Set still never reach Value. The compiler accepts c wherever a context is expected, so add a small go/analysis check that reports a *gin.Context passed to a context.Context parameter, and keep a test like the program's that sends a canceled request and asserts the store saw it.
sections.title: Decide on ContextWithFallback once, then review for c

reading.takeaway: Pass c.Request.Context() to stores and goroutines. *gin.Context is a pooled struct whose context methods go dead unless ContextWithFallback is set, c.Copy copies request data rather than a lifetime, and detached work needs WithoutCancel plus a deadline you own.

lessons.title: *gin.Context is a pooled struct, not your request context: pass c.Request.Context() to stores and goroutines

lessons.explanation: A client that wants to clear a due date sends {"due": null}; a client that only renames a note leaves due out entirely. If the server cannot tell those requests apart, it either ignores the clear or wipes a field nobody mentioned. JSON Merge Patch gives the three cases exact meanings, and Gin's struct binding cannot see one of them.
lessons.objective: Implement an RFC 7396 merge-patch endpoint in Gin that distinguishes absent from null, enforces application/merge-patch+json with 415, and validates the merged result before storing it.

cautions: Arrays are replaced whole and null cannot be stored as a value; use JSON Patch when that matters.
Read, merge and write still need If-Match or a version check across replicas.
designGuide.cost: A generic decode, a merge and a second strict decode per request, plus media-type checks and error mapping that plain struct binding does not need.
strengths: Clients can leave, clear or replace each member exactly as RFC 7396 defines.
Validation sees the resource the store will hold, not a fragment of it.

alternatives: ShouldBindJSON rejects null members with a 400
null decodes to a pointer to an empty string
quiz.correct: null and absent both leave the pointer nil
quiz.explanation: encoding/json sets a pointer to nil for JSON null, which is also what an absent member leaves behind, so the handler cannot tell "clear it" from "leave it alone". A map of json.RawMessage or a tri-state type keeps the two apart.
quiz.hint: Compare the field after decoding {} with the field after decoding {"due":null}.
quiz.question: A PATCH handler binds {"due": null} with ShouldBindJSON into a struct whose Due field is *string. Why can it not clear the due date correctly?

review.answer: null and absent both leave the pointer nil

sections.body: RFC 7396 defines a merge patch as a JSON document that mirrors the target. For each member of a patch object, an absent member leaves the target alone, null removes the member, an object merges recursively, and any other value, arrays included, replaces the member whole. A patch that is not an object replaces the entire target. The media type is application/merge-patch+json, and claiming merge-patch semantics means honoring all of these rules, not just the convenient ones. The crud-resource lesson used pointer fields for PATCH and noted that they cannot express removal; this lesson builds the full version, including nested objects, strict decoding and the error statuses a client can program against.
sections.title: Three meanings in one small document

sections.body: encoding/json sets a pointer field to nil when the member is null, and nil is also what an absent member leaves behind, so {} and {"due":null} bind to identical structs. ShouldBindJSON adds nothing that helps here: in v1.12.0 it runs a json.Decoder over the body and then the validator, and it never looks at Content-Type. c.ShouldBind is worse for this route, because it picks a binding from Content-Type through binding.Default, and application/merge-patch+json is not in that table, so it falls back to form binding and never decodes the JSON body at all. Two representations keep the information. A map[string]json.RawMessage records presence as a key and null as the four raw bytes null. A small tri-state type with an UnmarshalJSON method works too, because encoding/json calls UnmarshalJSON for a present null but not for an absent member.
sections.title: Why struct binding cannot hear null

sections.body: The program first decodes the same three bodies into a pointer field and into a raw map, so the difference is visible. The handler then checks the media type, decodes the patch generically, refuses members a client may not change, and merges the patch into the current note represented as a generic JSON document. It turns the merged document back into a Note with unknown fields disallowed and validates that Note with Gin's validator before storing it.
sections.title: Merge, decode strictly, validate
sections.walkthrough: The pointer is nil for both {} and null, while the map distinguishes absent from null. mime.ParseMediaType lowercases the type and drops parameters, so Application/Merge-Patch+JSON is accepted; c.ContentType() only strips parameters, so comparing its result to a lowercase constant would reject that client. decodeOne reads one value, keeps numbers as json.Number so large integers survive the round trip, and rejects trailing data, which is why the body with two objects is a 400. mergePatch is the RFC 7396 algorithm. Decoding the merged document with DisallowUnknownFields refuses a misspelled nested member such as colour instead of dropping it. Removing due makes it absent, and omitempty keeps it absent on output. {"title":null} removes a required member, so validating the merged note gives 422 naming the field. The 415 carries Accept-Patch, as RFC 5789 recommends.

sections.body: Whether a patch is acceptable depends on the state it lands on. {"title":null} is a perfectly formed patch that removes a required member, and a tag limit applies to the merged list, not to the members a client happened to send. So the rules live on the resource struct and run on the merged value through binding.Validator.ValidateStruct, the same validator ShouldBindJSON would have used. Read-only members such as id are refused before merging, because a merge would otherwise apply them. Pick statuses clients can act on: 415 with Accept-Patch for the wrong media type, 400 for malformed JSON, 422 for a well-formed patch that is not allowed or produces an invalid resource. The mutex makes read, merge and write one step inside this process. Across replicas the same read-modify-write needs a version check, and the optimistic-concurrency lesson adds If-Match for exactly this endpoint.
sections.title: Validate the result, not the patch

sections.body: A generic merge suits resources whose JSON shape matches the stored model. When the public shape differs, or only a few members are patchable, a typed patch DTO reads better. Optional records presence and null separately, and ShouldBindJSON can still decode it because it simply runs encoding/json. Apply the DTO to a copy of the stored resource, then validate the copy exactly as before.
sections.title: A tri-state field when you prefer a typed DTO
sections.walkthrough: This fragment plugs into the program's Note type; compile it inside your own service. UnmarshalJSON is never called for an absent member, so Set stays false and applyTo leaves the field alone. For a present null, encoding/json passes the literal bytes null, so Null is set and Value keeps its zero value. Validator tags cannot see inside Optional, which is one more reason to validate the patched Note rather than the DTO. Nested objects need their own Optional fields, or a map, to keep merge semantics below the top level.

sections.body: Go's decoder matches member names to struct fields case-insensitively, so {"Title":"x"} binds to Title even though the allow-list map checks exact names; decide which behavior is your contract and test it. For duplicate names, encoding/json keeps the last one, and another parser in front of you may keep the first, so a proxy that inspects patches can see a different document from the one you apply. Merge patch also has two semantic gaps: an array can only be replaced whole, so appending one tag means sending the full list, and null can never be stored as a value. When clients need either, use JSON Patch (RFC 6902) or a sub-resource such as POST /notes/7/tags. Cap the body with http.MaxBytesReader, as the binding-limits lesson explains. The test table writes itself: absent, null, value, nested null, a non-object patch, an unknown member, an invalid result and the wrong media type.
sections.title: What a reviewer should still look for

reading.takeaway: Accept only application/merge-patch+json, decode the patch into a representation that keeps absent and null apart, merge it into the current resource, and validate the merged result before storing it.

lessons.title: PATCH with JSON Merge Patch in Gin: keep absent, null and value apart, then validate the merged resource

lessons.explanation: List endpoints accumulate filters one release at a time: a status here, a search box there, a second sort key for the dashboard. Each one is a chance to splice a value into SQL text, to let a percent sign widen a search, or to send IN () to the database. Build the query in one function that owns every placeholder, and test that function without a database.
lessons.objective: Write a pure function that turns a Gin list request into SQL text and arguments, with allow-listed sorts, a placeholder for every value, escaped LIKE patterns, bounded IN lists and a unique tiebreaker.

cautions: Each IN list length is a new statement text; prefer = ANY($n) on PostgreSQL.
Leading-wildcard LIKE cannot use a B-tree index, however well it is escaped.
designGuide.cost: A builder type, explicit validation for every parameter and an index for each allowed sort combination.
strengths: The whole query is a pure function that table tests can pin exactly.
Equivalent requests produce identical SQL and arguments.

alternatives: Gin splits it into the two values open and closed
Gin answers 400 before the handler runs
quiz.correct: The pair is dropped silently: no status filter at all
quiz.explanation: URL.Query discards ParseQuery's error and keeps only the pairs it could parse. A semicolon is no longer a separator, so the whole pair is dropped and the query loses its filter. Parse RawQuery yourself and answer 400.
quiz.hint: Look at what URL.Query does with the error returned by url.ParseQuery.
quiz.question: A Gin handler reads filters with c.QueryArray("status"). In Go 1.17 and later, what happens to the request ?status=open;closed?

review.answer: The pair is dropped silently: no status filter at all

sections.body: The security.sql-injection lesson explains why statement text and values must reach the driver separately, and the pagination-filtering lesson covers cursors and why sort names go through an allow-list. What remains is the code in between: a function that takes the parsed query string plus the scope from the path or the authenticated principal and returns SQL text and an argument slice. Keeping it free of *gin.Context makes it a pure function, so a table test can assert the exact statement for each request. Keeping every filter in it gives a reviewer one place to check the invariant that matters: SQL text is assembled only from constants your code owns and placeholder numbers the builder generates.
sections.title: One function between url.Values and QueryContext

sections.body: c.Query, c.QueryArray and c.ShouldBindQuery all read c.Request.URL.Query(), which ignores the error from url.ParseQuery and keeps only the pairs it could parse. Since Go 1.17 a semicolon is not a separator, so ?status=open;closed loses its only pair and the client silently receives every status. Current Go releases also refuse a query with more than 10,000 pairs as a whole, controlled by the urlmaxqueryparams GODEBUG setting, so the handler sees no parameters at all. Parse c.Request.URL.RawQuery with url.ParseQuery yourself and answer 400 on error, then reject unknown names. Accept lists both as repeated keys and as comma-separated values, validate every element, and only then sort and dedupe. Canonical input means that equivalent requests produce byte-identical SQL and arguments, which keeps statement caches and query statistics small and lets a response cache keyed by the query reuse entries. The project scope comes from the path and is added first and unconditionally; it is not a filter the client may drop.
sections.title: Parse the raw query strictly, then canonicalize

sections.body: buildQuery validates each parameter, adds a predicate per filter through a builder whose bind method is the only way to add a value, then appends the allow-listed ORDER BY, the tiebreaker and a bound LIMIT. The handler returns the SQL and arguments as text so the output shows exactly what a driver would receive. No database is involved.
sections.title: Build the statement and print it
sections.walkthrough: bind appends the value and returns its placeholder, so numbering follows argument order across WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT. In the second request triaged,open becomes the sorted pair open, triaged, and the assignee list 42, 9, 42 becomes 9 and 42 after parsing as integers; the raw count is bounded before any parsing. q=100%25_done decodes to 100%_done, and the escaper turns it into the pattern %100!%!_done%, matched literally under ESCAPE '!'; ILIKE is PostgreSQL's case-insensitive LIKE. created_after is parsed as RFC 3339 and passed as a UTC time.Time, never as text. A sort key containing an encoded semicolon is simply not in the map. An unencoded semicolon makes url.ParseQuery fail, which is a 400 here and would have been a missing filter with c.QueryArray. Unknown names are checked in sorted order so the error is deterministic.

sections.body: A placeholder stops injection; it does not make a value mean what the user intended. LIKE treats % and _ in the bound value as wildcards, so escape them and name the escape character in the statement, as the security lesson shows, and cap the length. A pattern with a leading % cannot use an ordinary B-tree index, so contains-search over a large table needs a trigram index or full-text search, not a bigger timeout. IN lists need three guards: bound the raw count before doing work, refuse empty elements, and never emit IN (), which is a syntax error. Every distinct list length is also a distinct statement text, which multiplies prepared statements and plan-cache entries. PostgreSQL can take the whole list as one array argument instead.
sections.title: Lists and patterns are where bound values still go wrong
sections.walkthrough: This fragment extends the program's builder for PostgreSQL; run it against a real driver in your own environment. = ANY($2) compares the column with each element of one array parameter, so the statement text stays constant whatever the list length, and the bound on the list still applies because it limits the work and the size of the argument. pgx encodes Go slices as PostgreSQL arrays directly, while lib/pq needs the pq.Array wrapper. Keep the canonical sort and dedupe so equal requests still send equal arguments.

sections.body: The client chooses among names; the server owns the SQL. A leading minus selects DESC, and the column, direction and NULL placement all come from constants. Refuse a repeated key and cap the number of keys, because every allowed combination is an index you either build or a sort the database performs on every request. PostgreSQL sorts NULL as larger than any value, so NULLs come last ascending and first descending; writing NULLS LAST for nullable columns keeps undated issues at the end in both directions. An index serves the query without a separate sort only when its columns, directions and NULL placement match the ORDER BY or its exact reverse. Always append the unique id, so the order is total and a page boundary is a single row, which the pagination lesson relies on for cursors. Choose a default order when the client sends none rather than leaving it to the planner.
sections.title: Sort keys, directions and the tiebreaker

sections.body: Because buildQuery takes url.Values and returns a string and a slice, its tests need no database and no HTTP server. For each case, assert the full SQL text and the full argument list, not a substring. Include equivalence cases that must produce identical output, such as reordered and repeated list values, and hostile cases that must produce 400: an unencoded semicolon, an unknown parameter, an unknown or repeated sort key, an out-of-range limit, twenty-one assignees and an over-long search term. Then add a small integration suite against a disposable PostgreSQL that checks rows rather than strings: a title containing a literal percent sign, NULL placement in both directions, and EXPLAIN for each allowed sort combination to confirm the index you expect is used.
sections.title: Test the builder as a pure function

reading.takeaway: Parse RawQuery strictly, canonicalize and bound every list, let a builder generate every placeholder, take sort SQL only from constants and always end the order with a unique tiebreaker.

lessons.title: Gin list filters to parameterized SQL: parse strictly, bound IN lists, escape LIKE, end with a tiebreaker

lessons.explanation: A client asks for /posts?include=author,tags so that it can render a feed in one request. The obvious implementation looks up each post's author inside the loop that builds the response, and a page of fifty posts quietly becomes a hundred and one queries. The cost should depend on how many relations were requested, never on how many rows the page holds.
lessons.objective: Serve optional related data on a Gin list endpoint with one batched lookup per relation, bounded concurrent loads and deterministic output, and prove the query count by counting store calls.

cautions: errgroup v0.24.0 does not recover panics, and gin.Recovery cannot catch a loader panic.
The errgroup context is canceled once Wait returns; never reuse it.
designGuide.cost: A batch method per relation in the store, an include registry, and per-request concurrency that claims pool connections.
strengths: Round trips stay constant as the page grows.
Unknown includes fail loudly instead of silently returning less data.

alternatives: One list query plus one lookup per post per include
One list query plus one query per distinct author
quiz.correct: One list query plus one batch per include
quiz.explanation: Each loader receives every ID on the page and makes a single round trip, so the cost is one plus the number of includes whatever the page size; the N+1 shape grows with the page.
quiz.hint: Count how often each loader runs, not how many IDs it receives.
quiz.question: A client requests a page of 50 posts with ?include=author,tags. With batched loaders, how many store calls should the request make?

review.answer: One list query plus one batch per include

sections.body: In the N+1 shape, one query loads the list and then one more query runs per row for each relation. Each extra round trip adds latency in series and holds a pool connection while it waits, so under load the request spends most of its time queuing for connections, as the SQL pool lesson describes. Batching reverses the dependency. Collect the IDs the page refers to, load each relation for all of them in one query, and join the results in memory. The cost becomes one list query plus one query per requested include, whatever the page size. Independent relations can also load concurrently, which turns their latencies from a sum into a maximum, provided the concurrency is bounded.
sections.title: N+1 grows with the page, batching grows with the request

sections.body: Map each public include name to a loader that fetches one relation for the whole page and writes only its own field of a page struct. That map is the allow-list. An unknown name answers 400 and lists the valid ones, because a typo that silently returns less data is a bug nobody reports. Accept repeated and comma-separated forms through c.QueryArray and drop duplicates; the safe-filters lesson explains when to parse the raw query strictly instead. A loader is also an authorization boundary: an included author must expose exactly the fields a direct read of that author would, for the same caller. Nested includes such as author.organization multiply the work and the data exposed, so support them only deliberately, with a depth limit.
sections.title: Includes are an allow-list of loaders

sections.body: The store is an in-memory model that counts every method call. The naive route looks up authors one post at a time; the batched route parses the includes, loads the posts, runs the requested loaders through an errgroup limited to two at a time, and assembles the response in post order. A last request makes the tags store fail.
sections.title: Count the calls: naive versus batched
sections.walkthrough: The naive route makes one AuthorByID call per post, four for four posts, and that number grows with the page. The batched route makes one ListPosts call and one call per requested relation: AuthorsByIDs receives the deduplicated, sorted author IDs 7 and 9, and TagsByPostIDs receives every post ID. include=author,tags&include=author shows repeated and comma-separated forms merged with duplicates dropped. Each loader writes only its own field of page, so the goroutines never write the same memory, and they receive gctx rather than c. The response is built after Wait, in post order. A post without tags renders [] because the slice is non-nil, while a relation that was not requested is omitted by omitzero. An unknown include fails before any store call, and a failing loader turns into 503 with no partial body.

sections.body: errgroup.WithContext(c.Request.Context()) gives the loaders a context that is canceled when the client leaves and, through context.WithCancelCause in x/sync v0.24.0, the first time a loader returns an error, so the other loaders can stop early. Wait returns that first error. SetLimit(2) must be called before the first Go, because changing the limit while goroutines are active panics; once the limit is reached, Go blocks the handler until a slot frees. Size the limit against the connection pool: concurrent requests times loaders per request is how many connections includes can claim. Two traps are specific to running this inside Gin. The derived context is canceled as soon as Wait returns, so rendering or a follow-up query must use the request context, not gctx. And in v0.24.0, Go does not recover panics: a panic in a loader goroutine crashes the process, because gin.Recovery only protects the goroutine running the handler chain.
sections.title: Bounded concurrency with errgroup, and what it does not cover

sections.body: In PostgreSQL each loader becomes a single statement over an array of IDs. Let the database order the rows so that each slice arrives sorted, and build the response from the primary list, never by ranging over a map. Decide explicitly what a missing related row means: a deleted author can render as null, drop the post or fail the request, and each choice belongs in the API contract. Bound the ID list through the page limit; a page of at most 100 rows can never send more than 100 IDs to a loader.
sections.title: One query per relation in SQL, ordered by the database
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs against a real PostgreSQL database in your own environment; PG wraps a *sql.DB. post_id = ANY($1) takes the whole ID list as one array parameter. With the pgx stdlib driver a []int64 argument is encoded as an array directly, while lib/pq needs pq.Array(ids). ORDER BY post_id, tag makes every slice deterministic without sorting in Go. rows.Err is checked after the loop because iteration can fail midway, as the SQL rows lesson explains.

sections.body: Latency tests rarely catch an N+1 regression on a laptop with ten rows. A call count does. Run the list handler against a counting store with page sizes of 1, 10 and 50 and assert that the number of calls per relation is identical and equal to one. Add cases for an unknown include, a duplicated include, an included relation with no rows, a loader that fails and a client that cancels mid-request, and run the suite under go test -race so a loader that touches c or shares a map is reported. In production, record the number of queries per request as a span attribute or histogram, keyed by route template, so a regression shows up as a step in a graph rather than as a slow page.
sections.title: Make the call count a test assertion

reading.takeaway: Map each include to one batched loader keyed by the page's IDs, run the loaders through a bounded errgroup on the request context, and build the response in list order after Wait.

lessons.title: ?include= without N+1 in Gin: one batched loader per relation, a bounded errgroup and list-order output

lessons.explanation: A popular public endpoint renders the same page of articles thousands of times a minute, and each render costs a query and a JSON encode. Caching the finished response inside the service removes that work, but only if the cache never answers differently from the handler: not for another user, not for another query string and not after a write.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin middleware that caches public GET responses under a route-template key, never stores per-user responses, coalesces concurrent misses with singleflight and stays correct across writes, TTLs and conditional requests.

cautions: Invalidation is per process; other replicas serve old entries until their TTL ends.
A follower keeps waiting for the leader even after its own client has gone.
designGuide.cost: Memory for stored bodies, a capture writer, per-route allow-lists that must track what handlers read, and an invalidation call in every write path.
strengths: A popular public page costs one handler run per TTL per process.
Concurrent misses collapse into one fill, and 304s are answered from the entry.

alternatives: Cache it: the route template already identifies the content
Strip the header, then fill the cache as usual
quiz.correct: No, bypass: the response may depend on the caller
quiz.explanation: The key holds only the route, its params and the allow-listed query. A handler that reads Authorization can return per-user data, and caching it would serve one caller's response to the next, so the request must bypass the cache.
quiz.hint: Ask whether the key captures every input the handler can read.
quiz.question: A response-cache middleware keys entries by c.FullPath(), the path params and the allow-listed query. What should it do with a GET that carries an Authorization header?

review.answer: No, bypass: the response may depend on the caller

sections.body: One invariant drives every decision: the cache may answer only when the stored response is exactly what the handler would produce for this request. The key must therefore capture every input the handler reads, a request that carries identity must bypass the cache, and only a response that declares itself public may be stored. The conditional-requests lesson set Cache-Control and ETags for browsers and CDNs, which saves bandwidth. A server-side cache saves the handler's own work, the query and the render, and it lives inside your process, where you control the key, the lifetime and invalidation. The stampede and cache-aside lessons explain why concurrent misses are dangerous; this lesson builds the Gin middleware that handles them.
sections.title: The cache must never change the answer

sections.body: c.FullPath() returns the route template, such as /articles/:id, so the set of keys and the unit of invalidation follow routes rather than raw paths, and an unmatched request has an empty template and is never cached. Add the values from c.Params, then the query parsed with url.ParseQuery and re-encoded with Values.Encode, which sorts parameter names, so ?sort=new&page=1 and ?page=1&sort=new share an entry. Encode keeps the order of repeated values, because that order can be meaningful. Each route lists the parameters its handler reads. A request with any other parameter bypasses the cache instead of having the parameter dropped: dropping utm_source would be harmless, but dropping a parameter the handler does read would serve the wrong page. If you know some tracking parameters are ignored, strip them through a named list. Requests with Authorization or Cookie bypass, and a stored response must not carry Set-Cookie or Vary, because the key does not include the request headers it would vary on.
sections.title: Key by what the handler reads

sections.body: The program wraps one list route in the cache. A fake clock decides expiry. The handler counts its calls, reads the data version before doing slow work, and can be held at a gate so that misses overlap deterministically. The sequence covers a hit through a reordered query, three bypasses, a 304 served from the entry, a write, expiry, a write that lands during a fill, and two bursts of five concurrent misses, with and without coalescing.
sections.title: The middleware, a fake clock and a gated handler
sections.walkthrough: The first request misses and stores the response; ten seconds later the reordered query hits and Age reports 10. The bearer, cookie and utm requests bypass and each runs the handler. If-None-Match is answered 304 from the stored entry without a handler call. The POST bumps the version and invalidates /articles, so the next GET misses, and after the clock passes the 60 second TTL it misses again. In the write-during-a-fill step, the fill reads version 2 and waits; the POST invalidates the route meanwhile, so put discards the result and the next GET sees version 3 instead of a stale page for a minute. In the singleflight burst the gated leader is the only handler run: the other requests wait for it or hit the entry it stored. capture keeps its own header map, so headers that outer middleware set, such as a request ID, are never stored and replayed.

sections.body: group.Do runs the fill function on the calling goroutine, so the leader runs its own c.Next and no other goroutine ever touches its *gin.Context, as the context-fallback lesson requires. Followers block until the leader finishes and replay the same immutable entry onto their own writers, then Abort so their chains do not run. The fill re-checks the cache first, because a request that missed just before the previous flight ended would otherwise start a second fill. The flight key includes the route's generation, so a request that arrives after an invalidation never joins a flight that started before it. The limits are real. Do has no context, so a follower keeps waiting after its own client has gone; DoChan could select on cancellation, but it runs the function on a new goroutine, where calling c.Next would break the one-owner rule. If the leader's client disconnects and the handler fails, every follower receives that failed response, which at least is not stored. singleflight re-panics in the leader and in every follower; record restores the real writer in a defer so an outer Recovery can still answer 500, and registering Recovery inside the cache turns a panic into an ordinary 500 that is never stored. Coalescing is per process, so ten replicas still make ten fills.
sections.title: Coalescing misses inside Gin with singleflight

sections.body: A write handler commits and then invalidates the route templates whose responses it changed. Invalidating before the commit opens a window in which a read refills the entry with the old data. Even after the commit, a fill that read the old data before the write can finish afterwards and store it, which is the race the cache-aside lesson warns about.
