alternatives: application/json, because q=0 excludes text/csv
An empty string, so the handler should answer 406
quiz.correct: text/csv, because Gin discards q-values
quiz.explanation: parseAccept cuts every element at its first semicolon, so q=0 disappears and text/csv is the first accepted entry that matches an offer. RFC 9110 would exclude it and pick application/json through */*.
quiz.hint: Look at what parseAccept keeps from each element of the header.
quiz.question: A client sends Accept: text/csv;q=0, */* and a Gin v1.12.0 handler calls c.NegotiateFormat("application/json", "text/csv"). What does it return?

review.answer: text/csv, because Gin discards q-values

sections.body: parseAccept splits the header on commas, cuts each element at its first semicolon and trims spaces, so q-values and every other parameter are thrown away. NegotiateFormat caches that list in c.Accepted, which SetAccepted can replace, returns your first offer when the header is missing or empty, and panics if you pass no offers. Otherwise it walks the accepted entries in the client's order and compares each with your offers byte by byte: a * at the same position in either string matches the rest, and an accepted entry that is a prefix of an offer also matches, so even Accept: a selects application/json. Three consequences follow. Header order beats q: "application/json;q=0.1, text/csv" gets JSON. q=0 counts as acceptance: "text/csv;q=0, */*" gets CSV, the one type the client excluded. And media types compare case-sensitively although RFC 9110 says they are case-insensitive, so "Application/JSON" matches nothing. c.Negotiate switches on that result for JSON, HTML, XML, YAML, TOML, ProtoBuf and BSON; any other offer, including text/csv and even text/xml, falls to the default branch, AbortWithError with 406, which commits the status with an empty body.
sections.title: How Gin matches Accept, read from the source

sections.body: negotiate implements RFC 9110 section 12.5.1: each offer takes the q-value of the most specific media range that matches it, an exact type beating type/* and type/* beating */*, q=0 excludes, the highest q wins and ties go to the server's order. The program prints Gin's choice and the RFC choice side by side for seven Accept headers, then sends seven requests through the real router, including a ?format= override and a call to c.Negotiate.
sections.title: One handler, three representations, two negotiators
sections.walkthrough: ginChoice builds a fresh test context per header because NegotiateFormat caches the parsed list in c.Accepted. The table shows the three divergences described above; the browser header agrees in both because text/html comes first and has the highest q. In report, a format query parameter is checked against an allow-list and, when present, replaces negotiation entirely, so no Vary is sent. Without it the handler sets Vary: Accept before choosing, so even the 406 carries it. CSV is rendered with encoding/csv into a buffer and sent with c.Data; HTML uses the template installed with SetHTMLTemplate. image/png gets a 406 whose JSON body lists the available types. ?format=xml is a 400, because the URL itself is wrong. The last line is c.Negotiate offered text/csv and asked for text/csv: 406 with no body and no Content-Type, since it has no CSV renderer.

sections.body: An empty result means none of your representations is acceptable. Answer 406 Not Acceptable with a body listing what is available, as RFC 9110 suggests, written in your normal error format; a client that accepts only image/png will receive something it did not ask for either way. RFC 9110 also allows ignoring Accept and sending a default instead. Choose one behavior and document it, though for API clients 406 is kinder, because silent JSON delivered to a CSV importer fails later and more confusingly. A missing Accept means anything is acceptable, so put the safest default first in the offers. Browsers send text/html first with */*;q=0.8, so a person opening the URL gets HTML. Send Vary: Accept on every negotiated response so caches know the URL has several representations; without it, a CDN that stored the CSV serves it to the next JSON client. The price is fragmentation: every distinct Accept string becomes its own cache key, and many caches do not normalize it. Each representation also needs its own ETag, as the conditional-requests lesson requires.
sections.title: 406, defaults and Vary: Accept

sections.body: Negotiation hides the representation in a header, and sometimes it belongs in the URL. A "Download CSV" link in a page or an email cannot set Accept, and a browser's address bar always sends its own. A CDN keys on the URL without needing Vary, and logs and support tickets show exactly what was requested. So many APIs accept ?format=csv, or a suffix such as /sales.csv, as an explicit override validated against an allow-list, and fall back to Accept only when it is absent. An unknown value is a 400 because the URL is wrong; 406 is about the Accept header. Never copy the query value into Content-Type, or ?format=text/html turns your JSON into a page a browser renders, which is reflected XSS. CSV has a hazard of its own: a cell beginning with =, +, - or @ is evaluated as a formula when a user opens the export in a spreadsheet, so prefix such values with a single quote when people will open the file, as OWASP's CSV injection page describes.
sections.title: When ?format= beats the Accept header

sections.body: Turn the comparison table into a test against your real router. Include a missing header, curl's */*, a browser's full header, q=0 exclusions, a low q listed first, letter-case variants and a type you do not offer. Assert the status, the media type parsed from Content-Type and Vary: Accept, and decode each body with the matching reader, encoding/json for JSON and encoding/csv for CSV, so a renderer that writes the wrong format with the right header cannot pass. Add cases for ?format=: a valid override with no Vary, and 400 for an unknown value.
sections.title: Test every Accept header you claim to support
sections.walkthrough: This test fragment lives in your service package and runs with go test in your own project; newRouter is the constructor from the first lesson's pattern. Each row names an Accept header and the status and media type you promise for it. mime.ParseMediaType strips the charset parameter so the comparison is about the type alone. The q-value rows and the TEXT/HTML row fail with Gin's NegotiateFormat and pass with the q-aware negotiate function, which is exactly the regression this test exists to catch.

reading.takeaway: Treat Gin's NegotiateFormat as a first-match helper that ignores q-values and letter case, negotiate by q yourself when clients depend on it, answer 406 in your own format, send Vary: Accept on every negotiated response and offer ?format= where URLs must name the representation.

lessons.title: Content negotiation in Gin: what NegotiateFormat really matches, 406 in your format and Vary: Accept

lessons.explanation: A breaking change to a response shape cannot be deployed in place: some clients will keep sending yesterday's requests for months. The route-groups lesson put /v1 and /v2 groups side by side. This lesson adds what makes a second version manageable: a domain type that belongs to neither version, adapters that own each wire shape, standard headers that tell clients when v1 ends, and a route-table test that stops anyone from deleting v1 early.
lessons.objective: Serve two API versions from one service through per-version DTO adapters, mark v1 with Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version links, and test that v1 routes survive until the announced date.

cautions: Group middleware does not run for 404 and 405, so typos carry no Sunset.
Cross-origin clients cannot read the headers without Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
A test that fails because v1 still exists after a date is a date bomb.
designGuide.cost: Two DTO sets and their adapters to maintain until the sunset, one middleware, and a route-table test; the real cost is the months of supporting v1 that the headers announce.
strengths: A bug fix in the service reaches both versions at once.
Clients learn the end date and the replacement from standard headers.
One Retirement value keeps headers and tests in agreement.

alternatives: Once the Deprecation date passes, since it marks the end
As soon as v2 ships, because clients can follow the link
quiz.correct: After its Sunset date, once its remaining traffic is gone
quiz.explanation: Deprecation only discourages the resource and changes no behavior; Sunset is when it may stop responding. The route-table test enforces Sunset, and traffic per route template shows when removal hurts no one.
quiz.hint: One header announces a state; the other announces an end.
quiz.question: A v1 group sends Deprecation and Sunset headers and points to /v2 with successor-version links. When is it safe to delete a v1 route registration?

review.answer: After its Sunset date, once its remaining traffic is gone
review.prompt: When may a v1 route be deleted?

sections.body: Suppose v1 returned a numeric id, a flat author string and a date, and the product now needs string IDs, a nested author object and a full timestamp. Changing the v1 handler breaks every mobile app that has not updated, and those apps update on their users' schedule, not yours. Copying the whole service into a v2 package fails differently: every bug fix now has to land twice, and the copies drift. The stable middle is one application service and one domain type that know nothing about JSON, plus one small adapter per version that maps the domain value to that version's DTO. A v1 handler and a v2 handler differ only in which adapter they call. Additive changes, such as a new optional field, do not need a new version; reserve /v2 for changes an old client cannot ignore. The compatibility lesson in the Go course covers the other half of the problem, when old and new binaries run during one rollout.
sections.title: Version the wire shape, not the service

sections.body: The program keeps one Notes service and registers both groups on one engine. The v1 group carries a deprecated middleware built from a single Retirement value, which also feeds the route-table check, so the headers and the test can never disagree about the dates. The router receives its clock as a function, so the same engine can be asked what it does today and after the sunset.
sections.title: Two adapters, one service, and a v1 group that announces its end
sections.walkthrough: toV1 and toV2 are the only code that knows either wire shape; handlers fetch a Note and pick an adapter. deprecated computes both header values once: Deprecation is a structured-field date, an at sign followed by Unix seconds, and Sunset is an HTTP-date from http.TimeFormat. Per request it looks up the method and c.FullPath(), the route template, in Successors and fills the v2 template with this request's parameters, so /v1/notes/7 links to /v2/notes/7. Once the injected clock passes the sunset, v1 answers 410 Gone but keeps its links. checkRetirement reads r.Routes(): a v1 route missing before the sunset is a finding, after it the removal is allowed, and every successor must be registered.

sections.body: The three headers answer different client questions. Deprecation (RFC 9745) says the resource is deprecated, or will be, as of a date; it changes nothing about how the request is processed. Sunset (RFC 8594) says when the resource is expected to stop responding, and RFC 9745 adds that the sunset should not be earlier than the deprecation date; a sunset in the past means the resource may vanish at any moment. A Link with rel="successor-version" (RFC 5829) names the replacement, and rel="deprecation" points people at migration notes. Set all of them in group middleware before c.Next, because a header added after the handler has started the body is silently not sent. Know what the middleware cannot reach: Gin's 404 and 405 answers run only engine-level middleware, so a mistyped v1 path carries no Sunset. Browsers hide these headers from cross-origin scripts unless the CORS middleware lists them in Access-Control-Expose-Headers. After the sunset, 410 Gone with the successor link is kinder than 404: it tells a client the path was real and where it went.
sections.title: What Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version promise

sections.body: Adapters run in both directions. A v1 POST body should be decoded into a v1 request DTO and translated into the same domain command v2 uses, so validation and side effects stay in one place. Do not implement v1 by calling the v2 handler and rewriting its JSON: you pay two encodings, and v1 quietly inherits every later v2 change, including ones its clients must not see. Watch for semantic changes that no type shows: if v2 reports durations in milliseconds and v1 in seconds, the conversion belongs in toV1 and in a test. A golden test per adapter, with one captured v1 response checked in as a fixture, catches accidental changes to the old shape when someone edits the domain type. Path versioning, as here, is the easiest scheme to route, cache and label in metrics; with header or media-type versioning, every cache key, log query and dashboard has to learn the header too.
sections.title: Keep version differences inside the adapters

sections.body: checkRetirement takes the time as a parameter. Its own unit tests pin dates on both sides of the sunset, as the program does, so their outcome never changes. The guard on the real router passes time.Now(): until the announced date, deleting a v1 route fails CI, and from the sunset on the same test permits the deletion without anyone editing it. The opposite rule, failing the build because v1 still exists after the sunset, is a date bomb that breaks an unrelated pull request on a calendar day. Track the clean-up with traffic instead: count requests by c.FullPath() as the metrics lesson does, and remove the v1 group when its remaining callers are clients you have contacted, not merely when the date passes.
sections.title: A route-table test that cannot become a date bomb
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs in a _test.go file beside newRouter; retirement and seedNotes are the package's own values. The first test guards the real router with the real clock, so it relaxes by itself at the sunset. The second pins both sides of the boundary: an hour before the sunset the deleted list route is exactly one finding, and at the sunset instant, where Before is false, there are none. r.Routes() builds a fresh slice on every call, so DeleteFunc cannot change the engine.

reading.takeaway: Keep the domain version-free and give each version an adapter; put the retirement dates in one value that drives the Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version headers and a route-table test that receives its clock.

lessons.title: API versions in Gin: one service under /v1 and /v2, an adapter per version, and a v1 that announces its sunset

lessons.explanation: An OpenAPI document is a promise that clients, generated SDKs and gateway configurations build on, while the router is what actually answers. Nothing connects the two unless you write the check: a handler added on Friday never reaches the document, an operation deleted from code lingers in the SDK, and a handler that starts returning 422 contradicts a spec that says 400. A small test that reads both sides and prints sorted differences keeps them together.
lessons.objective: Write a test that converts engine.Routes() to OpenAPI path templates, reports routes and operations that exist on only one side, and checks recorded status codes against declared responses.

cautions: Catch-all routes have no faithful OpenAPI template.
Only exercised status codes are compared; 4XX and default accept anything in range.
designGuide.cost: About a hundred lines of test helpers and one recording middleware; it checks paths, methods and codes, not body schemas, which need a separate validator.
strengths: Undocumented routes and dead operations fail CI the day they appear.
Status checks reuse the API test table instead of new fixtures.

alternatives: URL.Path is empty once Gin has matched a route
FullPath includes the query string the spec declares
quiz.correct: It is the route template that matches a spec path key
quiz.explanation: c.FullPath() returns the template, such as /v2/notes/:id, which maps to /v2/notes/{id}; raw paths would give one key per ID. It is empty for unmatched requests, so the middleware skips NoRoute answers.
quiz.hint: Compare /v2/notes/7 with the keys of the paths object.
quiz.question: A drift test records the status of each test call and compares it with the OpenAPI responses. Why key the records by c.FullPath() instead of c.Request.URL.Path?

review.answer: It is the route template that matches a spec path key
review.prompt: Why record FullPath, not URL path?

sections.body: Drift comes in three shapes, and each hurts a different reader. A route missing from the document is invisible to client generators and API gateways that validate requests against the spec, so the new endpoint works in curl and fails behind the gateway. An operation in the document without a route ships as a method in every generated SDK that returns 404 at runtime. A status code the handler sends but the document does not declare breaks clients that switch on declared responses, and generated clients often treat an undeclared code as a decoding error. None of these fail a build by themselves. It does not matter whether the document is written by hand or generated from annotations: annotations drift from handler code in exactly the same ways, because they are comments that nothing executes. The cure is a test that reads both sides.
sections.title: How a document and a router drift apart

sections.body: The program parses a small OpenAPI 3.1 document, builds a router that disagrees with it in three ways, sends the calls an API test table would send, and prints each finding in sorted order. The document is a string constant only so the example fits in one file; the last section embeds the real file.
sections.title: Diff the route table against the document
sections.walkthrough: operations decodes paths into raw path items and reads only the eight HTTP method keys, because a path item can also hold keys such as parameters and summary. template rewrites each Gin segment: :id becomes {id}, *path becomes {path}, and the catch-all is reported. The observed middleware runs after c.Next, keys each response by method and converted c.FullPath(), and skips requests whose FullPath is empty because they matched no route. drift walks the routes against the operations, then each operation's observed statuses against its declared codes, accepting an exact code, a range such as 4XX or default. Map iteration order never reaches stdout, because only the sorted findings are printed.

sections.body: A Gin :param matches one path segment, which is exactly what an OpenAPI {param} means, so the conversion is mechanical, but the names must match: a document that says /notes/{noteId} for the route /notes/:id produces two findings, and that is correct, because generated clients use the parameter name. A catch-all is different. Gin's *path matches several segments and c.Param returns them with a leading slash, while an OpenAPI path parameter value cannot contain an unescaped slash, so no template describes the route faithfully. Either redesign it, for example as a query parameter, or keep it as a reviewed warning, as the program does. Watch the edges as well: OpenAPI method keys are lowercase, a servers URL such as /api is a prefix the router may or may not include, and the redirects and 405 answers Gin generates are not operations. Gin registers no implicit HEAD or OPTIONS routes, so engine.Routes() holds exactly what your code registered and nothing more.
sections.title: Translate Gin paths into OpenAPI templates

sections.body: Matching routes compares structure; status codes need behavior. The recording middleware observes what the handlers really send, and the natural source of calls is the table the API-tests lesson already runs through the real router, so each success and error case contributes its status for free. The check can only judge codes the table exercises: a 409 that no case triggers is never compared, which is one more reason to give every error kind a row. Use ranges such as 4XX and the default response deliberately, because each one accepts codes nobody reviewed. Requests that match no route have an empty FullPath and Gin's NoRoute answers them, so they are skipped rather than reported against an operation. Checking response bodies against the declared schemas is the next step and needs a JSON Schema validator; the problem-details lesson fixes the error body shape, which keeps that check small.
sections.title: Declared codes against observed codes

sections.body: In the service, embed the document so the binary and the test read the same bytes, and serve those bytes at /openapi.json if clients fetch the spec at runtime. Keep the allow-list of undocumented internal routes in the test file, where every exemption is visible in review. Because the findings are sorted, a CI failure is a stable list that diffs cleanly between runs instead of a different order every time.
sections.title: Run it as a test against the embedded document
sections.walkthrough: This fragment spans two files of the package. spec.go embeds openapi.json into the binary; go:embed patterns are relative to the package directory and cannot contain .., so the document lives beside the package or in a small package of its own that exports the bytes. The test replays the shared case table through a router built with the recording middleware, then reports one error per finding. internal is the reviewed allow-list, including the route that serves the document itself.

reading.takeaway: Treat the OpenAPI document as test input: convert engine.Routes() to templates, fail on routes or operations present on one side only, compare observed status codes with declared responses, and print findings sorted.

lessons.title: Keep the OpenAPI document and the Gin router honest: diff routes, operations and status codes in a test

lessons.explanation: A CPU profile or a goroutine dump from a live process can end an incident in minutes, so production services should be able to produce them. The same endpoints in the wrong hands publish the command line, internal function names and memory statistics, and let anyone start a 30-second CPU profile on demand. The safe arrangement is structural: a second Gin engine that serves only diagnostics, hosted by its own http.Server on an address the internet cannot reach.
lessons.objective: Mount net/http/pprof and expvar on an admin-only Gin engine behind a network and token guard, and prove with httptest that the public engine does not serve them.

cautions: A NoRoute fallback to DefaultServeMux leaks pprof with a 404 status.
pprof.Index only works under the exact /debug/pprof/ prefix.
Secrets passed as flags appear in cmdline and expvar output.
designGuide.cost: A second engine, http.Server and listener with their own budgets and shutdown, plus network policy to keep the port private; profiling itself costs CPU while a profile runs.
strengths: Profiles are available during an incident without a redeploy.
The public router cannot leak diagnostics by construction.

alternatives: Gin's engine serves them at /debug/pprof/ automatically
They are registered only for a blank _ import
quiz.correct: Registers /debug/pprof/ handlers on DefaultServeMux
quiz.explanation: Its init calls http.HandleFunc on http.DefaultServeMux, however you import it. Gin never consults that mux, so exposure depends on what serves it: a nil handler, a NoRoute fallback or a second server.
quiz.hint: Look at which mux the package's init function writes to.
quiz.question: A Gin service imports net/http/pprof. Which statement about the pprof handlers is true?

review.answer: Registers /debug/pprof/ handlers on DefaultServeMux

sections.body: The package's init function registers five handlers on http.DefaultServeMux: Index for /debug/pprof/ and the named profiles beneath it, Cmdline, Profile, Symbol and Trace, each with a GET method pattern since Go 1.22. expvar's init does the same for GET /debug/vars and publishes two variables, the command line and runtime memory statistics. The registration happens when the package is linked into the binary, whether you import it with a blank identifier or by name to call pprof.Index, and whether the import is in your code or in a dependency. Each endpoint leaks something: cmdline shows every flag, including any secret passed as one; goroutine?debug=2 prints every stack; profile and trace run the CPU profiler or the execution tracer, with their overhead, for as many seconds as the caller asks. A Gin engine never consults the default mux, so it is safe only as long as nothing else serves that mux.
sections.title: What importing net/http/pprof does to the process

sections.body: The program builds both engines and drives them only with httptest recorders, so no port is opened. It first asks the default mux which pattern would serve the debug paths, then shows the public engine's answers, a leaky variant, and the admin engine behind its guard.
sections.title: An admin engine, a guard, and proof that the public engine is clean
sections.walkthrough: http.DefaultServeMux.Handler reports the patterns GET /debug/pprof/ and GET /debug/vars, registered by the init functions of the two imports. The public engine answers every debug path with Gin's plain 404 body. The leaky engine adds NoRoute(gin.WrapH(http.DefaultServeMux)) and serves the whole pprof index, yet its status is still 404: Gin sets 404 before running NoRoute handlers, and the pprof index never calls WriteHeader. adminOnly checks c.RemoteIP() against the allow-list first, then the bearer token with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare. gin.WrapF adapts each pprof function, gin.WrapH adapts expvar.Handler(), and the decoded expvar JSON shows the custom counter next to the published command line.

sections.body: The leaky engine is the failure worth remembering. Someone adds a NoRoute fallback to the default mux so a legacy http.Handle registration keeps working, and every debug endpoint becomes public. A test that only checks for status 404 still passes, because Gin preset the status before the wrapped handler wrote its body. Assert the body and Content-Type too, for every path pprof and expvar register, as the program does. The other ways to serve the default mux are just as quiet: http.ListenAndServe(addr, nil), a metrics server built without a handler, or a second http.Server whose Handler field was left empty. If a service needs standard-library handlers next to Gin, give them a private http.NewServeMux and mount that, never the default one. A review rule that rejects a nil handler argument, plus the public 404-body test, closes both paths.
sections.title: A 404 status is not proof

sections.body: pprof.Index chooses a profile by cutting the literal prefix /debug/pprof/ from r.URL.Path. Mount it under /admin/debug/pprof/*any and every profile URL returns the HTML index with status 200, which looks like success and contains no profile. Keep the exact prefix on the admin engine, or wrap the handler in http.StripPrefix and gin.WrapH. In Gin 1.12 the :profile parameter route coexists with the static cmdline, profile, symbol and trace routes, and Gin redirects /debug/pprof to /debug/pprof/ with a 301. Profile and Trace extend the connection's write deadline by the requested seconds through http.ResponseController, which works through Gin because its response writer implements Unwrap. Only one CPU profile can run at a time; a second request gets a 500. The block and mutex profiles stay empty until the program calls runtime.SetBlockProfileRate and runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction.
sections.title: Mount pprof at exactly /debug/pprof/

sections.body: A separate listener is the real boundary; the guard is defense in depth. Bind the admin server to loopback and reach it with kubectl port-forward, or bind it to the Pod address on a port that no public Service or ingress selects and that a NetworkPolicy restricts. The guard uses c.RemoteIP(), not c.ClientIP(), because forwarded headers are client input, as the trusted-proxies lesson explains, and nothing should proxy the admin port anyway. Load the token from configuration rather than a flag, since a flag would appear in the cmdline endpoint it protects, and log every admin request.
sections.title: Two servers in one process
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment; listen is a small helper that calls ListenAndServe and treats http.ErrServerClosed as nil. Each engine gets its own http.Server with its own budgets, and the admin WriteTimeout is a floor that pprof raises per request. errgroup ties the two lifetimes together: if either listener fails, ctx is canceled and both servers shut down within one budget, so the process never keeps serving public traffic with its diagnostics gone, or the reverse.

reading.takeaway: Importing pprof or expvar registers handlers on http.DefaultServeMux; serve them only from a separate, guarded admin engine and listener, and test the public engine for a 404 body, not just a 404 status.

lessons.title: Debug endpoints in Gin: pprof and expvar on a separate admin engine and listener, never on the public router

lessons.explanation: The binary you test with go run is not the one you ship. A release build differs in Gin's mode, in what the toolchain stamps into the executable, in how it links and in the image around it. Each difference has a failure attached: request headers in debug logs, an incident where nobody can say which commit is running, a container that will not start because a C library is missing. This lesson follows the build from the mode switch to the final image.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin service for production with release mode, -trimpath, -ldflags -X and CGO_ENABLED=0, report its identity from runtime/debug build info, and package it in a minimal non-root image.

cautions: An unknown GIN_MODE panics in Gin init, before main.
With -trimpath the -ldflags value is absent from build info.
ARG and ENV values are readable in the image history.
designGuide.cost: A few build flags and a two-stage Dockerfile; you give up a shell in the runtime image, so debugging moves to logs, the admin listener and ephemeral debug containers.
strengths: /version answers which commit is running in one request.
A static binary on distroless has a tiny attack surface and no shell.

alternatives: The distroless image has no shell to start the binary
-trimpath removed paths the binary opens at startup
quiz.correct: A cgo build needs a C loader the static image lacks
quiz.explanation: With a C compiler present cgo is on, so net and os/user link dynamically and need a loader such as ld-linux. The static image has none, so exec reports no such file or directory; CGO_ENABLED=0 builds a static binary.
quiz.hint: Ask which file the kernel needs before main can run.
quiz.question: A Gin binary built in the golang image runs on the build host but fails in a distroless static container with "no such file or directory". What is the likely cause?

review.answer: A cgo build needs a C loader the static image lacks

sections.body: Gin reads GIN_MODE once, in its package init, and an empty value means debug, or test under go test. Debug mode prints the route table and warnings to stdout, re-parses templates loaded with LoadHTMLGlob on every render, and when Recovery catches a panic it logs the request's headers with only Authorization masked, so cookies and API-key headers reach the logs. Release mode drops all of that. An unknown value is not ignored: GIN_MODE=production makes SetMode panic inside Gin's init, before main runs and before your logger exists. Pick one owner for the mode. Either the deployment sets GIN_MODE=release and nothing calls SetMode, or validated configuration calls gin.SetMode before any engine is built, as the config-startup lesson does, and GIN_MODE stays unset. Two owners eventually disagree.
sections.title: What Gin's debug mode does in production

sections.body: debug.ReadBuildInfo returns the running binary's own record, which differs on every build, so the program parses a fixed record in the same text format with debug.ParseBuildInfo. It also validates a mode setting, shows what SetMode does with an unknown value, and serves /version twice: as go run links it, and with a version string as -ldflags -X would set it.
sections.title: Report the build identity at /version
sections.walkthrough: ginMode accepts the three names Gin knows and maps an empty setting to release, the opposite of Gin's own default. SetMode panics on anything else, and recover turns that into a printed line here. ParseBuildInfo reads the path, mod, dep and build lines but skips the go line, because ReadBuildInfo fills GoVersion from runtime.Version() separately, so the program sets it by hand. versionFrom prefers the linked string, falls back to the main module version, which go build derives from a VCS tag or reports as (devel), and copies vcs.revision, vcs.time and vcs.modified. Cache-Control: no-store stops caches from reporting a previous deploy's identity.

sections.body: -trimpath removes the build machine's directories from file names recorded in the binary, so stack traces do not reveal home directories and builds from different checkouts match. -ldflags "-X main.version=..." sets a package-level string variable at link time; for other packages it needs the full import path, it works only on a variable that is uninitialized or initialized to a constant string, and a misspelled name is silently ignored, which is why /version should be checked after every build. -s -w drop the symbol table and DWARF data: panics and pprof still name functions because they use the runtime's own tables, but a debugger has less to work with. CGO_ENABLED=0 matters because the golang image has a C compiler, so cgo is on by default and net and os/user link against the system C library.
sections.code:
VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty)
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
  go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=${VERSION}" -o bin/api ./cmd/api
go version -m bin/api | grep -E 'vcs\.|CGO_ENABLED|trimpath'
file bin/api
sections.title: Build flags that make the binary honest
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own checkout. git describe prints a tag-based version with a -dirty suffix when the tree has uncommitted changes. go version -m prints the record the /version handler reads; expect vcs.revision, vcs.time, vcs.modified, CGO_ENABLED=0 and -trimpath=true. One surprise: with -trimpath, go build leaves -ldflags out of that record, because linker flags can contain local paths, so the -X value is visible only through the variable it set. file should report a statically linked executable.

sections.body: The containers lesson builds a basic two-stage image on scratch. For a Gin API, the distroless static image is a better default runtime: it adds CA certificates for outbound TLS, time zone data, an /etc/passwd with a nonroot user and a /tmp directory, and still has no shell or package manager. A cgo-linked binary fails in it with a confusing no such file or directory, because the missing file is the dynamic loader, not your program. Use a numeric USER: when a Pod sets runAsNonRoot without a runAsUser, Kubernetes can verify only a numeric image user and refuses to start a container whose image names one. If .dockerignore excludes .git, as it usually should, go build has no VCS data inside the build, the vcs fields are empty and the version is (devel), so CI passes the version in as a build argument.
sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
ARG VERSION=dev
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -trimpath \
    -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=${VERSION}" -o /out/api ./cmd/api

# Pin the digest you reviewed: static-debian12:nonroot@sha256:...
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
USER 65532:65532
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
sections.title: A multi-stage image with a distroless, non-root runtime
sections.walkthrough: This Dockerfile runs in your own environment: docker build --build-arg VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty) -t notes-api:dev . The build stage holds the toolchain, module cache and source; only /out/api crosses into the runtime stage. Cache mounts keep downloads and compiled packages between builds without storing them in any layer. The exec-form ENTRYPOINT makes the binary PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM directly, which the rolling-deploys lesson relies on.

sections.body: Anything in a layer or in the image config is readable by everyone who can pull the image, forever. ARG and ENV values are recorded in the image history, so a token passed as a build argument is published; private module credentials belong in a BuildKit secret mount used by a single RUN step and never written to a layer. Environment-specific settings, such as database URLs, tokens, trusted proxy ranges or a debug mode, come from the orchestrator at runtime, so the same digest can be promoted from staging to production as the delivery lesson requires. The source tree, .git, .env files, fixtures and local binaries stay out through .dockerignore. Decide what /version itself may reveal: version, revision, commit time and the modified flag help operators, while hostnames, environment values or the full dependency list help attackers. A production response with modified true is itself a finding: someone shipped uncommitted code.
sections.title: What must not be baked into the image

reading.takeaway: Ship with release mode set by one owner, -trimpath, CGO_ENABLED=0 and a -X version; report vcs.revision, vcs.time and vcs.modified from build info at /version, and run as a numeric non-root user with no secrets in any layer.

lessons.title: Shipping a Gin binary: release mode, a /version endpoint from build info, static builds and a non-root image

lessons.explanation: During a rolling deploy every old replica is told to stop while traffic is still arriving. Calling Shutdown the moment SIGTERM lands closes the listener before every load balancer has heard the replica is leaving, and the requests they still send meet a refused connection. The fix is an ordered sequence with one owner, and because it is about time and ordering, it should be modeled with an injected clock and tested like any other code.
lessons.objective: Implement and test a SIGTERM sequence that flips readiness to 503, keeps serving while load balancers stop routing, disables keep-alives, and shuts the http.Server down within a grace period the platform honors.

cautions: Delay plus budget must fit inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Shutdown does not wait for hijacked connections or streams.
A main that returns when ListenAndServe does cuts the drain short.
designGuide.cost: Every Pod termination takes the drain delay plus in-flight time, which lengthens each rollout; the code is one Lifecycle flag, one Drain function and a grace period to keep in sync.
strengths: Rollouts complete without refused connections or cut requests.
An injected clock makes the sequence testable in milliseconds.

alternatives: Shutdown cancels in-flight requests unless it is delayed
SIGTERM arrives before the replacement Pod has started
quiz.correct: Load balancers still route until endpoint removal spreads
quiz.explanation: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM start together, and proxies learn of the removal late. Shutdown closes the listener at once, refusing connections still routed to the Pod; a short serving delay covers that window.
quiz.hint: Think about who still believes the old Pod is a valid target.
quiz.question: On SIGTERM a Gin service calls http.Server.Shutdown at once, and during rolling deploys some clients see connection refused. Why does a short drain delay before Shutdown fix this?

review.answer: Load balancers still route until endpoint removal spreads

sections.body: When Kubernetes deletes a Pod, two things start in parallel: the control plane removes the Pod's endpoints from its Services, and the kubelet runs any preStop hook and then sends SIGTERM. The endpoint change then has to reach every kube-proxy, ingress controller and cloud load balancer, which takes from milliseconds to several seconds. A process that closes its listener at once refuses connections routed during that window; one that exits drops requests mid-flight; and clients holding keep-alive connections keep reusing the old Pod's sockets. Kubernetes already marks a terminating Pod's endpoints not ready, so for a plain Service the readiness flip mostly confirms what the control plane did. It matters for load balancers and ingress controllers that health-check the Pod directly, and EndpointSlices still publish the probe result as their serving condition. The drain delay is what covers propagation. The server-lifecycle lesson sets the budgets; this one orders the steps.
sections.title: The window where requests get dropped

sections.body: Drain depends only on interfaces: a Clock with After, and the three methods of *http.Server it calls. The model supplies a clock that moves only when told and a server that runs the Gin engine through httptest recorders and refuses requests once Shutdown has closed its listener. main narrates two runs: a slow export that finishes inside the budget, and one that does not.
sections.title: Model the sequence with a fake clock and a fake server
sections.walkthrough: Drain waits for sigterm to close, stores the draining flag that Lifecycle.Readyz reads, disables keep-alives, and only then asks the clock for the delay, so the step message proves the timer exists before main advances. During the delay /readyz answers 503 while /orders is still served, with Connection: close as net/http adds when keep-alives are off. After Advance(5s), Drain registers the budget timer and calls Shutdown; the fake closes its listener, so the next request is refused, and waits for in-flight requests. In the first run the export finishes and Shutdown returns nil. In the second, Advance(20s) fires the budget, the watcher cancels the context and Drain falls back to Close. main prints every line after a channel receive, so scheduling never changes the order.

sections.body: Readiness goes first because it is the only signal some balancers act on; return 503, since Kubernetes HTTP probes count every status from 200 to 399 as success, and keep liveness at 200 throughout, as the metrics-health lesson explains. The delay should exceed a direct health checker's probe period times its failure threshold plus endpoint propagation; five to ten seconds is common, and every Pod in a rollout pays it. SetKeepAlivesEnabled(false) closes idle HTTP/1.1 connections at once and makes each active one close after its current response; HTTP/2 connections get a GOAWAY when their last open stream finishes. Shutdown disables keep-alives too, so the explicit call matters only during the delay, which is the point: clients reconnect while the listener still accepts, and the balancer sends the new connections elsewhere. Shutdown closes listeners and idle connections, then waits for active ones; it does not wait for hijacked connections, and an open Server-Sent Events stream simply holds it until the budget expires, so register a RegisterOnShutdown function that tells streaming handlers to finish.
sections.title: Why the order is readiness, keep-alives, delay, Shutdown

sections.body: Nothing in Drain changes for production. A real clock adapts time.After, *http.Server already has SetKeepAlivesEnabled, Shutdown and Close, and the Lifecycle value is injected into the Gin handler like any other dependency, so the model's tests keep covering the code that ships. The one new obligation is in main, which must not return while the drain is still running.
sections.title: Wire the same Drain to a real signal and server
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment. signal.Stop after the first signal restores default handling, so a second Ctrl-C ends a stuck drain at once. The comment marks the classic bug: ListenAndServe returns http.ErrServerClosed the moment Shutdown begins, and a main that returns then exits with requests still running. If ListenAndServe fails for another reason, such as a port already in use, serve returns that error immediately. Do not derive request contexts from the signal, as the config-startup lesson warns.

sections.body: The grace period countdown starts when the Pod is deleted, before any preStop hook runs, and SIGKILL arrives when it ends, whatever the process is doing. Keep the arithmetic true whenever the delay or budget changes: delay plus Shutdown budget plus the time to close pools and flush telemetry must fit inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds. A preStop sleep is the other place a delay can live, useful when you cannot change the application, but it counts against the same grace period, so never stack it on top of an in-app delay by accident. Pair the sequence with a rollout strategy that keeps capacity, such as maxUnavailable 0 with a surge, as the rollout lesson describes. To verify it in a real cluster, run steady load through kubectl rollout restart and count errors; the target is zero, and the model keeps the ordering from regressing.
sections.code:
# Pod template fragment: merge into a Deployment in your own cluster.
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 35   # delay 5s + Shutdown budget 20s + margin
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: registry.example.com/notes-api@sha256:<digest>
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: {path: /readyz, port: 8080}
        periodSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 1
      # Only if the app cannot delay on SIGTERM itself. Distroless images have
      # no shell, so use the sleep action, not exec: ["sleep", "5"].
      # lifecycle:
      #   preStop:
      #     sleep:
      #       seconds: 5
sections.title: Fit the sequence inside the Pod's grace period
sections.walkthrough: Apply this in your own cluster, not in the app. The comment beside terminationGracePeriodSeconds is the budget to recheck on every change. A 2-second probe period with failureThreshold 1 lets anything polling /readyz see the 503 well within the 5-second delay. The commented preStop block is the alternative owner of the delay; the sleep action needs Kubernetes 1.30 or newer, where it is enabled by default, and an exec sleep would fail in an image without a shell.

reading.takeaway: On SIGTERM flip readiness to 503, disable keep-alives and keep serving through a drain delay, then Shutdown within a budget and Close after it; fit delay plus budget inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds and wait for the drain before main returns.

lessons.title: Surviving a rolling deploy in Gin: fail readiness, keep serving through a drain delay, then Shutdown

summary: Upstream clients, retries and circuit breakers, compression, ranged downloads, content negotiation, versioning, contract tests, admin endpoints, release builds and rolling deploys.
title: Gin in the wider system
translationNote: Upstreams, listeners and signals are modeled in-process. Real deployments, load balancers and clusters belong to your own environment.

lessons.explanation: A blockchain's first job is evidence, not consensus: if a past record changes, the change must show. Each block stores the hash of its predecessor, so editing one block breaks the link that points at it. That guarantee holds only when every party hashes the same bytes for the same block, and only when the newest hash is kept somewhere the editor cannot rewrite.
lessons.objective: Link blocks with SHA-256 over a canonical byte encoding, verify the chain from genesis and report the first link that breaks.

cautions: Without a trusted tip, a rewritten chain verifies cleanly.
Re-serializing JSON before hashing breaks honest data.
designGuide.cost: One hash per block to write and to verify, an encoding you can never change casually, and a separate place to keep the trusted tip.
strengths: Any edit to history changes the tip hash.
Verification is linear and needs only the standard library.

alternatives: The first broken link that the verifier reports
Nothing, because consistent links prove integrity
quiz.correct: A trusted copy of the tip hash from before the edit
quiz.explanation: The tip hash commits to all of history. Relinking produces a different tip, so a copy held outside the attacker's reach no longer matches even though every internal link checks out.
quiz.hint: Compare what the attacker can recompute with what the attacker cannot reach.
quiz.question: An attacker edits an old block and recomputes every later hash so that all links verify again. What still exposes the edit?

review.answer: A trusted copy of the tip hash from before the edit

sections.body: A database row or a log line can be updated in place, and nothing about its neighbors changes. A hash pointer removes that silence. Block n stores H(block n-1), where H is SHA-256, a function for which no one knows how to find two different inputs with the same output. Change one byte of an old block and its hash changes, so the pointer stored in the next block no longer matches. This is tamper evidence, not tamper prevention: the bytes can still be edited, but a verifier notices. The rest of this unit adds the other pieces in order: Merkle trees commit to many transactions at once, signatures say who authorized them, proof of work makes extending the chain expensive, and fork choice decides which extension counts.
sections.title: Why a stored hash exposes an edit

sections.body: The program defines a block as a height, the previous block's hash and a payload. encode turns a block into bytes with a fixed field order, big-endian fixed-width integers and a length prefix in front of the variable payload; hash is sha256.Sum256 over exactly those bytes. firstBrokenLink checks every block against its predecessor and returns the first height where either the height sequence or the hash pointer fails. The run records the tip, edits an old payload, and then plays an attacker who rewrites every later pointer.
sections.title: Build and verify a chain with crypto/sha256
sections.walkthrough: build starts from the all-zero hash for genesis and feeds each block's hash into the next block. After the payload at height 1 changes, height 2 is the first block whose Prev no longer equals hash(chain[1]), so the verifier reports 2 rather than a bare false. Rewriting Prev at heights 2 and 3 makes every link consistent again, so the chain on its own looks valid; only the comparison with the tip recorded before the edit exposes it. The printed values are the first four bytes of each 32-byte digest.

sections.body: The hash covers bytes, not meaning. Two nodes that agree a block says alice pays bob 5 but serialize it differently compute different hashes and then disagree about the whole chain. encode avoids that by construction, and its length prefix also removes ambiguity at field boundaries: without it, a payload "ab" followed by a field "c" and a payload "a" followed by "bc" would hash identical bytes. Text formats are where this usually goes wrong. JSON objects are unordered, whitespace is insignificant, a number has several spellings (5, 5.0, 5e0), and Go's encoding/json adds its own choices: it sorts map keys, writes struct fields in declaration order and escapes <, > and & unless told otherwise.
sections.title: Pick one byte encoding and never let it drift
sections.walkthrough: The three literal strings decode to the same object yet print three different digests, 8cd4d93c, 560a0696 and 39350022, so a verifier that re-serializes before hashing accepts or rejects data depending on which form it happens to produce. json.Marshal sorts the map keys and writes the memo as a\u003cb; an Encoder with SetEscapeHTML(false) writes a<b and appends a newline, trimmed here. Both outputs are valid JSON, and neither is a hashing format unless one canonicalization scheme, such as RFC 8785, is applied everywhere.

sections.body: The relinking step in the first program is the realistic attack. Whoever can rewrite one block can usually recompute every later hash in microseconds. What the chain buys you is that one 32-byte value, the tip hash, commits to the entire history, so protecting history reduces to protecting that value. Publish it, sign it, store it in a system with different administrators, or make producing a replacement expensive, which is what proof of work and proof of stake do later in this unit. Audit logs, release manifests and blockchains share this structure and differ in who is trusted to produce or hold the tip. When verification fails, report the first broken height and treat every later block as unverified until it is checked against a trusted tip again; an operator needs to know which record and which neighbor disagree.
sections.title: Anchor the tip, or the chain proves nothing

sections.body: Check in known-answer vectors: a fixed block and its expected digest, so a refactor that reorders fields or changes an integer width fails a test instead of silently forking your history. Mutate each field in turn and assert that the hash changes. Fuzz pairs of blocks with go test -fuzz and assert that different blocks never encode to the same bytes, which catches a missing length prefix. Keep a single encode function shared by writer and verifier; two implementations of one format is how nodes come to disagree. Test the verifier on an empty chain, a lone genesis block, a height gap and an edited genesis. SHA-256 appears here because it is in the standard library; Ethereum uses Keccak-256, a different function, as the signing-boundaries lesson explains.
sections.title: Test the encoding like a consensus rule

reading.takeaway: Hash one canonical byte encoding of each block, verify every link from genesis, report the first break, and keep the trusted tip hash out of reach of anyone who can edit the data.

lessons.title: Hash chains: every block commits to the exact bytes of the block before it

lessons.explanation: A block header cannot carry every transaction, but it can carry one 32-byte Merkle root that commits to all of them. A client that trusts the header can then check that a particular transaction is included from a handful of sibling hashes instead of the whole block. The tree shape and hashing rules are consensus rules, and two classic mistakes let different transaction lists produce the same root.
lessons.objective: Build a domain-separated Merkle tree, generate and verify inclusion proofs, and explain the duplicate-leaf and second-preimage pitfalls.

cautions: Duplicating odd nodes lets two different lists share a root.
A root taken from the same untrusted response proves nothing.
designGuide.cost: About 2n hashes to build the tree and log2(n) per proof, plus a tree shape that becomes a frozen consensus rule once roots are published.
strengths: A proof costs about log2(n) hashes, not the whole block.
Verification needs only the leaf, index, size and a trusted root.

alternatives: Two lists sharing a root when the last leaf is duplicated
Finding SHA-256 preimages by brute force
quiz.correct: So no interior node can pose as a leaf
quiz.explanation: Without prefixes, H(left || right) is also the leaf hash of the 64-byte string left || right, so a shorter forged list reaches the same root. Prefixes make leaf and node inputs disjoint; the odd-leaf rule is a separate fix.
quiz.hint: Think about what a 64-byte leaf made of two sibling hashes would hash to.
quiz.question: A Merkle tree hashes leaves as H(data) and interior nodes as H(left || right). Which attack do distinct leaf and node prefixes stop?

review.answer: So no interior node can pose as a leaf

sections.body: The previous lesson chained blocks. Inside a block the problem is different: thousands of transactions, and a wallet or indexer that wants to check one of them without downloading the rest. A Merkle tree hashes each transaction into a leaf, then hashes pairs of nodes level by level until one root remains, and the header stores only that root. To prove leaf i, the prover sends the sibling at each level on the path from the leaf to the root, and the verifier recomputes the path and compares. For n leaves that is about log2(n) hashes, so 20 hashes cover a million transactions. A proof shows that the leaf is committed by this root; it says nothing about whether the header itself is canonical, which is the job of the chain and fork-choice lessons.
sections.title: One root for many transactions

sections.body: The program hashes leaves with a 0x00 prefix and interior nodes with a 0x01 prefix, and promotes a lone last node to the next level unchanged instead of pairing it with a copy of itself. prove collects one sibling per level when one exists; verify walks up from the leaf and uses the claimed index and the tree size to decide, at every level, whether the sibling sits left or right. The second half builds the classic tree, with no prefixes and duplication of the last hash, to show what the two rules prevent.
sections.title: Build, prove and verify in Go
sections.walkthrough: With five leaves, leaf 2 needs three siblings: leaf 3, the hash of leaves 0 and 1, and leaf 4, which was promoted from below. A changed leaf or a claimed index of 3 recomputes a different path and fails. verify derives each direction from index and size instead of trusting flags inside the proof, and it rejects proofs with too few or too many hashes. naiveRoot gives [a b c] and [a b c c] one root and accepts two 64-byte forged leaves built from interior hashes; the separated tree rejects both. Promotion yields the same tree shape as RFC 6962, which splits at the largest power of two below n.

sections.body: Bitcoin's tree pairs an odd last hash with a copy of itself, so the transaction lists [a, b, c] and [a, b, c, c] produce the same root, exactly as naiveRoot shows. This became CVE-2012-2459. The list with the repeated transaction is an invalid block, but its header hash equals the honest block's. A node that received the mutated version first, rejected it and remembered the header hash as invalid would then refuse the honest block too. Bitcoin Core now detects the mutation while computing the root and treats the block as malformed rather than marking the header invalid, and the comment above its Merkle code warns new designs not to copy the algorithm. In your own trees, promote the lone node or use the RFC 6962 split, and include the leaf count in whatever you sign or publish next to the root.
sections.title: The duplicate-last-leaf trap

sections.body: Without domain separation an interior node is SHA-256 of 64 bytes and a leaf is SHA-256 of arbitrary bytes. Anyone who knows two sibling hashes can present their 64-byte concatenation as a leaf, and the shorter, forged list reaches the same root: that is the second-preimage result in the program. Prefixing leaves with 0x00 and nodes with 0x01, as Certificate Transparency does in RFC 6962, makes the two kinds of input disjoint, so no interior node can satisfy a leaf proof. Bitcoin's tree has no such separation, and its known ambiguity around 64-byte transactions follows from that. Ethereum headers use Merkle-Patricia tries for transactions, receipts and state rather than this binary tree, and eth_getProof (EIP-1186) returns account and storage proofs. The principle is the same: verify the proof against a root you already trust, never against a root delivered in the same response.
sections.title: Separate leaves from interior nodes

sections.body: Take the root from a header you have already validated. Bind the index and tree size into verification so a proof for one position cannot be replayed for another. Reject proofs that are too long or too short instead of ignoring extra hashes. Hash leaves from their canonical bytes, as in the hash-chain lesson. Test every index for many sizes, including 1 and powers of two plus and minus one; a wrong index; swapped sibling order; truncated and extended proofs; and a leaf whose bytes equal an interior node. Fuzz verify with random proofs and require that it never panics. These tests are cheap: checking every index and every wrong index for all sizes from 1 to 40 runs in well under a second.
sections.title: Review checklist for proof code

reading.takeaway: Prefix leaves and interior nodes differently, never duplicate an odd node, and verify a proof from the leaf, its index and the tree size against a root you already trust.

lessons.title: Merkle proofs: show one transaction is in a block with about log2(n) hashes

lessons.explanation: A hash chain shows that data changed; a signature shows who approved it. Ethereum and Bitcoin use ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve, and Ethereum appends a recovery byte so that a verifier can compute the signer's public key from the signature instead of receiving it. Recovery always produces some key, so the code that matters is the comparison with the address you expected and the checks that reject malleable signatures.
lessons.objective: Sign a Keccak-256 digest with go-ethereum's crypto package, recover and check the signer's address, and enforce the low-s rule on untrusted signatures.

cautions: Recovery returns some key for any digest; compare the address.
SigToPub and Ecrecover accept high-s twins; validate values first.
designGuide.cost: One Keccak-256 and one public-key recovery per verification, plus explicit normalization of v at every boundary that accepts signatures.
strengths: The signer is computed, so no public key travels with the data.
Deterministic RFC 6979 nonces make signing reproducible in tests.

alternatives: Comparing the recovered address with the expected one
crypto.Ecrecover, which returns an error for high s
quiz.correct: ValidateSignatureValues with homestead true
quiz.explanation: Both signatures recover the same key, so the address comparison passes. ValidateSignatureValues(v, r, s, true) applies EIP-2's s <= N/2 rule, the same check go-ethereum's transaction signers run before recovery.
quiz.hint: Recovery succeeds for both; look for the function that compares s with half the curve order.
quiz.question: crypto.SigToPub recovers the same signer from a signature (r, s) and its twin (r, N-s). Which check rejects the twin before you trust it?

review.answer: ValidateSignatureValues with homestead true

sections.body: crypto.Sign returns 65 bytes: r and s, 32 bytes each, followed by a recovery id v of 0 or 1. r and s form an ordinary ECDSA signature; v tells the recovery algorithm which candidate curve point the signer used, so crypto.SigToPub and crypto.Ecrecover return exactly one public key. That is why an Ethereum transaction carries no public key and no from field: the sender is computed from the signature. The byte encoding of v varies by context. Legacy transactions store 27 or 28, EIP-155 transactions store chainID*2+35 or +36, typed transactions store a yParity of 0 or 1, and personal_sign signatures usually end in 27 or 28. Normalize to 0 or 1 at the boundary before calling the crypto package, and leave transaction encodings to the signers in core/types.
sections.title: What a recoverable signature contains

sections.body: The program derives a test key from 32 bytes of 0x01, a well-known throwaway value that must never hold funds, and it never contacts a network. It signs a Keccak-256 digest, recovers the public key, then edits the message and recovers again. Finally it builds the mirror-image signature (r, N-s) with the recovery bit flipped, where N is the curve order, and runs it through the checks go-ethereum offers.
sections.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"

	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/crypto"
)

func main() {
	// TEST KEY ONLY: fixed bytes, never funded, never used on a real network.
	key, err := crypto.ToECDSA(bytes.Repeat([]byte{1}, 32))
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	signer := crypto.PubkeyToAddress(key.PublicKey)
	fmt.Println("test signer:", signer.Hex())

	if _, err := crypto.Sign([]byte("not a digest"), key); err != nil {
		fmt.Println("raw message:", err)
	}

	digest := crypto.Keccak256([]byte("chain 1337: pay bob 5, nonce 7"))
	sig, err := crypto.Sign(digest, key)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	again, _ := crypto.Sign(digest, key)
	fmt.Println("signature:", len(sig), "bytes, v =", sig[64], "deterministic:", bytes.Equal(sig, again))

	pub, err := crypto.SigToPub(digest, sig)
	fmt.Println("recovered == signer:", err == nil && crypto.PubkeyToAddress(*pub) == signer)

	edited := crypto.Keccak256([]byte("chain 1337: pay bob 500, nonce 7"))
	other, err := crypto.SigToPub(edited, sig)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println("edited message: no error, recovered == signer:", crypto.PubkeyToAddress(*other) == signer)

	// Build the high-s twin (r, N-s) with the recovery bit flipped.
	n := crypto.S256().Params().N
	r := new(big.Int).SetBytes(sig[:32])
	s := new(big.Int).SetBytes(sig[32:64])
	twinS := new(big.Int).Sub(n, s)
	twin := make([]byte, 65)
	copy(twin, sig[:32])
	twinS.FillBytes(twin[32:64])
	twin[64] = sig[64] ^ 1

	twinPub, err := crypto.SigToPub(digest, twin)
	fmt.Println("twin recovers signer:", err == nil && crypto.PubkeyToAddress(*twinPub) == signer)
	pubBytes := crypto.FromECDSAPub(&key.PublicKey)
	fmt.Println("low-s rule accepts original:", crypto.ValidateSignatureValues(sig[64], r, s, true),
		"twin:", crypto.ValidateSignatureValues(twin[64], r, twinS, true))
	fmt.Println("VerifySignature original:", crypto.VerifySignature(pubBytes, digest, sig[:64]),
		"twin:", crypto.VerifySignature(pubBytes, digest, twin[:64]))
}
sections.title: Sign and recover with a fixed test key
sections.walkthrough: crypto.Sign refuses the 12-byte string because it requires exactly 32 bytes, so callers must hash first. Signing the same digest twice yields identical bytes because the nonce is derived from the key and the digest as in RFC 6979, with no random source. SigToPub on the edited digest returns no error and a valid but different public key; only the address comparison catches it. The twin recovers the same signer, so recovery alone does not make signatures unique. ValidateSignatureValues with homestead set to true and VerifySignature both reject the twin because its s is above N/2.

sections.body: ECDSA signs a number smaller than the curve order, so it needs fixed-size input; Ethereum uses Keccak-256 and Bitcoin uses double SHA-256. Size is the smaller reason. The go-ethereum documentation for Sign warns that the hash must not be chosen by an adversary. A service that signs whatever 32 bytes a caller supplies is a signing oracle, and those bytes may be the hash of a transaction that spends the service's funds. Hash your own structured message with a prefix that says what it is: accounts.TextHash implements the EIP-191 prefix "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" plus the message length, and EIP-712 hashes typed data under a domain. The signing-boundaries lesson covers key custody and domain policy; the rule at the primitive level is that the signer owns the hashing step.
sections.title: Why you sign a digest, never raw input

sections.body: For every valid ECDSA signature (r, s), the pair (r, N-s) is also valid for the same key and message. If any part of a system identifies data by the hash of its signed bytes, a third party can flip s and produce a second valid encoding with a different identifier, without the key. Bitcoin suffered this as transaction-ID malleability, and Ethereum's Homestead upgrade (EIP-2) made transactions with s above N/2 invalid. In go-ethereum the rule is crypto.ValidateSignatureValues(v, r, s, homestead), which the transaction signers call before recovering, and VerifySignature also rejects high s. Ecrecover and SigToPub do not, and EIP-2 deliberately left the on-chain ecrecover precompile accepting high s, so contracts must check it too. When you accept signatures from users, for logins or off-chain orders, validate the values yourself and never key a record by signature bytes.
sections.title: Malleability and the low-s rule

sections.body: Keep the test key fixed and labeled, and assert known answers: the 0x01-repeated key has the address 0x1a642f0E3c3aF545E7AcBD38b07251B3990914F1, so a regression in key derivation fails at once. Write negative tests for a wrong digest, a wrong expected address, the high-s twin, v outside 0 and 1, r or s equal to zero or N, a 64-byte signature without v and a digest of the wrong length. If you ship builds with and without cgo, run the suite both ways: go-ethereum uses the decred secp256k1 package when cgo is off and libsecp256k1 when it is on, and your checks should not depend on which one recovered the key. Prefer fixed vectors to crypto.GenerateKey in tests so that every failure is reproducible.
sections.title: Test the verifier, not just the signer

reading.takeaway: Sign only digests you computed, recover the key and compare its address with the one you expected, and reject high-s or malformed values with ValidateSignatureValues before trusting a signature.

lessons.title: secp256k1 signatures: sign a 32-byte digest, recover the signer and reject high-s twins

lessons.explanation: An Ethereum address is neither a public key nor a name. It is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of an uncompressed public key, written as 40 hex digits. Those digits carry no error detection unless their letter case follows EIP-55, so a validator has to decide what it accepts before value moves: the format, the checksum, and whether the zero address can ever be a destination.
lessons.objective: Derive an address from a public key, produce and check EIP-55 checksums, and validate user-supplied addresses, including the zero address.

cautions: HexToAddress pads, crops and never fails.
Lowercase input and missing JSON fields carry no protection.
designGuide.cost: One Keccak-256 per check and a documented decision about lowercase input, applied the same way at every boundary.
strengths: Mixed-case checksums catch almost all typos at no extra length.
One parser at each boundary makes the policy reviewable.

alternatives: Lowercase input always fails the EIP-55 check
HexToAddress returns an error for the typo
quiz.correct: None; a typo just names another valid address
quiz.explanation: EIP-55 hides the checksum in letter case. An all-lowercase string has no case information, so it is valid unchecked hex, and a changed digit simply names a different 20-byte account.
quiz.hint: Where does EIP-55 keep its check bits?
quiz.question: Why can an EIP-55 validator not catch a mistyped digit in an all-lowercase address?

review.answer: None; a typo just names another valid address

sections.body: The signatures lesson recovered a public key: an uncompressed secp256k1 point serialized as 0x04 followed by the 32-byte X and Y coordinates. Ethereum drops the 0x04 prefix, hashes the 64 coordinate bytes with Keccak-256 and keeps the last 20 bytes. crypto.PubkeyToAddress does exactly that, and so does go-ethereum's transaction sender recovery. The mapping is one-way, so an address never yields a key, and not every address belongs to a key at all: a contract's address comes from its creator's address and nonce (CREATE) or from a salt and the init code hash (CREATE2), and nothing in the 20 bytes says which kind you are looking at. Ask the chain for the code at that address when the difference matters.
sections.title: From public key to address

sections.body: The program derives the test key's address by hand and compares it with PubkeyToAddress, re-implements the EIP-55 rule and compares it with common.Address.Hex, then feeds six inputs through parseAddress. That validator requires the 0x prefix and exactly 40 hex digits, enforces the checksum when the input mixes cases, and rejects the zero address. The last three lines show library behavior that regularly surprises reviewers.
sections.title: Derive, checksum and validate in one program
sections.walkthrough: eip55 hashes the 40 lowercase ASCII hex characters, not the 20 raw bytes, and uppercases a letter when its nibble in that hash is 8 or more; digits never change. The flipped input differs from the signer only in the case of one letter and is rejected. The lowercase typo is accepted and names a different account, because lowercase input carries no checksum. MixedcaseAddress.ValidChecksum compares the input with Hex(), so it reports false for any all-lowercase input. A JSON body without a to field, and HexToAddress given non-hex text, both produce the zero address with no error.

sections.body: EIP-55 stores its checksum in letter case: each of the letters a to f is uppercase exactly when the matching nibble of the hash is 8 or more. An address carries about 15 check bits on average, and the EIP estimates that a mistyped checksummed address passes by accident about 0.0247% of the time. An all-lowercase or all-uppercase string has no case information, so EIP-55 treats it as unchecked, and most wallets accept it. Your service has to choose: accept lowercase from machines that produced it, such as an RPC response or your own database, but for destinations a person typed or pasted, require the checksummed form or add a confirmation step. Always display addresses with Hex() so that whatever people copy is checksummed. A few networks use EIP-1191, which mixes the chain ID into the checksum, so a valid case pattern there can fail plain EIP-55.
sections.title: What EIP-55 protects and what it cannot

sections.body: common.HexToAddress never fails. It strips an optional prefix, decodes what hex it can, and pads or crops to 20 bytes, so 0x1234 becomes an address ending in 1234 and garbage becomes the zero address; the abi-calls lesson already warned that it converts rather than validates. common.IsHexAddress checks length and digits but accepts input without a prefix or with 0X and ignores case. Address.UnmarshalJSON requires the prefix and 40 digits but not the checksum, and a missing field leaves the zero value. Put one parser like parseAddress at every boundary: HTTP handlers, CLI flags and configuration. Give the zero address an explicit policy, too. ERC-20 tokens emit it as the sender of a mint and conventionally as the recipient of a burn, and many token contracts reject transfers to it, so as a payout destination it almost always means a missing value rather than an intent.
sections.title: Parsing is not validation

sections.body: Use the mixed-case vectors published in EIP-55, such as 0x5aAeb6053F3E94C9b9A09f33669435E7Ef1BeAed, as known answers for both Hex() and your parser. Add cases for a missing prefix, an uppercase 0X prefix, 39 and 41 digits, non-hex characters, surrounding whitespace, an all-uppercase body, the zero address, and a lowercase address with one digit changed, which passes format checks and must then be caught by an allow-list or a confirmation step downstream. Store addresses as 20 raw bytes or as the canonical Hex() string, never in whatever case the user typed, so that equality checks and unique indexes do not depend on letter case.
sections.title: Test the validator at its edges

reading.takeaway: Derive addresses with PubkeyToAddress, display them with Hex(), and validate input with one explicit parser that checks prefix, length, the checksum on mixed case and the zero address.

lessons.title: Ethereum addresses: 20 bytes of Keccak-256, an EIP-55 checksum and strict input validation

lessons.explanation: Every ledger must answer one question before it accepts a payment: has this value already been spent? Bitcoin answers with a set of unspent transaction outputs that each transaction consumes and creates. Ethereum answers with a balance and a nonce per account that each transaction updates. Neither stores a wallet's balance as a primary fact; both derive it from accepted history, and that choice shapes every indexer built on top.
lessons.objective: Implement minimal UTXO and account ledgers in Go, reject double spends in each, and explain what each model makes easy or hard for an indexer.

cautions: Skipping the duplicate-input check creates money.
Contract-internal transfers never appear as top-level transactions.
designGuide.cost: UTXO indexers maintain an owner index over outputs and spends; account indexers need logs or traces and per-block undo journals.
strengths: UTXO spends are explicit, so provenance and undo are mechanical.
Account balances are a direct read at a chosen block.

alternatives: Its nonce is lower than alice's next nonce
Alice's stored balance is too low for it
quiz.correct: The spent output is deleted from the set
quiz.explanation: The first spend deleted genesis:0 and created new outputs. A UTXO ledger keeps no per-account nonce or stored balance; the second spend names a coin that no longer exists.
quiz.hint: Look at what UTXOSet.Apply does to each input once validation passes.
quiz.question: In the UTXO ledger, why is a second transaction that spends genesis:0 rejected?

review.answer: The spent output is deleted from the set
review.prompt: How does UTXO stop a double spend?

sections.body: In the UTXO model the state is a set of coins: outputs of earlier transactions, each with an amount and a locking condition. Bitcoin locks outputs with scripts; this lesson uses an owner name. A transaction names the exact outputs it consumes, which disappear, and creates new outputs, usually including change back to the sender, and whatever the inputs hold beyond the outputs is the fee. In the account model the state maps each address to an account with a balance, a nonce and, for contracts, code and storage. A transaction says from, to, value and nonce, and the ledger debits one balance and credits another. The double-spend defense follows from the shape: a UTXO ledger deletes the coin, so a second spend names something that no longer exists; an account ledger demands the next nonce, so a replay is stale.
sections.title: Two shapes of state

sections.body: UTXOSet.Apply checks every input before it changes anything: each must exist, belong to the signer and appear only once, and the outputs may not exceed the inputs. Ledger.Apply checks the nonce and the balance, then debits, credits and increments the nonce. Owner fields stand in for the signature checks that the signatures lesson covers. After the transfers, the program rebuilds the account state from the history of accepted transfers and compares it with the live state.
sections.title: Both ledgers in one program
sections.walkthrough: Alice spends the 50-unit genesis output into 30 for bob and 19 change, and the missing 1 is the fee. Spending genesis:0 again fails because the first Apply deleted it. A transaction listing t1:1 twice would count those 19 units twice; the seen map rejects it before any sum is used. The account ledger rejects the replayed nonce 0 and then a correctly numbered transfer that exceeds the 20 remaining. UTXO balances are computed on demand by summing unspent outputs, and the account state rebuilt from history matches.

sections.body: The seen map in UTXOSet.Apply looks redundant until you remove it.
