Without it, one transaction can reference the same output twice, the input sum counts the coin twice, and the ledger creates money. This is not hypothetical: CVE-2018-17144 was a Bitcoin Core bug in which an optimization skipped the duplicate-input check during block validation. Nodes running 0.14 could be crashed by such a block, and versions 0.15.0 to 0.16.2 would have accepted one that inflated the supply. Validate everything first and mutate only after every check passes, as both Apply functions do, so that a rejected transaction leaves no partial state. Production code also range-checks every amount (Bitcoin caps values at 21 million coins) and guards unsigned addition against overflow; this model uses small numbers and leaves that out.
sections.title: The duplicate-input check is not optional

sections.body: UTXO makes provenance easy: every payment names its inputs, so tracing where a coin came from is a direct walk, and undoing a block is mechanical, re-adding the outputs it spent and deleting the ones it created, which is what Bitcoin Core's per-block undo data stores. Per-address balance and history are the hard part. An indexer must maintain an owner index over outputs and their spends, and one wallet uses many addresses and change outputs, so a user's balance is an aggregation the chain knows nothing about. The account model makes balances easy, a single read at a chosen block, and hides history: value moves inside contract execution without a top-level transaction, token balances live in contract storage and surface only through logs such as the ERC-20 Transfer event, and full history needs logs or traces. Undoing a block needs the previous value of every key it touched, which the fork-choice lesson uses.
sections.title: What each model means for an indexer

sections.body: The rebuild at the end of the program is the most valuable test either model can have: start from genesis, replay accepted history and compare with the live state. Run it in CI against fixtures and periodically against production projections. Add property tests: total supply stays constant apart from issuance and fees in the UTXO model, or explicit mints and burns in the account model; a rejected transaction changes nothing; applying an accepted transaction a second time is rejected. If a projection keeps a balance column, treat it as a cache of a derivation and keep the means to recompute it, because the chain will never tell you the column drifted.
sections.title: Balances are derived; test that they stay derivable

reading.takeaway: Validate every input or nonce before mutating state, treat balances as derived from accepted history, and choose indexing structures that match how the model records spends.

lessons.title: Account model versus UTXO: two ledgers and two ways to stop a double spend

lessons.explanation: Ethereum hashes and signs bytes, so every value needs exactly one byte form. On the execution layer that form is Recursive Length Prefix (RLP): transactions, headers and receipts are RLP, and typed transactions are a type byte followed by an RLP payload. RLP encodes byte strings and nested lists and nothing else. go-ethereum's decoder is deliberately strict, because accepting a second spelling of a value means accepting a second hash for it.
lessons.objective: Encode and decode Go structs with go-ethereum's rlp package, recognize the canonical-form rules, and bound untrusted input before decoding it.

cautions: rlp.Decode on an arbitrary io.Reader sets no input limit.
Typed decode errors do not match ErrCanonInt with errors.Is.
designGuide.cost: Reflection-based encoding is slower than generated code, and a format without field names makes every schema change a versioning decision.
strengths: One canonical byte form per value keeps hashes and signatures stable.
The decoder rejects non-canonical sizes, integers and trailing data.

alternatives: RLP stores integers as fixed 8-byte words
Leading zeros are legal but slower to parse
quiz.correct: One value must have exactly one encoding
quiz.explanation: 0x05 and 0x820005 would decode to the same integer but hash differently. Accepting both gives one transaction two identities, and nodes that disagree about acceptance split consensus.
quiz.hint: Think about what happens to a transaction hash when two byte strings mean the same value.
quiz.question: A lax decoder reads the bytes 0x820005 as the integer 5. Why must a consensus decoder reject them?

review.answer: One value must have exactly one encoding

sections.body: A single byte below 0x80 is its own encoding. A string of 0 to 55 bytes is 0x80 plus its length followed by the bytes; a longer string is 0xb7 plus the length of the length, the length in big-endian, then the bytes. Lists follow the same pattern from 0xc0 and 0xf7. Integers are not a separate type: they are big-endian strings with no leading zero bytes, so zero is the empty string 0x80. go-ethereum maps Go types onto this. Structs become lists of their exported fields in declaration order, unsigned integers and *big.Int become minimal strings, byte slices and arrays become strings, other slices become lists. Signed integers, floats and maps are refused because they have no canonical form, and a negative big.Int returns an error. The hash-chain lesson made these choices by hand; RLP is the standardized version.
sections.title: Two kinds of item and a length prefix

sections.body: The program prints the specification's own examples, round-trips a struct holding an address, a *big.Int and an empty byte slice, then decodes five malformed inputs into a uint64 and one oversized value from a reader with an explicit limit. No network or chain is involved; these are pure functions over bytes.
sections.title: Encode, decode and feed the decoder bad input
sections.walkthrough: 0 encodes as 80, 15 as the single byte 0f and 1024 as 82 04 00; dog is 83 followed by its ASCII bytes, and [cat dog] is the list header c8 over two strings. The 27-byte transfer starts with da (0xc0 + 26), then 07 for the nonce and 94 for the 20-byte address. Each malformed input breaks a different rule: 8105 wraps a byte that must stand alone, 820005 has a leading zero, b80105 uses the long form for a short string, 0f0f leaves trailing bytes, and bbffffffff claims a 4 GiB string inside 5 bytes. io.MultiReader hides the underlying bytes.Reader, as a network connection would, so only the explicit 64-byte limit stops the 100-byte value, and it does so before allocating.

sections.body: Each rejected input is something a lax decoder could interpret: 8105 and 820005 as the integer 5, b80105 as the one-byte string 05. If a node accepted them, one transaction would have several byte forms and therefore several hashes. A node that accepted a form and a node that rejected it would disagree about a block's validity, which is a consensus split. The property that protects everyone is a bijection: decoding b succeeds only if encoding the result gives back b. go-ethereum's Stream enforces it with ErrCanonSize for a size that should have used a shorter form, ErrCanonInt for leading zeros and, in DecodeBytes, ErrMoreThanOneValue for trailing data. Struct decoding also rejects too few or too many list elements unless trailing fields carry the optional or tail tags.
sections.title: Why consensus decoders refuse non-canonical bytes

sections.body: An RLP header can claim a length up to 2^64-1, and a naive decoder allocates what the header says. DecodeBytes, and NewStream over a bytes.Reader, bytes.Buffer or strings.Reader, know the input length and return ErrValueTooLarge for larger claims. Over any other io.Reader, such as a connection or an HTTP body, the stream has no limit unless you pass one, and rlp.Decode offers no way to pass one, as its documentation warns. Cap the raw message first (go-ethereum's eth protocol caps messages at 10 MiB, and its legacy transaction pool refuses transactions over 128 KiB), then decode with NewStream(r, limit). After decoding, bound the values: RLP puts no size limit on *big.Int, so check BitLen, as the transaction pool does for fee caps over 256 bits. One API surprise: when DecodeBytes fills a typed value, canonical-form failures come back wrapped in a descriptive error that errors.Is does not match against ErrCanonInt or ErrCanonSize, so treat any decode error as invalid input.
sections.title: Bound untrusted input before you decode it

sections.body: Check in the specification examples and the RLP fixtures from the ethereum/tests repository as known answers. For every type you decode from outside, fuzz with go test -fuzz: when DecodeBytes succeeds, re-encode and require identical bytes; when it fails, require no panic and no large allocation. Add cases for each rule above, for a nested list whose inner length exceeds its parent (ErrElemTooLarge), for structs with missing or extra elements, and for optional trailing fields. For hot paths, go-ethereum's rlpgen generates reflection-free encoders. Keep RLP where it belongs: it is the execution layer's consensus encoding, the consensus layer uses SSZ, and your own service APIs are better served by formats with field names and explicit schemas.
sections.title: Test with vectors and round trips

reading.takeaway: Let the rlp package define the bytes, cap untrusted input and decode with an explicit stream limit, bound decoded big integers, and treat every non-canonical form as invalid.

lessons.title: RLP: Ethereum's canonical encoding, and why its decoder rejects every other spelling

lessons.explanation: A hash chain reveals that history changed, but anyone can rebuild a chain. Proof of work makes rebuilding expensive: a block counts only if its header hashes below a target, and the only known way to find such a header is to try nonces. Bitcoin still works this way; Ethereum left proof of work at the Merge in 2022. The idea to keep is the asymmetry between expensive search and cheap verification.
lessons.objective: Mine a toy block against a big.Int target, verify it with one hash, compute its expected work and retarget from observed block times.

cautions: Security is probabilistic and assumes an honest hash-rate majority.
Timestamps are miner-supplied and need explicit bounds.
designGuide.cost: Real proof of work spends energy and hardware in proportion to the security it buys; the toy costs milliseconds only because its difficulty is tiny.
strengths: Verification cost is constant regardless of difficulty.
Cumulative work gives an objective rule for comparing chains.

alternatives: About 2^16 hashes, repeating the search
About 2^8 hashes, the square root of the search
quiz.correct: One header hash compared with the target
quiz.explanation: The verifier does not search. It hashes the header, including the found nonce, once and compares the integer with the target. That asymmetry is what makes proof of work usable.
quiz.hint: The winning nonce is inside the header; what does Valid do with it?
quiz.question: A miner needed about 2^16 attempts to find a valid nonce. How much work does a node spend verifying that header's proof of work?

review.answer: One header hash compared with the target
review.prompt: PoW: cost to verify a block?

sections.body: Read a SHA-256 digest as a 256-bit unsigned integer. A header is valid when that number is below a target, and lowering the target makes valid headers rarer. With a target of 2^(256-k), a valid hash starts with k zero bits, so a miner expects about 2^k attempts while a verifier hashes once and compares. The nonce is the field the miner is free to change. Everything else in the header is fixed: the parent hash, the height, the difficulty and a commitment to the body, such as the Merkle root from the second lesson. Finding a nonce therefore proves work spent on this exact header. Change the body and the commitment changes, the old nonce stops working, and the cheap relinking attack from the first lesson now costs a fresh search for every block rewritten.
sections.title: A target turns hashing into a lottery

sections.body: Header.Hash encodes fixed-width fields in a fixed order, as in the hash-chain lesson, and Valid compares the digest with target(Bits) using math/big. Mine increments the nonce from zero, so the run is deterministic: the same header always yields the same nonce. Work reports the expected number of hashes a target represents, and Retarget scales the target by observed over expected time, clamped to a factor of four. Difficulty stays at 16 bits or less so the run takes milliseconds.
sections.title: Mine, verify and retarget a toy chain
sections.walkthrough: At 8, 12 and 16 bits the expected work is 255, 4095 and 65535 hashes, computed as 2^256 divided by target+1, the formula Bitcoin Core uses for chain work. The 16-bit search took 205064 attempts, about three times the mean; attempt counts are geometrically distributed, so single blocks vary widely. Verification is one Valid call, and flipping one bit of the body commitment makes the same nonce fail. Retarget keeps the target when ten blocks take the expected 6000 seconds, halves it when they take half as long, and clamps a 60-fold speed-up to a factor of four. The spans are fixed numbers, not clock readings.

sections.body: Hash rate rises and falls as hardware joins or leaves, so a fixed target would let block intervals drift from seconds to days. Bitcoin recomputes its target every 2016 blocks from the time those blocks took, aiming at ten minutes per block, and limits each adjustment to a factor of four in either direction; Retarget is that rule in miniature. Timestamps are written by miners, so real rules also bound them: Bitcoin rejects a header whose time is not later than the median of the previous eleven blocks or lies more than two hours in the future. A toy that reads the wall clock is neither deterministic nor representative. Treat timestamps as untrusted data, as the program does, and test the rules that bound them.
sections.title: Difficulty adjustment keeps block time, not security, constant

sections.body: Because work is costly to produce, nodes follow the valid chain with the most cumulative work, and rewriting a block buried under k later blocks means outpacing the rest of the network for k blocks. That security is probabilistic: an attacker with a minority of hash rate can still win a short race, and one with a majority can rewrite at will. Bitcoin's real header is 80 bytes hashed with double SHA-256, its target is packed into a 4-byte bits field, and it accepts a hash equal to the target, where this toy uses a strict comparison so that Bits reads as leading zero bits. Ethereum's proof-of-work era ended with the Merge (EIP-3675); validators now propose blocks and stake finalizes them, which the next lesson relies on. And do not reinvent proof of work as an API rate limiter: puzzles cost honest low-end devices more than attackers with GPUs.
sections.title: What proof of work does and does not secure

sections.body: Keep difficulty tiny in tests and pin the expected nonce for a fixed header as a known answer, so a changed encoding changes the nonce and fails loudly. Test Valid at the boundary: under a strict comparison a hash equal to the target must fail, and a target of zero or above 2^256 must be refused before use; real chains also enforce a maximum target, the proof-of-work limit. Test Retarget at, above and below both clamps, and check integer division, whose rounding compounds over many periods. Benchmark mining separately from unit tests, and never let a test search at a difficulty whose runtime depends on luck you have not measured: the 16-bit search here already needed three times its average.
sections.title: Testing work-based code

reading.takeaway: Proof of work is asymmetric: a nonce below a 2^(256-k) target takes about 2^k hashes to find and one hash to check, so chains compare cumulative work and retarget from timestamps treated as data.

lessons.title: Proof of work: finding a nonce takes thousands of hashes, checking it takes one

lessons.explanation: Two valid blocks can extend the same parent, and nodes need a rule that makes them converge on one branch. Proof-of-work chains follow the branch with the most cumulative work; when a heavier branch appears, the node reorganizes, and blocks it had accepted stop being canonical. Anything an indexer derived from those blocks must be undone, and anything irreversible should have waited for finality.
lessons.objective: Implement a heaviest-chain fork-choice rule, compute a reorganization's undo and apply path, apply confirmation depth, and use Ethereum's safe and finalized tags.

cautions: Confirmations are a probability; recompute them from the head.
latest and safe can both move backwards; only finalized is final.
designGuide.cost: Undo journals for every block, an atomic undo-apply-checkpoint transaction, and roughly 13 minutes of waiting for finality on Ethereum.
strengths: Cumulative work makes every honest node converge on one head.
Per-block undo data turns a reorg into a mechanical replay.

alternatives: latest, once six blocks have built on top of it
safe, because safe blocks can never be reorganized
quiz.correct: finalized: reverting it would slash stake
quiz.explanation: latest can reorg, and safe reflects the consensus client's current view of justified checkpoints. A finalized block can only be reverted if at least a third of all stake is slashed.
quiz.hint: Only one tag is backed by an economic penalty rather than an expectation.
quiz.question: After the Merge, which block tag should an indexer wait for before releasing an irreversible withdrawal?

review.answer: finalized: reverting it would slash stake

sections.body: Forks happen without any attacker: two miners find blocks at nearly the same moment, or a proposer's block arrives late. Each node keeps every valid block in a tree keyed by hash, and a fork-choice rule picks one leaf as the head. Longest chain is the informal name, but the rule that resists manipulation is most cumulative work, using the Work value from the proof-of-work lesson, so a branch of fewer, harder blocks beats a branch of more, easier ones. Ties keep the block seen first. The events-finality lesson in the next unit shows an indexer refusing a block that does not extend its tip; this lesson supplies the step that follows, walking both branches back to their common ancestor.
sections.title: Forks are normal; the rule decides

sections.body: Node.Add rejects a block whose parent is unknown or whose height is not the parent's plus one, computes cumulative work and switches head only on strictly more work. route walks the old and new tips back to their common ancestor and returns the blocks to undo, newest first, and to apply, oldest first. The Indexer keeps a small projection, deposit to including block, that it applies and undoes per block, and computes confirmations as head height minus inclusion height plus one.
sections.title: A node and an indexer that survive a reorg
sections.walkthrough: dep-7 lands in A3 and has two confirmations at head A4, below the policy of three, so it is not credited. B2 brings its branch to work 3, not more than 4, so the head stays. B3 brings it to 5, and the node reorganizes via A1: it undoes A4, A3 and A2 and applies B2 and B3, even though A4 is higher. dep-7 then has no canonical block. X9 is rejected because its parent is unknown; a real node would hold it as an orphan until the parent arrives. When B4 re-includes dep-7, its confirmations restart from one.

sections.body: Waiting for k confirmations means waiting until the including block and k-1 blocks after it are all canonical. Under proof of work, the chance that an attacker with a minority of hash rate overtakes a k-block lead falls exponentially with k; the Bitcoin whitepaper works through the numbers, and six confirmations became the convention. It is still a probability, and the right k depends on what is at stake. Recompute confirmations from the current canonical head on every change instead of storing a counter, because a reorg can remove the including block, as happened to dep-7 after B3, or move the transaction to a different height, as B4 did. Identify transactions by their hash, never by block and position.
sections.title: Confirmation depth is a probability policy

sections.body: Ethereum's proof of stake picks the head with LMD-GHOST and finalizes checkpoints with Casper FFG. When validators holding two thirds of the stake attest to a checkpoint pair, the earlier checkpoint is finalized, and reverting it would require at least one third of all stake to be slashed. Normally that takes about two epochs, 64 slots of 12 seconds, a little under 13 minutes. The JSON-RPC tags expose this: latest is the head and can reorg; safe is the block the consensus client expects not to reorg under normal conditions, which clients derive from the latest justified checkpoint; finalized is the latest finalized block. Release irreversible effects such as withdrawals from finalized, and use safe or latest only for views that tolerate rollback.

sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in the reader's own native environment against their own node; it is not executed by the app. ethclient turns the negative rpc.BlockNumber constants into the finalized and safe tags (FinalizedBlockNumber is -3 and SafeBlockNumber is -4 in go-ethereum v1.17.10), so no heights are guessed. store.Finalize is a placeholder for your projection. A stored hash that differs from the finalized hash at the same height means the indexer followed another chain or a misbehaving provider, which calls for an alert, not an automatic rollback.

sections.body: For every block the projection applied, keep enough to reverse it, keyed by block hash: the rows it inserted, or the previous values of rows it updated, like the account journal from the ledger lesson. Undo newest first, then apply the new branch oldest first, in one database transaction together with the checkpoint, so a crash cannot leave a half-reorganized state. Bound the depth you support: below finalized no reorg should happen, and a deeper one is an incident. Finality can also stall when too few validators participate, which has happened on mainnet; then finalized lags far behind latest, and the right response is to wait and alert, not to fall back to latest. Test with scripted block trees like the program's: a one-block replacement, a deep reorg, a heavier but shorter branch, an unknown parent, a re-included transaction and a crash between undo and apply.

lessons.explanation: Since the London upgrade an Ethereum transaction no longer names one gas price. It carries two caps chosen by the sender, while the protocol sets a per-block base fee that is burned. The price actually paid is decided only when a block includes the transaction, so the code that builds it has to reason about the worst case. This lesson computes those numbers exactly and puts a ceiling in front of the signer that no fee oracle can raise.
lessons.objective: Derive maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas with big.Int, predict the effective gas price for any base fee and enforce a fee ceiling before signing.

cautions: A capped transaction can wait indefinitely while the base fee keeps rising.
Blob gas has a separate fee market that this policy does not bound.

strengths: Exact integer arithmetic that agrees with go-ethereum's EffectiveGasTip.
A policy ceiling bounds spend even when an oracle or node misbehaves.

sections.body: A type-2 transaction, types.DynamicFeeTx in go-ethereum, carries GasTipCap (maxPriorityFeePerGas, the most the sender offers the block producer) and GasFeeCap (maxFeePerGas, the most it will pay per unit of gas in total). The block header carries BaseFee. A block can include the transaction only if maxFeePerGas is at least that base fee, and the price per gas is then min(maxFeePerGas, baseFee + maxPriorityFeePerGas). The base-fee part is burned; only the remainder reaches the producer. The base fee follows demand: geth's CalcBaseFee changes it by parentBaseFee * (gasUsed - target) / target / 8, so a completely full block raises it by 12.5 percent and an empty one lowers it by the same fraction. Every value here is an integer number of wei that can exceed 64 bits, which is why go-ethereum uses *big.Int throughout and why float64 has no place in the calculation; the exact-units lesson shows that failure for token amounts.

sections.body: The program takes an observed base fee of 30 gwei and a 2 gwei tip and derives a fee cap of twice the base fee plus the tip, the same headroom go-ethereum's bind/v2 transactor uses when no cap is given. It runs the policy check a signing service would own, builds an unsigned DynamicFeeTx for local chain 1337, and replays the inclusion formula at three possible base fees, cross-checking each result against go-ethereum's own Transaction.EffectiveGasTip.

sections.walkthrough: gwei multiplies by params.GWei (1e9) inside big.Int, and formatGwei divides with QuoRem so 61.5 gwei prints exactly. checkPolicy rejects a tip above the cap, a fee cap above 100 gwei and a worst case (gas limit * fee cap) above 0.003 ether: the oracle spike to a 120 gwei base fee yields a 242 gwei cap and is refused, and so is a 200000-gas call even at the normal cap. At base 30 the sender pays 32 gwei and the producer keeps 2. At 61.5 the cap binds, so the producer gets only 0.5. At 63 geth returns ErrGasFeeCapTooLow (fee cap less than base fee) and the transaction simply waits. tx.Cost() is gas * GasFeeCap + value, the balance a node demands up front, not the amount finally charged.

Both are hints from an external dependency, so they are inputs to the policy rather than values the signer trusts. FeeHistory returns one more base fee than the number of blocks requested: the last entry is the node's projection for the next block, a better starting point than the latest header when blocks are full.
sections.title: Take inputs from the node, but let the policy decide
sections.walkthrough: This fragment talks to a real node, so run it in your own native environment against an endpoint whose chain ID you have verified; it is not executed here. HeaderByNumber(ctx, nil) asks for the latest header, and BaseFee is nil before London, which deserves an explicit error instead of a nil-pointer panic. SuggestGasTipCap maps to eth_maxPriorityFeePerGas; the 50th-percentile rewards in hist.Reward are an alternative tip source. hist.BaseFee has blockCount+1 entries, the last one for the next block. Whatever the source, checkPolicy has the last word.

sections.body: Treat the fee ceiling as configuration with an owner, reviewed like any spending limit, and alert when the guard trips instead of raising it automatically. A transaction with 2x headroom can still wait if the base fee keeps climbing; that is the safe failure, because the alternative is paying whatever the market demands. When you do speed up a pending transaction, the replacement rules from the nonces lesson apply: geth's default pool accepts a same-nonce replacement only if both the fee cap and the tip rise by at least 10 percent, so bump both and pass the new values through the same policy. Reconcile budgets from the receipt, EffectiveGasPrice * GasUsed, not from the caps; unused gas and unused headroom are never charged. The gas limit is a separate guard: estimating it is a simulation against current state, and the worst-case fee multiplies it. Blob transactions add an independent fee market, maxFeePerBlobGas, that this policy does not bound.
sections.title: Ceilings, replacements and what is finally charged

sections.body: The fee path needs no node to test. Table-test effectivePrice at base fees below, at and above the point where the cap binds, and assert agreement with EffectiveGasTip in each case so a library upgrade that changes the rules is noticed. Test the guard with a tip above the cap, a zero cap, a cap exactly at the limit (allowed) and one wei above it (refused), and a gas limit that pushes the worst case over the total ceiling. Add a regression test that oracle values are copied rather than aliased: big.Int methods mutate their receiver, so a helper that writes into a *big.Int taken from a header can silently change the next transaction's fees. types.NewTx copies its TxData, which protects the built transaction, but not the policy inputs you keep. In review, check that nothing between the policy check and the signer can change the fields.
sections.title: Test the guard at its edges

reading.takeaway: Compute EIP-1559 fees in wei with big.Int: the price paid is min(maxFee, baseFee + tip), and a policy-owned ceiling on maxFee and on gasLimit * maxFee must reject a transaction before it is signed.

lessons.title: EIP-1559 fees: compute the effective gas price exactly and refuse to sign above a ceiling

lessons.explanation: eth_sendRawTransaction takes one opaque byte string. Everything that matters about a transfer, including its chain, nonce, fees, destination, the signer and its future on-chain hash, is fixed when those bytes are produced, before any node sees them. Producing, checking and storing the bytes offline turns a network call with an unknown outcome into a lookup you can repeat.
lessons.objective: Sign a typed transaction with a test key, round-trip its raw bytes, recover the sender and use the precomputed hash to make retries safe.

cautions: Remote signers with random nonces produce new hashes for the same fields.
A fresh nonce on retry is a second payment, not a retry.
designGuide.cost: A durable record per signed transaction (intent, nonce, raw bytes, hashes) and a receipt lookup before every resend.
strengths: The hash is known before broadcast, so retries can be idempotent.
Decoding and recovering the sender verifies bytes from other systems offline.

alternatives: Only after a node accepts it into its pool
Only after a block includes the transaction
quiz.correct: As soon as it is signed: keccak256 of the raw bytes
quiz.explanation: Transaction.Hash is keccak256 of the signed EIP-2718 envelope, so it is fixed before broadcast and lets the service look up a receipt after a timeout instead of signing again with a new nonce.
quiz.hint: Ask what the transaction hash is computed from.
quiz.question: A service signs a transaction and its eth_sendRawTransaction call times out. When could it first have known the hash to look up?

review.answer: As soon as it is signed: keccak256 of the raw bytes
review.prompt: When is a tx hash known?

sections.body: go-ethereum distinguishes three artifacts. The signing hash, returned by Signer.Hash, is keccak256 over the type byte and the RLP list of fields without a signature; that is what the private key signs. The raw transaction, returned by MarshalBinary, is the EIP-2718 envelope: one type byte (0x02 for EIP-1559) followed by the RLP list that now includes V, R and S. The transaction hash, Transaction.Hash, is keccak256 of exactly those raw bytes. Because the hash is a pure function of the signed bytes, it is known the moment signing finishes, before broadcast, and it does not depend on which node accepts it. The signing-boundaries lesson built an unsigned intent; here it goes through the whole offline lifecycle.
sections.title: One transaction, two hashes and a byte string

sections.body: The example derives a throwaway key from 32 bytes of 0x01, a well-known test key that must never hold funds, and signs an EIP-1559 transfer for local chain 1337. It then plays the receiving side: decode the raw bytes into a fresh Transaction, recover the sender and compare hashes. Two final checks show what stays stable across signing and what changes.
sections.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"

	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/common"
	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/core/types"
	"github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/crypto"
)

func main() {
	// TEST KEY ONLY: 32 bytes of 0x01. Never fund it or reuse it outside a local chain.
	key, err := crypto.ToECDSA(bytes.Repeat([]byte{1}, 32))
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	from := crypto.PubkeyToAddress(key.PublicKey)
	signer := types.LatestSignerForChainID(big.NewInt(1337))

	to := common.HexToAddress("0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000aa")
	intent := &types.DynamicFeeTx{
		ChainID:   big.NewInt(1337),
		Nonce:     7,
		GasTipCap: big.NewInt(2_000_000_000),
		GasFeeCap: big.NewInt(62_000_000_000),
		Gas:       21_000,
		To:        &to,
		Value:     big.NewInt(1_000_000_000_000_000),
	}
	signed, err := types.SignTx(types.NewTx(intent), signer, key)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	raw, err := signed.MarshalBinary() // the bytes eth_sendRawTransaction carries
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("sender %s\n", from.Hex())
	fmt.Printf("raw: %d bytes, first byte 0x%02x (type %d)\n", len(raw), raw[0], signed.Type())
	fmt.Println("tx hash  ", signed.Hash().Hex())
	fmt.Println("sign hash", signer.Hash(signed).Hex())
	fmt.Println("hash == keccak256(raw):", signed.Hash() == crypto.Keccak256Hash(raw))

	// The receiving side: decode untrusted bytes, then recover who signed them.
	var decoded types.Transaction
	if err := decoded.UnmarshalBinary(raw); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	got, err := types.Sender(signer, &decoded)
	fmt.Println("recovered sender matches:", got == from, err)
	fmt.Println("decoded hash matches:", decoded.Hash() == signed.Hash())

	_, err = types.Sender(types.LatestSignerForChainID(big.NewInt(1)), &decoded)
	fmt.Println("verify as chain 1:", err)

	again, _ := types.SignTx(types.NewTx(intent), signer, key)
	fmt.Println("re-signed same fields, same hash:", again.Hash() == signed.Hash())

	bump := *intent // shallow copy is enough: we replace the big.Int pointers
	bump.GasTipCap = big.NewInt(2_200_000_000)
	bump.GasFeeCap = big.NewInt(68_200_000_000)
	replacement, _ := types.SignTx(types.NewTx(&bump), signer, key)
	fmt.Println("replacement: same nonce", replacement.Nonce() == signed.Nonce(),
		"new hash", replacement.Hash() != signed.Hash())
}
sections.title: Sign with a fixed test key and round-trip the bytes
sections.walkthrough: LatestSignerForChainID(1337) returns the newest signer in this release, the Prague signer, which accepts every typed transaction and binds signatures to chain 1337. SignTx computes signer.Hash, signs it with crypto.Sign and attaches V, R and S. MarshalBinary yields 119 bytes starting with 0x02, and keccak256 of those bytes equals Hash(). UnmarshalBinary rebuilds the transaction from untrusted bytes, and types.Sender recovers the address; the same bytes checked with a chain-1 signer fail with ErrInvalidChainId. Re-signing identical fields reproduces the hash because go-ethereum signs with deterministic RFC 6979 nonces. Raising both fee caps by 10 percent for the same nonce produces a new hash.

sections.body: The precomputed hash is what makes an unknown send outcome manageable. Store the intent, nonce, raw bytes and hash durably before the first network call, then treat sending as an attempt to publish those exact bytes. After a timeout, ask for a receipt by hash before deciding anything. If none exists yet, resending the stored bytes cannot create a second transfer, because the nonce allows at most one transaction from that account at that position to be included.
sections.title: Persist the bytes and the hash before you send
sections.walkthrough: This fragment needs a node and a database, so it runs in your own native environment; store is a placeholder for your persistence layer. SendTransaction is MarshalBinary plus eth_sendRawTransaction, so the bytes on the wire are the stored ones. The receipt lookup uses the precomputed hash whether or not the send returned an error, and ethclient reports ethereum.NotFound while no receipt exists. On a resend, geth answers already known for a transaction it holds and nonce too low once that nonce is used; the second means some transaction took the slot, so look up the receipt by hash to learn whether it was yours.

sections.body: Three retry strategies look alike and behave very differently. Resending the stored raw bytes is idempotent: same hash, same nonce. Re-signing the same fields is safe only because the result occupies the same nonce. With go-ethereum's deterministic signer it even reproduces the hash, but a remote signer, HSM or KMS that uses random ECDSA nonces returns a different valid signature and therefore a different hash for the same intent, so the record must accept several hashes per nonce. Building a transaction with a fresh nonce is a second payment and belongs to a new business intent, never to a retry; the nonces lesson covers who owns that decision. A fee-bumped replacement deliberately produces a new hash for the same nonce. Whichever version is included wins and the others become permanently invalid, so reconcile by account and nonce as well as by hash.
sections.title: Resend, re-sign or replace: three different retries

sections.body: Services that receive raw transactions from elsewhere, such as a relayer, a co-signer or an approval queue, should decode and check them instead of forwarding bytes blindly. After UnmarshalBinary, compare Type, ChainId, To, Value, Data, Nonce, Gas and both fee caps with the approved intent, recover the sender with a signer for the configured chain and compare it with the expected account. Two details from go-ethereum 1.17 matter in review. Sender rejects a chain mismatch, but SignTx stamps the signer's chain ID onto a typed transaction whose ChainID is zero instead of failing, so the signer, not the intent, picks the chain unless your policy checks ChainID first. And LatestSignerForChainID follows the newest fork of each release, so pin the module version and rerun these round-trip tests on every upgrade.
sections.title: Decode untrusted bytes like a verifier

reading.takeaway: Sign offline, persist the raw bytes and their hash before broadcast, and retry by resending those exact bytes; a fresh nonce is a second payment, not a retry.

lessons.title: Raw transactions offline: sign, encode, decode and recover the sender before anything is broadcast

lessons.explanation: A receipt is the node's report of what a transaction did: whether execution succeeded, how much gas it used and which events contracts emitted. Deposit detectors, payment processors and indexers turn those events into balances, which makes the decoding rules security rules. Anyone can deploy a contract that emits a log shaped exactly like a token transfer, and a log from a block that is later reorganized away has to be reversed.
lessons.objective: Interpret receipt status and gas, decode an ERC-20 Transfer log with accounts/abi, and reject impostor or removed logs before crediting a balance.

cautions: Log position fields come from the provider and are not consensus-checked.
Reversal works only while credits are internal; irreversible effects need finality.
designGuide.cost: A per-chain token allow-list, an idempotency key per delivered log and reversal logic in every projection that consumes events.
strengths: Impostor contracts and look-alike events are rejected before money moves.
Duplicate and removed deliveries keep the projection consistent.

alternatives: Topic 0 equals the Transfer event hash; nothing else
The ABI decodes the Data section without an error
quiz.correct: Success status, token address, topic0 and 3 topics
quiz.explanation: Topic 0 only names the event shape. The emitting address proves which contract spoke, the topic count separates ERC-20 from ERC-721, and a reverted receipt has no effects to credit.
quiz.hint: Anyone can deploy a contract that emits the same event signature.
quiz.question: Which checks must pass before a log is credited as an ERC-20 deposit?

review.answer: Success status, token address, topic0 and 3 topics

sections.body: Receipt.Status is 1 (types.ReceiptStatusSuccessful) or 0 (types.ReceiptStatusFailed). A failed transaction is still included: the sender paid GasUsed * EffectiveGasPrice, the nonce is consumed, and every state change and log from the execution was discarded, so Logs is empty. A successful status only says execution did not revert; whether your business effect happened depends on which logs were emitted and by which contract. Each Log carries the emitting contract Address, zero to four Topics and an opaque Data section. Its block number, block hash, transaction hash and log index are derived fields filled in by the node; go-ethereum's own comment says they are not secured by consensus, so they are only as trustworthy as the provider that served them.
sections.title: What a receipt proves, and what it does not

sections.body: For a non-anonymous Solidity event, topic 0 is keccak256 of the canonical signature, Transfer(address,address,uint256) for ERC-20. Each indexed parameter takes one further topic as a 32-byte word, and the non-indexed parameters are ABI-encoded into Data. The program builds a successful receipt in memory with three logs (a genuine transfer from the expected token contract, the same bytes from an impostor contract and a four-topic log), adds a reverted receipt, then pushes the genuine log through a reorg.
sections.title: Indexed fields live in topics, the rest in data
sections.walkthrough: abi.JSON parses the event, and Event.ID is the topic-0 hash computed from Event.Sig. decodeTransfer checks the emitting address first, then requires exactly three topics with the right topic 0: an ERC-721 Transfer has the same signature and topic 0 but indexes tokenId as a fourth topic and leaves Data empty. UnpackIntoInterface fills only the non-indexed Value from Data, and abi.ParseTopics fills From and To from topics 1 and 2. The reverted receipt is charged a fee and credits nothing. Credits are keyed by block hash and log index, so the duplicate delivery is a no-op, the Removed copy reverses the credit, and the re-inclusion in block B is credited once under its new key.

sections.body: Unpacking event data never reads topics. ABI.UnpackIntoInterface and Arguments.Unpack skip indexed arguments entirely, so a struct decoded only from Data has zero-value From and To fields and no error. ParseTopics wants the indexed arguments alone and the topics after topic 0, and it sets struct fields by reflection from the camel-cased ABI names; if the struct lacks a field, it panics rather than returning an error, so keep the struct next to the ABI and cover it with a test. Indexed strings, bytes and arrays cannot be decoded at all, because the topic holds keccak256 of the value instead of the value. When the ABI comes from a third party, decode with the ABI you reviewed for that deployed address, not with whatever interface the contract claims; the abi-calls lesson makes the same point for calls.
sections.title: Two decoding traps in accounts/abi

sections.body: Push the cheap filters to the node with an ethereum.FilterQuery: the contract address and topic 0 limit what you download, and a topic-2 filter restricts results to transfers into your own addresses. Then repeat every check in the handler anyway. A provider can be buggy or hostile, a query can be widened later by someone else, and the handler is where the money moves.
sections.title: Filter in the query, verify again in the handler
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own native environment against a node for the expected chain. Topics is positional: the first inner slice matches topic 0, nil accepts any sender in position 1, and the third restricts topic 2, the recipient, to the watched address. FilterLogs returns []types.Log by value, so the loop passes the address of each element. Keep the range bounded, because providers cap block spans and result counts; the events-finality lesson covers backfill and checkpoints.

sections.body: Logs from FilterLogs reflect the canonical chain at query time. Logs delivered through SubscribeFilterLogs or polling filters can arrive twice: once when the block is imported and again with Removed set to true when a reorganization takes that block off the canonical chain. The handler must reverse exactly what it applied, which is why the example keys credits by the delivered log's block hash and log index rather than by transaction hash: the same transaction is often re-included on the new branch at another position and deserves its own credit. Reversal is only possible while the credit is still internal. Anything irreversible, such as shipping goods or withdrawing to another chain, should wait for the confirmation or finality policy from the events-finality lesson. Test the handler with a reverted receipt, an impostor contract, a four-topic Transfer, truncated Data, a duplicate delivery and a removed log whose credit was never applied.
sections.title: Removed logs and what a credit should wait for

reading.takeaway: Credit a token transfer only from a successful receipt, the expected contract address, the exact topic 0 and topic count, and key the credit so a Removed log reverses precisely what was applied.

lessons.title: Receipts and logs: decode ERC-20 transfers from the right contract and reverse them on reorg

lessons.explanation: Wallets can sign arbitrary text as well as transactions, and many services use that to log users in without passwords. The cryptography is the easy part. A recovered address only says that some key signed some bytes; whether those bytes were meant for your site, for now and for exactly one login is decided by the message format and by state your server keeps. This lesson verifies both halves with a fixed test key and an in-memory nonce store.
lessons.objective: Verify an EIP-191 personal signature, normalize its V byte, and accept an EIP-4361 sign-in only for this domain, chain and expiry with an unused server nonce.

cautions: ecrecover cannot verify smart-contract wallets; EIP-1271 needs an RPC call.
A login signature must never double as authorization to move value.
designGuide.cost: A nonce table with a TTL and atomic consume, a strict message parser and a test matrix for V, s, domain, expiry and concurrency.
strengths: Password-free logins verified offline with go-ethereum primitives.
Domain binding and single-use nonces defeat relayed and replayed signatures.

alternatives: The signature no longer recovers the same address
Wallets never produce the same signature twice
quiz.correct: A server-issued nonce consumed once, atomically
quiz.explanation: Recovery is stateless and succeeds again for the same bytes. Only the nonce record, deleted when the first login committed, distinguishes the replay from the original.
quiz.hint: The bytes and the signature are identical to the accepted login; only server state has changed.
quiz.question: An attacker resubmits a user's valid Sign-In with Ethereum message and signature a minute after the user logged in. What makes the server reject it?

review.answer: A server-issued nonce consumed once, atomically

sections.body: EIP-191 version 0x45, the personal_sign format, prefixes the message with "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" and its decimal byte length, then hashes with keccak256; go-ethereum exposes exactly this as accounts.TextHash. The 0x19 prefix keeps the signed bytes from ever parsing as a valid transaction, so a site cannot get a wallet to sign a transfer by calling it a message. The signature is 65 bytes: R, S and a recovery byte V. crypto.Sign returns V as 0 or 1, while wallets and geth's own eth_sign return 27 or 28 for historical reasons, and crypto.SigToPub accepts only 0 or 1. The signing-boundaries lesson argued that recovery is not authorization; this lesson adds the rules that turn a recovery into a login.
sections.title: What personal_sign actually signs

sections.body: The program plays both parties. The wallet side builds an EIP-4361 message, hashes it with TextHash, signs it with a fixed test key and shifts V to 27 or 28 as wallets do. The server side parses the fields it relies on, checks them against its own configuration and clock, recovers the signer and consumes the nonce last. Five attempts show which rule stops which attack.
sections.title: Verify a sign-in end to end
sections.walkthrough: recoverPersonal copies the signature before normalizing V, rejects high-s values with ValidateSignatureValues and recovers with SigToPub over TextHash of the exact message text. Swapping V between 27 and 28 is not detected as malformed: it recovers a different, valid-looking address, so only the comparison with the claimed address catches it, and the nonce survives that failure. The genuine login succeeds and deletes the nonce, so the identical replay fails. A message signed for evil.example fails the domain check even though its signature is perfect, and a message presented six minutes later fails its five-minute expiration. The clock is a fixed value so the output is deterministic.

sections.body: A Sign-In with Ethereum message is plain text with a fixed layout: the requesting domain, the account in EIP-55 checksum form, an optional statement for the user, then URI, Version (1), Chain ID, Nonce, Issued At and optional Expiration Time, Not Before, Request ID and Resources lines. Every value the server compares must come from server state, never from the message: the expected domain and URI from configuration, the chain ID from the deployment, the time from the server clock and the nonce from the server's own store. EIP-4361 requires at least eight alphanumeric characters of nonce; crypto/rand.Text returns 26 base32 characters, which fits. The domain check defeats a phishing site that relays a genuine signature: the wallet shows the user which domain is asking, and your server refuses any domain but its own. Parse strictly against the specification's ABNF and reject duplicate fields, because two parsers that disagree about which Nonce line counts are a vulnerability. The example's parser is deliberately small and skips Issued At and Not Before checks that a real verifier performs with a bounded clock skew.
sections.title: The EIP-4361 fields the server must own

sections.body: The in-memory map and mutex model a single process. A real deployment issues nonces from a shared store with a time-to-live and consumes them with one atomic operation, so two concurrent submissions of the same signed message cannot both succeed. Run the stateless checks and signature recovery first, and make the consume the final step that commits the login.
sections.title: Store nonces so a replay loses the race
sections.walkthrough: This fragment needs a PostgreSQL database, so it runs in your own native environment; db is a *sql.DB and sessionID identifies the pre-login browser session. Binding the nonce to that session stops a signed message captured from one session from being redeemed in another. The DELETE with the expiry condition is the atomic test-and-consume: when two requests race, exactly one sees RowsAffected equal to 1. After a successful login, issue a fresh session identifier instead of promoting the pre-login one.

sections.body: ecrecover verifies only externally owned accounts. A smart-contract wallet has no single private key; it validates signatures through EIP-1271 isValidSignature, which needs an eth_call on the chain named in the message, so supporting those wallets adds an RPC-dependent path with the timeouts and trust questions of the rpc-boundaries lesson. KMS and HSM signers can return a high s value; normalize it (s becomes n - s and V flips) before publishing, because EIP-2 makes high-s transactions invalid and many message verifiers, including this one, reject them. Sign-in proves control of an address at login time and nothing more: map it to an account, issue your own session with its own expiry, and require a fresh, purpose-specific signature or EIP-712 typed data for anything that moves value. Test the verifier with a wrong domain, URI or chain, a missing or past expiration, an unchecksummed address, V of 0, 1, 27 and 28, a high-s signature, a duplicate Nonce line and two concurrent submissions.
sections.title: Limits worth stating in a review

reading.takeaway: A valid signature only recovers an address; a login also needs your domain, URI and chain, an unexpired message and a server-issued nonce that is consumed atomically exactly once.

lessons.title: Signed messages and Sign-In with Ethereum: recover the right address and refuse replays

lessons.explanation: Production services rarely trust one JSON-RPC endpoint: providers have outages, rate limits, stale replicas and occasionally wrong data. Adding a second URL does not fix that by itself. Reads must agree on which block they describe, a provider that disagrees must be detected rather than averaged in, and retries must stop before they turn a provider incident into your outage. This lesson models providers in memory behind the same interface ethclient implements.
lessons.objective: Pin multi-provider reads to an agreed block hash, quarantine providers that disagree or lag, and fail over with bounded retries and backoff.

cautions: Agreement among providers that share one upstream is a single vote.
AtHash helpers send requireCanonical false; use the raw client when it matters.
designGuide.cost: Extra header calls per pinned read, a provider pool with health state and metrics, and a retry policy that must be tuned and reviewed.
strengths: A lagging or forked provider is detected instead of silently trusted.
Fakes behind the ethclient interface make outage drills instant and deterministic.

alternatives: Average the values returned by all providers
Retry each call until two providers return equal values
quiz.correct: Pin every read to one agreed block hash
quiz.explanation: A block number can name different blocks on different forks and latest moves between calls; a hash names one block, and a provider that lacks it fails loudly instead of answering from another state.
quiz.hint: Think about what names one chain state unambiguously, even across forks.
quiz.question: Two providers answer latest for different blocks. What makes reads across several providers consistent?

review.answer: Pin every read to one agreed block hash

sections.body: Two providers asked for latest at the same moment can answer for different blocks, and a load-balanced endpoint can serve two consecutive calls from two different backends. A balance from one call and an allowance from the next may then describe states that never coexisted. Pick the block first, usually head minus your confirmation depth or the finalized tag, resolve it to a hash, and make every later read refer to that hash. A read by number lets a provider on another fork answer quietly from its own state; a read by hash, as EIP-1898 allows, fails loudly when the provider does not have that block. The rpc-boundaries lesson already verifies the chain ID and bounds each call; pinning is the next layer.
sections.title: Latest is not a coordinate

sections.body: The program defines Reader as the two ethclient methods the service needs, and a compile-time assertion proves that *ethclient.Client satisfies it, so fakes and the real client are interchangeable. Five fake providers cover the cases: three agree on block 100, one serves a forked header, one is still at block 99, and the first healthy one is rate limited. pin computes each header hash locally and requires a strict majority of all configured providers; balance then reads at the pinned hash with bounded per-provider retries.
sections.title: Outvote, then fail over
sections.walkthrough: Header.Hash() is keccak256 over the RLP of the returned fields, so the client computes it rather than trusting a quoted hash. epsilon has no header 100 and returns ethereum.NotFound, which is what ethclient reports for a null block, so it is excluded rather than counted as dissent. delta's header differs and so does its hash; it is quarantined. Three of five agree, a strict majority. alpha answers every balance call with an rpc.HTTPError of status 429; retryable treats 429 and 5xx as transient, waits 100ms and then 200ms, and after the third attempt moves on. beta answers at the pinned hash. Sleep is injected, so the run is instant and the total backoff of 300ms can be asserted instead of waited for.

sections.body: With real endpoints the shape stays the same: dial each provider with an explicit HTTP client, verify its chain ID before it joins the pool, and wrap it with a client-side limiter so your own traffic stays under the provider's quota instead of discovering the quota through 429 responses.
sections.title: Wire real clients behind the same interface
sections.walkthrough: This fragment dials real endpoints, so run it in your own native environment with URLs from configuration and never with credentials in source. rpc.WithHTTPClient supplies an http.Client whose Timeout caps every HTTP exchange, in addition to per-call contexts. A provider reporting another chain ID never joins the pool. rate.NewLimiter(20, 5) allows 20 requests per second with bursts of 5, and Wait returns an error instead of sleeping past the context deadline. rpc.FinalizedBlockNumber selects the finalized tag; pin then confirms that block hash across providers before any read.

sections.body: Agreement is evidence only if the providers are independent: three brands reselling one upstream are one vote, and the strongest single check is a node you operate or a light client that verifies consensus. Pinning by hash has a subtlety in this release: ethclient's BalanceAtHash, CallContractAtHash and the other AtHash helpers send requireCanonical as false, so a node may answer from a block it still stores after a reorg removed it from the canonical chain. When that matters, call the raw rpc.Client with rpc.BlockNumberOrHashWithHash(hash, true); geth then fails with hash is not currently canonical. Retry only reads and only transient classes (429, 5xx, timeouts), with a per-attempt timeout, an attempt cap per provider and an overall deadline, and add random jitter so many workers do not retry in lockstep; the example omits jitter to stay deterministic. go-ethereum's HTTPError carries the status and body but not response headers, so honoring Retry-After needs a custom http.RoundTripper. Never fail over a send by assuming a timeout meant failure; the raw-transactions lesson explains why.
sections.title: Quorum, canonical hashes and retry budgets

sections.body: Because the service depends on an interface, failure modes are cheap to script: a provider one block behind, one on a fork, one returning 429 for a minute, one that hangs until the context expires, one that returns a malformed header, and all of them at once. Assert outcomes rather than just errors: which provider was quarantined, how many attempts ran, the total backoff, and that no read used a block other than the pinned hash. Export the same facts as production metrics: per-provider error rate by class, head lag in blocks, disagreements per hour and retry budget spent. A disagreement is an incident to investigate, not noise to retry away.

lessons.explanation: SQL injection happens when a value supplied by a user becomes part of the statement the database parses. database/sql gives you a second channel: the query text reaches the driver as one string and every argument travels beside it as a typed value. The SQL rows lesson stated that placeholders bind values, not grammar; this lesson makes that separation visible with a recording driver and covers the places where binding alone is not enough: identifiers, sort direction and LIKE patterns.
lessons.objective: Send untrusted values as database/sql arguments, pick identifiers from allow-lists in code and escape LIKE wildcards with an explicit ESCAPE clause.

cautions: Raw-SQL methods in ORMs and query builders reintroduce concatenation.
A bound LIKE, regex or full-text value is still interpreted by its operator.
designGuide.cost: Almost nothing at run time; the cost is review discipline and a small allow-list map for every dynamic identifier.
strengths: The database never parses user input as SQL syntax.
Constant statements are easy to review, grep and prepare once.

alternatives: Bound column names are quoted, so ORDER BY $1 sorts safely
Escaping quotes in the sort key makes concatenation safe
quiz.correct: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers or keywords
quiz.explanation: A parameter is always a value. ORDER BY $1 either fails or sorts by a constant, so the column must come from a fixed map in code and every other key is rejected.
quiz.hint: Think about where in the SQL grammar a parameter is allowed to appear.
quiz.question: A list endpoint lets clients choose the sort column. Why does a placeholder not solve the injection risk?

review.answer: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers or keywords

sections.body: Build a statement with + or fmt.Sprintf and the database receives one string. It cannot know which characters came from your code and which came from a form field, so a name such as x' OR '1'='1 closes the string literal and appends a condition that is always true. Escaping quotes by hand looks like a fix until a different character set, a backslash rule or a numeric position that needs no quotes at all defeats it. The durable fix is structural: keep the statement constant and pass values through the driver's parameter mechanism, so a value never passes through the SQL parser as syntax. Placeholder syntax belongs to the driver, not to database/sql: PostgreSQL drivers use $1, $2 and so on, while MySQL and SQLite drivers use ?.
sections.title: Concatenation hands the parser your user's syntax

sections.body: A database driver implements a few interfaces from database/sql/driver. This program registers a tiny fake whose connection implements QueryerContext: database/sql calls it with the query string and a slice of driver.NamedValue, and the fake prints both instead of contacting a server. Four calls show a concatenated statement, a parameterized one, an allow-listed ORDER BY and a LIKE search for text that itself contains wildcard characters.
sections.title: Record what database/sql actually hands the driver
sections.walkthrough: In the first call the attacker's quote marks are inside the sql line and args is empty: the OR clause is now part of the statement. In the second call the statement is constant and the same characters arrive as a string argument bound to $1, so the database compares name with that exact string. database/sql converts each argument to a driver.Value before the driver sees it, which is why the untyped 20 arrives as int64. The sort key is looked up in a map of fixed SQL fragments, so the hostile key never reaches the driver at all. The LIKE pattern is still an argument, but its % and _ were escaped with ! first and the statement declares ESCAPE '!'. The fake parses nothing; it models the interface boundary, not database behavior.

sections.body: A placeholder can stand only where the grammar expects a value. Table names, column names, ASC and DESC are part of the statement's structure, so a database either rejects ORDER BY $1 or sorts every row by the same constant value, which silently does nothing. When a request legitimately chooses among columns, map public keys such as newest or name to SQL fragments written in your code, reject anything else with a 400 and keep the map next to the query so a reviewer sees the complete set. The same rule covers table names chosen for partitioning or tenancy: take them from configuration you own, never from the request. IN lists are the other common case: generate one placeholder per element from the count, and pass the elements as arguments.
sections.title: Identifiers and keywords need an allow-list, not a placeholder
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own service against a real PostgreSQL driver. The SQL text is built only from a number your code controls, so this concatenation is safe; every id still travels as an argument. The empty-list check matters because IN () is a syntax error, and the upper bound matters because every database limits how many parameters one statement may carry. Drivers that encode slices can bind a whole array instead, as in id = ANY($1) with PostgreSQL.

sections.body: Binding a search term stops injection into the statement, but LIKE interprets the bound value: % matches any run of characters and _ matches exactly one. A user searching for 100% or snake_case gets wrong results, and a pattern that begins with % cannot use an ordinary B-tree index, so a public search box needs length and rate limits anyway. Escape the wildcards and the escape character itself, then name that character in an ESCAPE clause instead of relying on a default: PostgreSQL and MySQL default to backslash, SQLite has none, and in MySQL a backslash inside a string literal is itself an escape, which is why the example uses !. Treat other embedded languages the same way: regular expressions, full-text query syntax and JSON path expressions accept operators inside a bound value, so validate their size and shape too.
sections.title: A bound LIKE pattern is still a small language

sections.body: Most real injections in Go services come through escape hatches. Query builders and ORMs offer raw-SQL methods for ORDER BY, WHERE fragments and JSON operators, and a fmt.Sprintf passed to one of them is exactly as dangerous as concatenating in db.QueryContext. Second-order injection is the delayed version: a value is stored safely through a parameter, then a reporting job or migration reads it back and splices it into dynamic SQL, trusting it because it came from your own database. Stored procedures that assemble EXECUTE strings move the problem into SQL instead of removing it. Some drivers can be configured to interpolate arguments on the client rather than using server-side parameters, which shifts escaping into the driver; keep the default unless you have measured a reason. Finally, limit the blast radius: the application's database role should not own the schema or read tables it never queries.
sections.title: Where injection survives in code that uses placeholders

sections.body: In review, look at every QueryContext, ExecContext and QueryRowContext call and ask whether its query argument is a constant or is assembled only from fragments your code owns. Static analysis helps: gosec reports SQL built with string formatting or concatenation (rules G201 and G202). In tests, send hostile values such as quotes, semicolons, comment markers and wildcard characters through the real queries against a disposable database and assert on the rows returned, not merely on the absence of an error. A recording driver like the one above is useful in unit tests to assert that a function sends a constant statement and exactly the expected arguments.
sections.title: Review and test the boundary

reading.takeaway: Keep every statement constant and pass untrusted values as arguments; choose identifiers and sort order from an allow-list in code, and escape LIKE wildcards with an explicit ESCAPE clause.

lessons.explanation: Cross-site scripting happens when data from one user becomes markup or script in another user's browser. Escaping is the defense, but the correct escaping depends on where a value lands: a text node, a quoted attribute, a URL, a JavaScript string and a CSS value each have different metacharacters. Go's html/template parses your template, tracks that context at every action and applies the matching escaper automatically. text/template does none of this, and typed strings such as template.HTML tell html/template to stop.
lessons.objective: Render untrusted data with html/template, read its context-specific escaping and treat every typed-content conversion as a reviewed trust decision.

cautions: template.HTML, JS and URL conversions disable escaping without checking anything.
Frontend code that uses innerHTML is outside html/template's protection.
designGuide.cost: Templates must be valid, analyzable HTML and rich user content needs a separate sanitizer; the escaping itself is cheap.
strengths: The escaper follows text, attribute, URL, JS and CSS contexts automatically.
Unsafe URL schemes are neutralized instead of rendered as clickable links.

alternatives: html/template could not parse the URL syntax
The value was percent-encoded beyond recognition

quiz.hint: Look at the scheme of the value the user saved, not at its characters.

sections.body: Take a display name such as . In a text node its angle brackets must be entity-encoded. In a quoted attribute the quote character matters most. Inside a
sections.title: One payload, four different meanings

sections.body: The program parses one template text with both packages and executes it with the same hostile data: a name carrying an event-handler payload, a javascript: link, a search query with spaces and an ampersand, and a staff-written biography typed as template.HTML. Comparing the two outputs line by line shows what html/template decided in each context.
sections.title: Render the same data with text/template and html/template
sections.walkthrough: text/template copies every value verbatim: the image tag would run in the paragraph, a payload containing a double quote would break out of the title attribute, and the script block becomes invalid JavaScript containing markup. html/template entity-encodes the name in both the text node and the attribute. In the first href it inspects the scheme, refuses javascript: and substitutes #ZgotmplZ, a deliberately meaningless marker. In the query string it percent-encodes the value, so & cannot start a new parameter. Inside <script> it emits a quoted JavaScript string with < and > written as \u003c and \u003e, so the browser never sees a tag. The Bio line is identical in both outputs because template.HTML told html/template the value is already safe markup.

sections.body: ZgotmplZ is the innocuous word html/template emits when an unsafe value reaches a URL, CSS or attribute-name position at run time. In URL attributes the filter passes relative references and the http, https and mailto schemes; javascript:, data: and every other scheme become #ZgotmplZ. Seeing it in rendered HTML means the data and the template disagree about what is allowed, so fix the data or the design instead of reaching for a conversion. html/template also refuses templates it cannot analyze: a template that ends inside an unclosed tag or attribute, an action in an ambiguous part of a URL, or if branches that leave the parser in different contexts make Execute return an error. Treat those errors as defects caught before any browser saw the page.
sections.title: #ZgotmplZ is a refusal, not a bug to silence

sections.body: html/template skips escaping for values of type template.HTML, HTMLAttr, URL, JS, JSStr, CSS and Srcset in their matching contexts. The conversion checks nothing; it is a claim, made by whoever wrote it, that the string is already safe there. That claim is correct for markup your own code generated, for the output of another executed template and for the output of a maintained HTML sanitizer. It is wrong for user input, for rows another service wrote, for Markdown rendered without sanitizing and for JSON pasted into a script as template.JS. Keep conversions rare, next to the code that produced the value and easy to search for, so a reviewer can list every place the escaper is switched off.
sections.title: Typed content is a trust assertion
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own service; markdownToHTML and policy stand for a Markdown renderer and an allow-list HTML sanitizer such as bluemonday, neither of which is in the standard library. The first function keeps the conversion beside the sanitizer that justifies it. The last line is the pattern to search for in review: a request value converted to template.HTML reintroduces exactly the XSS that html/template was preventing.

sections.body: html/template assumes the template text is trusted and only the data is not, so never parse a template from user input. Its guarantees end at the HTML it writes. A JSON API whose data the frontend inserts with innerHTML is DOM-based XSS, and the fix lives in that JavaScript. A handler that writes user bytes with w.Write or Gin's c.Data and a text/html content type bypasses templates entirely, and an uploaded file served from your origin needs a correct Content-Type plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, ideally from a separate download domain. In Gin, c.HTML renders through html/template, so templates loaded with LoadHTMLGlob get contextual escaping, while c.String responds as text/plain. A Content-Security-Policy, covered in the headers lesson, is the second layer for the day an escaping decision goes wrong.
sections.title: What html/template does not cover

sections.body: In review, look for text/template imports in packages that produce HTML, for template.HTML, JS and URL conversions, and for handlers that set Content-Type to text/html by hand. In tests, render each template with a fixed set of hostile values: angle brackets, both quote characters, a javascript: URL and a closing </script>. Assert on the exact output, as the program prints it, so an edit that moves an action into a new context shows up as a diff. A golden-file test per template is cheap and catches the regression a human reviewer is least likely to notice.
sections.title: Review and test escaping

reading.takeaway: Render HTML only with html/template, let it choose the escaper for each context, and treat every template.HTML, JS or URL conversion as a reviewed claim that the value is already safe.

lessons.title: html/template escapes by context, and template.HTML is where that protection switches off

lessons.explanation: Cross-site request forgery abuses ambient credentials. A page on another site submits a form or calls fetch toward your service, the browser attaches your session cookie, and your handler sees an authenticated request it never meant to accept. Since Go 1.25 the standard library ships http.CrossOriginProtection, which rejects non-safe cross-origin browser requests using the Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin headers instead of a per-form secret. This lesson shows what that check decides, where SameSite fits and what stays your responsibility.
lessons.objective: Protect cookie-authenticated endpoints with net/http's CrossOriginProtection, know what SameSite cookies add and recognize when a synchronizer token is still required.

cautions: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS always pass, so they must never change state.
Requests without Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin are allowed as non-browser clients.
designGuide.cost: One wrapper at startup; the ongoing cost is keeping GET handlers free of side effects and reviewing every bypass pattern.
strengths: No per-session token state and no changes to forms are required.
One wrapper protects every route, including routes added later.

alternatives: Allowed, because SameSite cookies treat it as the same site
Allowed whenever an Origin header is also present
quiz.correct: Rejected: a sibling subdomain is another origin
quiz.explanation: Only same-origin and none pass the Sec-Fetch-Site check; same-site and cross-site are rejected unless a trusted origin or a bypass pattern applies.
quiz.hint: Compare what site means for cookies with what origin means for this check.
quiz.question: CrossOriginProtection receives a POST from blog.example.com to app.example.com with Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site. What happens?

review.answer: Rejected: a sibling subdomain is another origin

sections.body: A forged request is genuine HTTP from the victim's own browser, with the victim's cookie and network address, so authentication succeeds. What differs is the initiator: a document from another origin started it. Modern browsers say so. Sec-Fetch-Site carries same-origin, same-site, cross-site or none (the user typed the URL or opened a bookmark), and the Origin header names the initiating origin on POST and CORS requests. Page scripts cannot set either header. A server that refuses state-changing requests initiated by another origin removes the attack without storing anything per session. Credentials that are not ambient, such as a bearer token the client adds to an Authorization header, are never attached by the browser on its own, so they are not exposed to CSRF in the first place.
sections.title: The browser attaches the cookie; the server must ask who initiated

sections.body: The program wraps a ServeMux with http.NewCrossOriginProtection, trusts one partner origin, exempts a single-sign-on endpoint that receives a cross-site form post by design and replaces the default 403 body. Each probe sets the headers a particular client would send. httptest.NewRequest uses example.com as the Host, which is what the Origin fallback compares against.
sections.title: Wrap the mux and probe it with every kind of client
sections.walkthrough: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS pass unconditionally, which is why the cross-site GET succeeds: handlers behind those methods must never change state. A POST with Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin passes, and so would none; cross-site and same-site are both rejected, because a sibling subdomain is a different origin even though cookies treat it as the same site. Without Sec-Fetch-Site the check compares the Origin host with the Host header, and a request with neither header is treated as a non-browser client such as curl and passes. AddTrustedOrigin matches the full scheme://host[:port] string exactly. AddInsecureBypassPattern uses ServeMux pattern syntax, and a bypassed handler must authenticate the request another way; here the identity provider's signed assertion does that.

sections.body: SameSite=Lax tells the browser to omit the cookie on cross-site subrequests and cross-site POST navigations while still sending it on top-level GET navigations, so a user following a link arrives logged in. Strict withholds it on those navigations too. Both are worth setting on a session cookie, as the session lesson does, but neither replaces an origin check. Site is not origin: blog.example.com and app.example.com are the same site, so a compromised or user-generated subdomain still gets your cookies attached to its requests. Browsers also disagree about the default when SameSite is omitted, and Lax still sends the cookie on top-level GETs, which leaves any state-changing GET handler exposed. Use SameSite to shrink the attack surface and CrossOriginProtection to make the decision.
sections.title: SameSite cookies narrow exposure; they do not make the decision

sections.body: Wrap the outermost handler so a route added next quarter is protected automatically, and keep exemptions to a short, reviewed list. Because a *gin.Engine implements http.Handler, cop.Handler(router) protects every Gin route without Gin-specific middleware. If a reverse proxy rewrites the Host header, the Origin fallback for older browsers compares against the wrong host; preserve Host at the proxy or register the public origin with AddTrustedOrigin. Review CORS separately: it decides which origins may read responses, a different question from which may send writes, and a credentialed CORS policy that reflects any origin leaks GET responses even while writes are blocked.
sections.title: Put the check outside everything else
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own environment. AddTrustedOrigin returns an error for a value with a path, query or fragment, or without a scheme or host, so check it at startup. Call SetDenyHandler if clients expect a JSON error body; otherwise rejections get a plain-text 403. For a decision inside one handler, Check(r) returns the same error without writing a response.

sections.body: Header-based protection depends on the browser.
