In the experiment the report read: round trip changed 01308000 into 013000, that is count 1, tag 0x30 and the two-byte encoding of length zero that Encode shortens to one byte. The saved file starts with the line go test fuzz v1 followed by the input as a Go literal; the hash in its name will differ on your machine.

sections.body: Limits belong at every layer that can expand data. http.MaxBytesReader caps the compressed request body, but a gzip body inflates after that check, so wrap the decompressor in a LimitReader as readAtMost does and treat hitting the limit as an error rather than silently truncating. The net/http Transport transparently decompresses gzip responses it asked for, so outbound response bodies need the same cap. For zip archives, the sizes in the headers are claims made by whoever built the archive: limit the number of entries and the bytes read per entry and in total, and leave entry names to the path-traversal lesson. Never preallocate from a declared length without a cap. Fuzzing proves nothing about inputs it never reached, so check the seed run with go test -coverprofile and add seeds for the branches it misses.
sections.title: Bound decompression and allocation everywhere

reading.takeaway: Give every parser of untrusted input a fuzz test with seeds and invariants (no panic, bounded output, canonical round trip), commit the failures it finds, and cap every declared length and every decompressed byte.

lessons.title: Fuzz the parsers that read untrusted bytes, and bound what they may allocate or inflate

lessons.explanation: Most of the code in a Go binary was written by someone else. The toolchain provides strong defaults: go.sum pins exact module content, the checksum database exposes a module version that changed after publication, and every binary records the modules it was built from. Supply-chain security in Go is mostly about not weakening those defaults, and about reacting quickly and precisely when a dependency has a known vulnerability.
lessons.objective: Run govulncheck in CI, rely on go.sum and the checksum database correctly, pin tools with tool directives, build with -trimpath, and audit a binary's embedded build information.

cautions: The checksum database proves consistency, not that code is benign.
Tool directives add tool dependencies to the application's module graph.
designGuide.cost: A govulncheck step and a build-information gate in CI, plus reviewer time for every dependency update; keeping the defaults on costs nothing.
strengths: Reachability analysis keeps vulnerability reports short and actionable.
Embedded build information makes every shipped binary auditable after the fact.

alternatives: The version was reviewed and contains no malware
The version has no known vulnerabilities
quiz.correct: Everyone gets the same content for a module version
quiz.explanation: The checksum database makes content tampering and per-user substitution detectable; whether the published code is safe still needs review and govulncheck.
quiz.hint: The database is a transparent log of hashes; think about what a hash can and cannot say about code.
quiz.question: A new version of a dependency is listed in the Go checksum database. What does that establish?

review.answer: Everyone gets the same content for a module version

sections.body: govulncheck compares your dependencies, and the Go version itself, against the Go vulnerability database. In source mode it builds a call graph and reports a vulnerability as affecting you only when your code can reach a vulnerable function, which turns a long list of advisories into the few that matter now. Vulnerable modules that you import but never call are summarized separately. Binary mode inspects a compiled executable, which is the right check for what you actually ship, but it cannot show call stacks. Standard-library vulnerabilities are fixed by moving to a newer Go patch release, so scan with the same Go version you release with.
sections.code:
# Pin the scanner in go.mod (Go 1.24+), so developers and CI run one version:
go get -tool golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest

go tool govulncheck ./...                       # source mode: reachable findings
go tool govulncheck -show verbose ./...         # also list imported but unreached ones
go tool govulncheck -mode=binary ./bin/orders   # audit what you actually ship
sections.title: Report the vulnerabilities your code can reach
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own module; govulncheck fetches advisories from the Go vulnerability database. go get -tool records the resolved version in go.mod and go.sum, and go tool runs exactly that version, building it on first use. In its default text output, govulncheck exits with a non-zero status when it finds vulnerabilities your code reaches, so a CI step fails on the findings that matter. Reachability is a static approximation: reflection and some indirect calls can hide a path, so schedule upgrades for unreached findings instead of ignoring them.

sections.body: go.sum records a hash of each module version's file tree and of its go.mod file. When the go command first downloads a module version that go.sum does not list, it checks the hash against sum.golang.org, a transparent log that lets every user confirm they see the same content for the same version. That defends against a compromised proxy or origin serving you different code from everyone else, and against a version tag moved after publication. It does not say the code is benign: a malicious version published openly is logged faithfully. Private modules must not be looked up in public services, which is what GOPRIVATE controls.
sections.code:
go env -w GOPRIVATE='*.corp.example.com'   # no public proxy or checksum DB for these
go mod verify                               # module cache still matches go.sum
go mod tidy -diff                           # non-zero exit if go.mod or go.sum would change
go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -o bin/orders ./cmd/orders
go version -m bin/orders                    # the embedded module and build record
sections.title: What go.sum and the checksum database prove
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own environment. GOPRIVATE takes comma-separated glob patterns of module path prefixes and keeps those modules away from proxy.golang.org and sum.golang.org; GONOPROXY and GONOSUMDB override it for finer control. go mod verify detects tampering in the local module cache. go mod tidy -diff prints needed changes and exits non-zero, so CI catches a go.mod that drifted from the imports. -mod=readonly is already the default without a vendor directory, but stating it guards against a GOFLAGS=-mod=mod in the environment quietly rewriting requirements. -trimpath replaces file system paths with module paths, so binaries do not reveal the build machine's layout and are easier to reproduce.

sections.body: Tools that run in CI or through go generate, such as linters, code generators and govulncheck, execute with your repository's credentials, so they deserve the same pinning as libraries. Since Go 1.24 a tool directive in go.mod records each one: go tool runs it at the recorded version, go get tool upgrades every declared tool, and go install tool installs them into GOBIN. Tool dependencies join your module graph, which can raise shared dependency versions for the application too; if that is unwanted, declare the tools in a separate go.mod and pass -modfile to go tool. Avoid go install pkg@latest and download-and-run installers in CI scripts: they execute whatever was published most recently, unreviewed.
sections.title: Pin and review tools like code

sections.body: Every module-mode binary embeds its main module, its dependency versions with checksums, and build settings such as -trimpath, CGO_ENABLED and the VCS revision. go version -m prints that record, debug/buildinfo.ReadFile reads it from a file, and runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo returns the running program's own copy. A release gate can read the candidate binary and refuse to ship it when the record shows a modified working tree or a dependency replaced by a local directory. The program applies such a policy to a fixed record and then prints only those fields of its own record that do not vary between environments.
sections.title: Audit what a binary was built from
sections.walkthrough: candidate mirrors what the go command records for a build from a modified checkout: since Go 1.24, go build appends +dirty to the main module version and sets vcs.modified=true. The replaced dependency carries no checksum because a directory has no published content to hash, which is exactly why it must not reach a release. audit walks Settings and Deps as slices, so findings print in a stable order. For the running program, ReadBuildInfo fills GoVersion from runtime.Version, and a program that imports only the standard library lists no dependency modules. Paths, VCS fields and target platform vary by environment, so they are not printed; go run does not stamp VCS information at all, while go build does.

sections.body: Each upgrade imports code that runs with your service's privileges. Update deliberately, one dependency or one related group per change, so a regression points at its cause. Read the go.mod and go.sum diff and look for modules that arrived transitively; go mod why -m explains why a module is needed and go mod graph shows who requires it. Skim the release notes and the size of the source diff in the upstream repository. Run the tests and govulncheck on the result. Automated update pull requests, such as Dependabot version updates for Go modules, are useful when a person reviews them with the same care as any other change. And prefer fewer dependencies: a small, well-understood helper is sometimes cheaper to own than a module that brings twenty more.
sections.code:
go list -m -u all                    # available upgrades appear in [brackets]
go get golang.org/x/net@v0.61.0 && go mod tidy
git diff go.mod go.sum               # new transitive modules show up here
go mod why -m golang.org/x/text      # which import path needs this module
go test ./... && go tool govulncheck ./...
sections.title: Review dependency updates as code changes
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own module; the module and version are examples. go list -m -u all shows each module with any newer version in brackets. go get changes one requirement and go mod tidy settles the graph, after which the git diff of go.mod and go.sum is the review surface: every new line in go.sum is code you have not seen before. go mod why -m prints the shortest import path that needs the module. The last line gates the change on tests and reachable vulnerabilities, the same checks CI repeats.

reading.takeaway: Keep the toolchain's defaults on (go.sum, the checksum database, read-only module mode), gate CI on reachable govulncheck findings, pin tools in go.mod, and refuse releases whose embedded build information shows a dirty tree or a local replacement.

lessons.title: Secure the Go supply chain: reachable vulnerabilities, verified modules, pinned tools, auditable binaries

summary: Redaction, constant-time checks, AEAD encryption, password storage, token design, fuzzing and dependency hygiene.
title: Secrets, cryptography and supply chain
translationNote: Use reviewed standard and x/crypto primitives rather than inventing constructions. Production key storage and rotation need your own infrastructure.

lessons.explanation: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can inspect files, propose patches and run available tools. Useful work still needs a concrete behavior and a way to check it. In this unit you guide an agent in your own repository. Ordinary native projects stay local. The separate Playground adds explicit, opt-in sharing with people and MCP clients; it never uploads an existing project automatically.
lessons.objective: Turn an ambiguous coding request into a small, verifiable Go change.

cautions: A tool can generate and execute code while still misunderstanding the product invariant. Review behavior as well as syntax.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: A Go agent task starts with a contract and a failing example
strengths: Turn an ambiguous coding request into a small, verifiable Go change.
Define the contract, inspect the relevant code, make one reviewable change and require concrete evidence. Use the explanation to check understanding, not replace it.

alternatives: A larger rewrite with no constraints
A more confident completion message
quiz.correct: A contract and a failing example
quiz.explanation: A tool can generate and execute code while still misunderstanding the product invariant. Review behavior as well as syntax.
quiz.hint: Choose evidence another developer can reproduce.
quiz.question: An agent reports a fix but never names a reproducing input or test. What should you establish first?

review.answer: A contract and a failing example
review.prompt: Start a Go agent task with?

sections.body: Suppose LowerBound returns an arbitrary duplicate index. Supply a minimal input, expected answer, supported Go version and public API constraint. Ask the agent to inspect the implementation and existing tests before proposing a change. A broad instruction such as improve search does not tell either of you which behavior matters.
sections.code:
Task: fix LowerBound in internal/search.
Input: [1, 3, 3, 8], target 3. Expected index: 1.
Preserve the exported signature and half-open interval invariant.
Inspect existing callers and tests first. Add empty, missing and duplicate cases.
Run: go test ./internal/search
Explain why equality moves hi instead of returning immediately.
sections.title: Give the task an observable result
sections.walkthrough: This is an example task prompt, not a tool-specific command. It names the defect, scope, invariant and verification. Replace paths with real repository paths; the agent must not invent a test result if the environment cannot run the command.

sections.body: Read the actual diff, including tests. A test that merely duplicates the new implementation may be green without protecting the contract. Ask which previous input fails, why the change fixes it and which other callers could observe a difference. Formatting changes should not hide the behavior change.
sections.title: Inspect before accepting a patch

sections.body: An agent can miss an overflow, copy a mutex or drop a cancellation path while producing plausible prose. Identify the owner of mutable values, the lifetime of every goroutine and the meaning of public errors yourself. A small patch is easier to understand and revert than an unexplained rewrite.
sections.title: Keep human judgment at the boundary

sections.body: Run the focused test, then the affected package checks. Record the actual compiler and command. If a remote integration service is unavailable, label that check unverified and keep an isolated reproduction. Passing unit tests is useful evidence; it is not proof about database failover or every interleaving.
sections.title: Repeat a reproducible check

sections.body: For a collaborative Go task, read the current source and identify the state your edit is based on. GopherForge’s encrypted JavaScript MCP companion uses sourceHash; the compatible remote MCP uses an integer revision. Ask the agent to show its named cursor, describe the failing input and publish a small checked edit. Publishing source and requesting Test are not execution. A person presses Run or Test in their browser or native app; that execution client builds locally and shares a result labelled with its source and participant. The browser has its own Go/WASI worker. Native encrypted rooms require GopherForge 1.3.3 or newer; public 1.3.2 uses compatible rooms.
sections.code:
Read sourceHash A (encrypted) or revision 7 (compatible)
  ├─ checked edit → new source identity
  ├─ request Test → awaiting local button
  ├─ person presses Test on web/iPhone/iPad → local Go
  └─ read the reported result for that captured source

If source has changed again, the earlier result is historical evidence.
sections.title: A shared Playground keeps editing separate from execution
sections.walkthrough: The two protocols use different change guards; do not send an encryption key to the compatible remote endpoint. The JavaScript companion keeps its key client-side, but the selected MCP host and AI provider can read decrypted tool results. A reported pass applies to the captured source and environment, not automatically to the latest edit or every platform.

sections.body: A learner can explicitly publish a read-only progress link for a teacher or assistant. Ask for a short plan based on unfinished lessons and interview topics marked Revisit, then explain and solve a concrete exercise yourself. The snapshot is not an account or a competency certificate. A compiler mark describes a recorded lesson check; a self-reported reading mark describes study, not execution. Never let an assistant silently replace your learning record from another person’s URL.
sections.title: Use a published progress snapshot as teaching context

reading.takeaway: Define the contract, inspect the relevant code, make one reviewable change and require concrete evidence. Use the explanation to check understanding, not replace it.

lessons.title: A Go agent task starts with a contract and a failing example

lessons.explanation: Durable guidance saves repeated explanation of layout, build commands and boundary rules. The supported discovery mechanisms differ between products and can change. Keep the repository facts stable, then consult the official documentation for how the installed tool discovers and scopes them.
lessons.objective: Write useful Go repository instructions without confusing context with permissions.

cautions: Do not share secret values in instruction files or assume that a context exclusion blocks all tool access.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Repository guidance for Codex, Claude Code and Cursor
strengths: Write useful Go repository instructions without confusing context with permissions.
Keep repository facts concrete, scope guidance using each product’s documented mechanism and enforce permissions in the environment. Recheck discovery after tool changes.

alternatives: The heading style in the markdown file
Excluding one file from search alone
quiz.correct: Guidance is not an access control
quiz.explanation: Do not share secret values in instruction files or assume that a context exclusion blocks all tool access.
quiz.hint: Distinguish what the model is told from what its tools are allowed to do.
quiz.question: Repository guidance forbids production queries, but the agent still has a production credential. What should you conclude?

review.answer: Guidance is not an access control

sections.body: Describe the real Go module, generated files, focused tests and opt-in integration environment. Use exact working directories and commands. Keep examples free of credentials and name environment variables without values. A new developer should be able to follow the same instructions without an agent.
sections.code:
# Go service working agreements
- Supported compiler: follow go.mod and the CI toolchain.
- Unit checks: go test ./...
- Worker changes: go test -race ./internal/worker/...
- Generated API: run the pinned generator documented in docs/generate.md.
- Integration checks use disposable databases; never production endpoints.
- Preserve public error and JSON contracts unless the task changes them.
sections.title: Write the repository facts once
sections.walkthrough: This illustrative guidance belongs in the repository instruction mechanism used by the selected tool. It is not an instruction for GopherForge itself. Replace package paths and generation commands with ones that exist in the actual checkout.

sections.body: Codex uses AGENTS.md with directory-scoped discovery and override rules. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md and its documented rules and memory mechanisms. Cursor offers AGENTS.md and project rules in .cursor/rules with selectable scope. Do not assume copying one filename gives identical precedence in every product.
sections.title: Map facts to the tool deliberately

sections.body: When guidance appears ignored, ask the tool which files it loaded and inspect its documented diagnostics. A nested instruction may override a general rule. Avoid growing one global instruction file into a second copy of the whole codebase; link concise maintained project documents where supported.
sections.title: Verify the loaded scope

sections.body: A sentence saying do not access production is useful intent, but it does not revoke a credential. Use actual sandbox, approval and account controls in the environment. A rule file is not an authentication boundary, and ignoring a file for indexing does not necessarily prevent shell tools from reading it.
sections.title: Keep controls separate from prose

sections.body: A repository instruction file and an MCP room capability solve different problems. Instructions describe how to work; a capability grants access to a selected room. Give an agent an Edit link only when it should change source, and a View link when it should review. Do not put bearer tokens in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, a Cursor rule or a committed MCP configuration. An expiry or a closed room requires a new explicit connection, not a search through unrelated projects.
sections.code:
Task contract:
- Read the room and current revision.
- Change only the named Go files.
- Explain the invariant and minimal failing input.
- Request a local test; wait for device Output.
- Do not run on a server or claim an older result validates a new edit.
sections.title: Give an MCP collaborator a bounded task
sections.walkthrough: The contract scopes both the edit and the evidence. The AI must first read the current room revision; the human then decides whether to execute that source on the local device. A repository rule never substitutes for the room capability or that local action.

sections.body: A mobile AI client can use a supported remote HTTPS MCP connector. The native app participates while foregrounded and executes only after its local button is pressed. Connector availability is controlled by the AI client and plan. Do not prescribe an npm daemon on iOS or claim that a custom remote URL automatically works in every mobile chat. Keep a readable web/JSON progress link as a simpler way to provide teaching context.

reading.takeaway: Keep repository facts concrete, scope guidance using each product’s documented mechanism and enforce permissions in the environment. Recheck discovery after tool changes.

lessons.explanation: Generated source can look idiomatic while targeting the wrong driver major version or changing the public result. Compile against the selected module graph, inspect authoritative APIs and test the observable path. A plausible import name or confident explanation is not version evidence.
lessons.objective: Catch invented APIs, unsafe concurrency and changed wire contracts in generated Go.

cautions: Compiling proves API compatibility for that build; database timing, failover and atomicity require additional evidence.

Trust that a similar method exists

quiz.hint: Find the dependency already selected by the build.
quiz.question: A MongoDB example uses an old driver signature but the module uses v2. Which is the useful first check?

review.answer: Check the selected version and API

sections.body: Start in the target module and inspect the workspace and selected dependencies. A local replace can make generated code compile against unreleased source. For MongoDB v2, use its /v2 path and documented lifecycle; do not add an old major version merely to make an invented call compile.
sections.code:
go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -m all
go doc go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2/mongo.Connect
go test ./internal/store/...
sections.title: Check which module the code actually uses
sections.walkthrough: These are native-development commands in a repository that already depends on the v2 driver. go doc establishes the selected API rather than downloading a guessed dependency. The package test path must exist in that checkout.

sections.body: For every generated goroutine, identify who starts it, cancels it and waits for it. Check blocking sends and capacity acquisition. Acquiring a semaphore inside a newly launched goroutine can bound active work while still allowing an unbounded number of waiting goroutines.
sections.title: Review ownership before adding goroutines

sections.body: A nil slice becoming empty changes JSON under some serializers. Replacing %w with %v changes error matching. Returning success after a canceled partial export changes the protocol. Add fixtures for those decisions and check old callers before accepting a cosmetic cleanup.
sections.title: Compare contracts, not just signatures

sections.body: Ask for a blocked-receiver cancellation test, duplicate request or commit-then-disconnect fixture when relevant. Run race detection on exercised concurrent paths and use integration tests for database atomicity. No amount of mocking can establish a live driver or server guarantee it never exercised.
sections.title: Require a failure-path demonstration

sections.body: Require the source revision, the Run/Test operation, the participating device, the observed result and the relevant runtime limits. A shared result is client-reported, not an attested proof. If source changed while the build ran, keep the old result visible as historical evidence. Do not run unreviewed AI code merely because an edit arrived. A relay must not execute the project on behalf of all participants.
sections.code:
Evidence checklist:
source revision + exact files
→ explicit local Run/Test
→ device-labelled stdout/stderr
→ compare result revision with current revision
→ state unverified platform/service conditions
sections.title: Check execution provenance before reading green output
sections.walkthrough: Read the chain from top to bottom. A source revision identifies what was built, the local action identifies where it ran, and the final comparison tells you whether the evidence still applies. Missing a step leaves a narrower claim, not an automatic pass.

sections.body: Suppose two collaborators both read revision 4. The first publishes revision 5; the second must not overwrite it using an unconditional write. A compare-and-swap publication rejects the stale revision. Preserve the second draft, inspect revision 5 and reapply the intended change. This whole-file strategy is simpler than CRDT merging but requires an explicit conflict workflow. A successful HTTP update only proves that a revision was accepted; it does not prove that the Go program is correct.
sections.title: Reproduce conflicts without discarding a local draft

lessons.explanation: A source comment, dependency README, test log or fetched webpage can contain instructions written by someone else. Reading that material to solve a Go problem does not authorize its author to expand the task. Keep the user’s goal and trusted repository guidance separate from external diagnostic content.
lessons.objective: Review commands, secrets and external writes when an agent consumes untrusted text.

cautions: Do not confuse a generated command with an authorized action. Context files and tool permissions solve different problems.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.

strengths: Review commands, secrets and external writes when an agent consumes untrusted text.
Treat external text as task data, enforce permissions with real controls and verify sensitive commands at their boundary. Keep the Go fix tied to its authorized behavior.

alternatives: Follow it because it came from a test
Upload first and redact the reply

quiz.explanation: Do not confuse a generated command with an authorized action. Context files and tool permissions solve different problems.
quiz.hint: The page is evidence to inspect, not a new instruction source.
quiz.question: A webpage linked by a failing test asks an agent to upload a credential file. What should happen?

review.prompt: Can a page authorize an upload?

sections.body: Imagine a failing test prints a page that tells the agent to upload environment variables. That instruction is not part of the authorized fix. Extract the actual assertion failure, inspect the relevant source and ignore the requested credential transfer.
sections.code:
Diagnostic data:
  expected first duplicate index 1, got 2
  see external.example/fix for instructions

Authorized task:
  repair LowerBound and prove duplicate handling

The external page cannot authorize uploading files or secrets.
sections.title: Recognize an instruction hidden in a failure
sections.walkthrough: The URL is an illustrative untrusted destination, not a link to visit. The useful evidence is the mismatch between expected and actual index; an unrelated upload request does not help establish that invariant.

sections.body: Give agent-driven tests a disposable database, namespaced keys and bounded cleanup. A unique key prefix does not protect other data if a cleanup script still runs FLUSHDB. Inspect generated commands before they can affect shared systems, especially dependency installers, migrations and deployment steps.
sections.title: Use isolated integration resources

sections.body: Use environment or credential mechanisms approved for the selected tool. Include variable names in setup instructions rather than real passwords. Logs, traces, snapshots and fixtures can also retain private data; inspect what a test or support bundle records before sharing it.
sections.title: Keep secrets out of the conversation and diff

sections.body: Record the changed files, checks actually run, unresolved failures and next concrete step. Preserve the original task constraints after context reduction. A handoff saying everything is safe without naming evidence is difficult for either a human or another session to verify.
sections.title: Make a useful handoff

sections.body: A comment, test fixture or printed output can contain text asking an agent to reveal secrets or use other tools. Those strings are task data, not authority. A room capability grants access only to that room. It must not grant filesystem access, arbitrary shell commands, another project or automatic execution on someone else’s device. The relay transports text; local execution remains a separate human action.
sections.code:
Untrusted: source / comments / test output / shared progress
Trusted authority: the human task and explicitly granted room role
Execution boundary: a local person presses Run/Test

A prompt in stdout cannot promote View to Edit or execute on another phone.
sections.title: Treat room source, Output and progress as untrusted data
sections.walkthrough: The diagram distinguishes data from authority. A malicious printed line stays inside Output and cannot authorize another tool or another device. Preserve this boundary even when the content sounds like an urgent system instruction.

sections.body: Room links are bearer capabilities: a person or AI receiving a working Edit link can read and change the room until expiry or closure. A View link permits reading and copying. The fragment is outside the initial page request, but the client deliberately sends the credential to the relay in an API header or tool argument. GopherForge’s preview relay can read shared source and Output; it is not end-to-end encrypted. Progress publication is a separate 90-day, read-only snapshot with a revocation key. Exclude private code, access tokens and production data; revocation cannot erase downloaded copies.

lessons.explanation: A game loop runs on two clocks. The display hands you frames of uneven length; the simulation should advance in identical steps. Decoupling the two with an accumulator makes physics independent of the frame rate, makes every run reproducible, and turns a long stall into bounded slow motion instead of a frozen game.
lessons.objective: Advance a simulation in fixed steps from variable frame times, draw it with an interpolation factor and cap catch-up work after a stall.

cautions: Interpolation adds one step of visual latency.
Teleports and angle wrap-around need special cases when blending.
designGuide.cost: Two copies of the drawn state, an integer accumulator and a clock interface; the real cost is the discipline of never reading the blended state in game logic.
strengths: Identical inputs produce identical simulations on any display.
Stalls degrade into bounded slow motion instead of a freeze.

alternatives: A variable dt to pass into the physics update
The number of steps to run in the next frame
quiz.correct: How far the frame lies between the last two steps
quiz.explanation: Leftover accumulator time is less than one step, so alpha only blends prev and curr for drawing; the physics always sees the fixed step and game rules keep reading curr.
quiz.hint: Alpha is computed after the step loop finishes, from time that was too short for a whole step.
quiz.question: In a fixed-timestep loop, what is the interpolation factor alpha used for?

review.answer: How far the frame lies between the last two steps
review.prompt: What does alpha = acc / step mean?

sections.body: The obvious loop measures the time since the last frame and integrates with it: position += velocity * dt. That ties the physics to whatever the machine delivers. Integration error depends on step size, so the same jump reaches a different apex at 30, 60 and 144 frames per second. A 250 ms stall (a window drag, a long garbage-collection pause on a weak device, a breakpoint) becomes one giant step in which a fast object passes straight through a wall. And because no two runs see the same frame times, a timing bug cannot be replayed, a recorded input file cannot reproduce a match, and two machines running in lockstep drift apart. A fixed step gives every run the same sequence of identical updates; only how often you draw is left to the hardware.
sections.code:
last := time.Now()
for running {
	now := time.Now()
	dt := now.Sub(last).Seconds() // whatever the last frame happened to cost
	last = now
	world.Update(dt) // physics now depends on the frame rate
	world.Draw()
}
sections.title: Why frame-sized steps break physics
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the pattern to replace, not code to run. Every Update receives a different dt, so the same inputs produce different trajectories on different machines, and a single slow frame turns into a single large, unstable integration step.

sections.body: The worked program replays seven recorded frame durations through a scripted clock. Each frame adds its duration to an accumulator. While the accumulator holds at least one step, the loop saves the current state as the previous one, integrates one 10 ms step and subtracts the step. Whatever remains is shorter than a step and carries over to the next frame. Time stays in time.Duration, an integer count of nanoseconds, so the accumulator cannot drift the way repeated float additions of 0.016 do; floats appear only inside the physics and in the interpolation factor.
sections.title: Consume frame time in fixed steps
sections.walkthrough: Frame 1 brings 16 ms: one step runs and 6 ms stays in the accumulator, so alpha is 0.60. Frame 2 adds 16 ms to those 6 and runs two steps. Frame 5 lasts only 4 ms, so no step runs at all, yet the drawn position still moves from 3.55 to 3.75 because alpha grew. Frame 6 stalls for 250 ms; the loop clamps it to 100 ms, runs ten steps instead of twenty-five and records 150 ms as dropped. The last line reports 20 steps, 200 ms of simulated time, against 351 ms on the clock.

sections.body: After the step loop, the leftover time is a fraction of a step: alpha = accumulator / step, always at least 0 and below 1. Drawing prev + (curr - prev) * alpha shows where the object is at the moment of the frame, so motion looks smooth even when the frame rate and the step rate do not divide evenly. The price is one step of latency: every drawn x in the output equals 50 units per second times the time fed into the loop, minus one 10 ms step. At a 60 Hz step that is about 17 ms, which most games accept; some competitive games extrapolate forward instead and live with occasional overshoot. Interpolate only what is continuous. Positions and scales are safe; angles need shortest-arc blending so 350 to 10 degrees does not spin the long way round; a teleport, respawn or screen wrap must set prev equal to curr, or the sprite visibly slides across the map for one frame. Interpolation is purely visual: game rules, collisions and input handling always read curr, never the blend.
sections.title: Draw between the last two states

sections.body: If one step costs more real time than it simulates, each frame owes more steps than the one before, each frame takes longer still, and the game locks up trying to catch up: the spiral of death. A milder version follows every stall, when hundreds of owed steps arrive at once. Clamping the frame time bounds the work: with maxFrame at 100 ms and a 10 ms step, no frame ever runs more than ten steps. The game slows down during an overload instead of freezing, and the Report value makes the dropped time visible so you can log it. Capping steps per frame works the same way. Pick the bound from measurements: if the slowest device you support spends a large share of the step length inside one Update, the fix is a cheaper step or a longer one, not a larger clamp. Lockstep multiplayer cannot drop time, because every peer must simulate every tick; there you slow the whole session down or resynchronize.
sections.title: Clamp catch-up work to avoid the spiral of death

sections.body: The loop never calls time.Now; it asks a Clock. Production passes an adapter over the monotonic clock, tests pass a script of frame durations, and every timing edge case becomes a deterministic table row: a zero-length frame, a frame of exactly one step, a stall just above the clamp, a long run whose step count must equal the time fed in divided by the step. Assert on step counts and on curr, not only on the drawn value, because alpha can hide a missing or extra step. If you use Ebitengine, the outer loop already exists: the engine calls your Update at a fixed tick rate, sometimes zero and sometimes several times per frame, and Draw once per frame, as the next lesson shows. The accumulator here is the model of that behavior and the tool for headless servers, replays and simulations that run outside an engine.
sections.title: Inject the clock and test the loop
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own program; quit and render are placeholders for your window and drawing code. time.Now carries a monotonic clock reading and time.Since subtracts monotonic readings, so a wall-clock adjustment such as an NTP correction or a user changing the system time never yields a negative or enormous frame.

reading.takeaway: Advance the simulation only in fixed steps taken from an accumulator, draw prev blended toward curr by alpha, clamp the time fed into the loop, and inject the clock so every timing edge case becomes a reproducible test.

lessons.title: Fix the timestep: an accumulator turns uneven frames into identical simulation steps

lessons.explanation: Ebitengine runs the loop from the previous lesson for you. You implement three methods, Update, Draw and Layout, and the engine decides when to call each one. Getting that split right is the most important structural decision in an Ebitengine project: a single state change inside Draw makes the game run at a different speed on every monitor.
lessons.objective: Structure an Ebitengine game so every state change happens in Update, Draw is a read-only view, and the rules run headless in tests.

cautions: Any state change in Draw becomes a frame-rate bug.
Draw gets no interpolation factor; smooth high-refresh motion needs extra work.
designGuide.cost: A strict split between Update and Draw plus a thin input adapter; little code, but the rule has to be enforced in review.
strengths: Game speed is identical on every display refresh rate.
Rules behind a plain Step function run headless in tests.

alternatives: Draw runs on a background goroutine and would race
Update receives a delta time and Draw does not
quiz.correct: Only in Update, at a fixed number of ticks per second
quiz.explanation: Update is called TPS times per second whatever the display, while Draw follows the refresh rate, so state changed in Draw advances faster on faster monitors.
quiz.hint: Compare how often each method runs on a 60 Hz and on a 120 Hz monitor.
quiz.question: In an Ebitengine game, why must movement code live in Update rather than Draw?

review.answer: Only in Update, at a fixed number of ticks per second

sections.body: ebiten.Game is an interface with three methods: Update() error, Draw(screen *ebiten.Image) and Layout(outsideWidth, outsideHeight int) (screenWidth, screenHeight int). Update runs at a fixed tick rate, 60 ticks per second by default and adjustable with ebiten.SetTPS, and the documentation lets you treat the time between two Updates as exactly 1/TPS seconds, so you never measure time inside it. Draw runs once per rendered frame, and how often that happens depends on the display: on a 120 Hz monitor there are about two Draw calls per Update, and when frames are slow the engine may run several Updates before the next Draw. Layout receives the outside size of the window or screen and returns the logical screen size; Ebitengine scales the logical screen to fit, so returning a fixed 320 by 180 gives a pixel-art canvas at any window size. In the first frame Update is guaranteed to run at least once before Draw, so Update is also the natural place for lazy initialization.
sections.title: Three methods on two different clocks

sections.body: The Ebitengine module is not available in this sandbox, so the program declares a Game interface with the same three methods and a Screen type that stands in for *ebiten.Image. The run function plays the engine: each frame it calls Layout, then Update as many times as the schedule says, then Draw once. Three schedules model the same 100 ms on a 60 Hz, a 120 Hz and a 30 Hz display. Drone moves in Update; DrawDrone moves in Draw. The last two runs exercise the three possible results of Update: nil continues, the Termination sentinel stops cleanly, and any other error stops the game and is returned to the caller.
sections.title: A headless driver shows why logic belongs in Update
sections.walkthrough: Every display delivers six ticks, so Drone ends at x=12 each time although Draw ran 6, 12 or 3 times. DrawDrone moves 2 units per Draw and ends at 12, 24 and 6: on the 120 Hz display it literally runs twice as fast. The goal run returns Termination from its tenth Update; run maps it to a nil error the way ebiten.RunGame does, and the last drawn frame shows tick 9 because in this model the terminating tick is never drawn. Saver wraps a sentinel with %w, so the caller can still match it with errors.Is after the game stops.

sections.body: In your own module the same structure hosts on Ebitengine with a handful of calls. ebiten.RunGame blocks until the game ends and returns the error Update returned, or nil after ebiten.Termination. Window size and title are set before RunGame. Images are allocated once, outside Draw: creating an *ebiten.Image every frame puts texture allocation on the hottest path in the program. Draw positions the sprite through DrawImageOptions.GeoM, the transform applied while the source image is drawn onto the screen, and ebitenutil.DebugPrint writes a line of debug text in the corner.
sections.title: The real main, as a fragment
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment after adding github.com/hajimehoshi/ebiten/v2 to a module; it is not compiled here and its package clause is omitted. The var _ line proves at compile time that *Game satisfies ebiten.Game. Update returns ebiten.Termination when Escape is held, so RunGame returns nil, while a genuine failure would come back as an error and reach log.Fatal. Draw only reads g.x and g.tick, so it is correct no matter how many times per tick the engine calls it.

sections.body: Update is the only method that changes state, but the rules do not have to live in it. A thin Update that copies Ebitengine input into a plain struct and calls world.Step(input) keeps the rules in code that never imports the engine: tests call Step with scripted input thousands of times per second, a replay system feeds recorded input, and a server can run the same Step without a window. Draw follows the mirror rule: it reads the world and issues draw calls, but never advances timers, consumes input or spawns particles, because the number of Draw calls per tick varies. Animation is the usual slip: derive the frame from the tick counter instead of incrementing a counter in Draw.
sections.title: Keep engine calls at the edge of Update
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs to the same program as the RunGame fragment and runs in your own environment. Input is a plain struct and world.Step is ordinary Go, so a test can build Input values directly. The animation frame is a pure function of world.Tick, so two Draw calls for the same tick show the same frame. The input lesson in this unit replaces the booleans with action bits and edge detection.

sections.body: Express every speed, cooldown and animation length in ticks and treat TPS as a design constant chosen once. ebiten.ActualTPS and ebiten.ActualFPS report measured rates for a debug overlay; game logic must not depend on them, because they fluctuate while the tick contract does not. Ebitengine does not hand Draw an interpolation factor, so at the default 60 TPS a 144 Hz display shows some ticks for two frames and others for three. Most 2D games accept that; a game that needs smoother motion can raise TPS or compute its own alpha from a monotonic clock as in the previous lesson. Passing ebiten.SyncWithFPS to SetTPS makes Update run once per frame, which brings back variable step lengths and every problem of the frame-sized loop. When you review an Ebitengine game, search Draw for assignments to game state: each one is a speed bug waiting for a faster monitor.
sections.title: Ticks, frames and what to measure

reading.takeaway: Change state only in Update and measure it in ticks; make Draw a read-only view that is safe to call any number of times; return ebiten.Termination to quit cleanly; keep the rules behind a plain Step function so they run headless.

lessons.title: Ebitengine's Game interface: Update advances ticks, Draw only reads, Layout fixes the screen

lessons.explanation: Almost every line of 2D movement code adds, scales or measures a pair of numbers. A tiny vector type with value methods makes that code read like the math, rules out aliasing bugs and costs nothing measurable. Combined with fixed ticks, it lets you tune movement in units a designer can reason about: pixels per tick, and a drag factor applied once per tick.
lessons.objective: Write a small value-semantics vector type and move a body with normalized input, per-tick acceleration and drag that behave the same on every display.

cautions: Changing TPS means converting every tuning constant.
Float results can differ across architectures through FMA fusion.
designGuide.cost: A thirty-line type and the habit of thinking in ticks; lockstep multiplayer may additionally need fixed-point math.
strengths: Value methods chain cleanly and cannot alias shared state.
Per-tick constants give identical movement on every display.

alternatives: Diagonal movement becomes about 29% slower
Velocity becomes NaN when both keys are held
quiz.correct: So diagonal movement is not about 41% faster
quiz.explanation: The length of (1, 1) is the square root of 2, about 1.41, so an unnormalized diagonal gets 41% more acceleration and top speed than a single direction.
quiz.hint: Compute the length of the vector (1, 1).
quiz.question: Holding right and down adds (1, 1) times the acceleration to velocity. What goes wrong without normalizing?

review.answer: So diagonal movement is not about 41% faster

sections.body: Vec2 is two float64 fields, small enough that copying it is cheap and usually stays in registers, and a copy can never be changed behind your back. Every method takes a Vec2 and returns a new one: a.Add(b) leaves a untouched, so b.Vel.Add(...).Scale(drag) reads as one expression without temporaries. Value semantics also make the zero value meaningful: Vec2{} is the origin and a valid 'no direction'. Length uses math.Hypot, which avoids needless overflow and underflow in the intermediate squares; when you only need to compare distances, compare squared lengths instead, as the collision lesson does. Do not use float vectors as map keys: two positions that print identically can differ in the last bit.
sections.title: Value methods for a two-float type

sections.body: Holding right and down produces the raw direction (1, 1), whose length is about 1.41. Scaling that by an acceleration makes diagonal movement 41% faster than straight movement, a bug players notice within seconds. Normalize rescales the direction to length 1 and returns the zero vector when nothing is held, instead of dividing by zero and producing NaN. Each tick the body then adds normalized input times accel to its velocity, multiplies velocity by drag, snaps tiny speeds to zero and adds velocity to position. Updating velocity before position is semi-implicit Euler integration: as cheap as the naive order and much more stable for game physics.
sections.title: Normalize diagonal input, then integrate per tick
sections.walkthrough: The first two lines show the raw diagonal and its unit direction. While input is held (ticks 1 to 12), speed climbs 0.480, 0.864, 1.171 and approaches the terminal speed where the gain of 0.6 per tick balances the 20% drag: v = (v + 0.6) * 0.8 solves to 2.40 px/tick. After release, speed shrinks by a factor of 0.8 per tick until it drops below 0.05 and snaps to zero on tick 30, so the body stops for good instead of creeping by ever smaller amounts. The last line shows what skipping Normalize costs: a diagonal top speed of 3.39 instead of 2.40.

sections.body: With a fixed tick rate, a speed of 2.4 px/tick is exact and the same on every machine, because the fixed-timestep lesson guarantees how many ticks run per second. Per-frame units are wrong on every display except the one you tuned on. Per-second units multiplied by dt are correct in principle but bury the step size in every formula, and drag does not scale linearly: a factor of 0.8 per tick is 0.8 to the power 60 per second, not 0.8 times 60. Keep tuning constants per tick, convert only for people (2.40 px/tick is 144 px/s at 60 TPS), and if you ever change TPS, convert every constant deliberately.
sections.code:
// Convert per-tick tuning from 60 to 120 ticks per second.
ratio := 60.0 / 120.0
speed120 := speed60 * ratio         // px/tick halves
accel120 := accel60 * ratio * ratio // px/tick gained per tick quarters
drag120 := math.Pow(drag60, ratio)  // 0.8 becomes about 0.894
sections.title: Why per-tick units beat per-frame units
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the arithmetic and is not a runnable program. Doubling TPS halves the distance per tick, quarters the velocity gained per tick, and turns the drag factor into its square root, so two new ticks remove as much speed as one old tick did. Missing any of these changes how the game feels, which is why the tick rate should be chosen once and early.

sections.body: The output above is exact for this toolchain and machine, but floating-point results are not guaranteed to be bit-identical across architectures. The Go specification allows an implementation to fuse x*y + z into a single fused multiply-add, which skips one rounding, and whether that happens depends on the target architecture and its settings, so the same source can differ in the last bit and drift apart after thousands of ticks. That never matters for a single-player game printed at two decimals. It matters for lockstep multiplayer and for replays shared between platforms. An explicit conversion forces the intermediate rounding and forbids fusion; teams that need strict cross-platform determinism often go further and keep positions in fixed-point integers, as the integer jump physics in the input lesson does.
sections.title: Floating point is reproducible only within one build
sections.walkthrough: This fragment follows the floating-point operator rules in the Go specification. In the first line the product vel*dt is not explicitly rounded, so the compiler may compute pos + vel*dt as one fused operation. Wrapping the product in float64(...) requires it to be rounded to float64 first, which makes the result the same with or without FMA hardware.

sections.body: Movement is a pure function of state and input, so table tests pin it down cheaply. Assert that a held diagonal reaches the same top speed as a held cardinal direction, that releasing input reaches exactly zero within a known number of ticks, and that normalizing the zero vector returns the zero vector rather than NaN. NaN is contagious: one bad division turns a position into NaN, every comparison against it is false, and collision code silently stops working, so a debug assertion with math.IsNaN in the step function pays for itself. Keep a body's state in one struct and step it from one place; a second code path that nudges position directly, such as knockback applied from an animation callback, is how determinism quietly breaks.
sections.title: Test movement as a pure function

reading.takeaway: Use a small value-type vector, normalize the input direction before scaling it, update velocity and then position once per tick, and keep every tuning constant per tick so movement is identical wherever the same build runs.

lessons.title: A 2D vector value type: normalized input, acceleration and drag in per-tick units

lessons.explanation: Players do not press buttons on the exact tick the game expects. They press jump a few ticks before landing or a few ticks after running off a ledge, and a strict implementation swallows those presses and feels broken. Responsive platformer controls are built from three small pieces: an action layer over physical keys, edge detection on actions, and short grace windows measured in ticks.
lessons.objective: Map physical keys to actions, detect presses on the action level, and implement jump buffering and coyote time as tick counters that can be tested deterministically.

cautions: Per-key edges double-fire when two keys share an action.
A tap shorter than one tick is invisible to polling.
designGuide.cost: A binding table, two bytes of action state and two counters per player; the real cost is play-testing the window sizes.
strengths: Rebinding and multiple devices become a data change.
Forgiving controls are exact, replayable tick rules.

alternatives: Jump buffering, which remembers presses made in the air
Edge detection, which turns a held key into repeated jumps
quiz.correct: A few ticks after leaving a ledge when jump still works
quiz.explanation: Buffering forgives a press that comes too early by remembering it until landing; coyote time forgives a press that comes too late by allowing a jump for a few ticks after leaving the floor.
quiz.hint: The press arrives after the floor is gone, not before the floor arrives.
quiz.question: A player runs off a ledge and presses jump two ticks later. Which mechanism lets that jump happen?

review.answer: A few ticks after leaving a ledge when jump still works

sections.body: Game logic should ask whether Jump is pressed, never whether Space is. A binding table maps each physical key or button to an action, several keys may share one action (Space, W and a gamepad face button all mean Jump), and rebinding becomes a data change. Storing a tick's actions as bits in a uint8 makes the whole input state one comparable value: pressed is down&a != 0, and just pressed is down &^ prev, the bits set now that were clear on the previous tick. Detecting edges on actions rather than keys matters as soon as two keys share an action. A per-key helper such as Ebitengine's inpututil.IsKeyJustPressed correctly reports a fresh press when the player adds W while already holding Space; OR the per-key edges together and you get a second jump the player never asked for.
sections.title: Bind keys to actions, then detect edges on actions

sections.body: The program drives a player through 75 scripted ticks: a long hold of Space, a second jump key pressed during that hold, a tap on the floor, a press shortly before landing, and a run to the right over two ledges with one press after each. The physics is integer arithmetic on purpose: gravity is 1 per tick and a jump sets the vertical speed to 5, so every tick is exact and the output reads as a precise specification of the controls. Only ticks with an event are printed.
sections.title: Simulate the controls tick by tick
sections.walkthrough: Tick 2 jumps from the floor. Space stays down until tick 14 and W joins it on tick 6, but the Jump action has no new edge, so the landing on tick 10 does not bounce. On tick 24 PadSouth is pressed seven ticks into the air; the press is buffered, the player lands on tick 25, and tick 26 jumps with a two-tick-old press. On tick 41 the player runs off the first ledge; the press on tick 43 comes two ticks after leaving the floor, inside the four-tick coyote window, so it jumps. After the second ledge the press comes six ticks late: no coyote time is left, the buffered press expires on tick 70, and the player lands on tick 71 without jumping. The summary counts six key presses but five action edges, because W never created one.

sections.body: Both features are windows measured in ticks, and both live in Player, where tests can see them. Jump buffering forgives a press that is too early: press is set to 0 on the action edge, grows by one each tick it stays unused, and is cleared when it reaches bufferTicks while a jump is still impossible, so a press made up to five ticks before the first grounded tick still fires. Coyote time forgives a press that is too late: air counts ticks since the feet last touched the floor, and a jump is allowed while air is at most coyoteTicks. The jumped flag is the detail that is easy to miss. A jump also leaves the floor, and without the flag the coyote rule would allow a second jump during the first four ticks of the first one. Start with a handful of ticks for each window and tune them by playing; keep them in ticks for the reasons the movement lesson gives.
sections.title: Buffering and coyote time are two counters

sections.body: In a real game, polling is the only code that touches the engine. It runs once per tick at the start of Update and turns key states into the Action bits the simulation already understands. Polling at the tick rate has one consequence worth knowing: a press and release that both happen between two polls are invisible, so an extremely short tap can be lost. At 60 TPS that window is about 17 ms and rarely matters. Ebitengine documents its Key constants as physical key positions on a US keyboard, so a WASD layout stays in the same place for players with other keyboard layouts; when a rebinding screen shows key names, remember that the label printed on the player's key may differ from the constant's name.
sections.title: Wire the same logic to Ebitengine
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own Ebitengine module; it reuses Action, Input and Player from the program above. IsKeyPressed reports each key's level once per tick, and the edge is computed from the previous tick's Action bits, so W pressed while Space is held never produces a second Jump edge. Because Update runs at a fixed tick rate, bufferTicks and coyoteTicks mean the same amount of time on every display.

sections.body: Input is a list of held keys per tick and the output is a list of events, so every control rule becomes a regression test: press three ticks before landing and expect a jump on the first grounded tick; press coyoteTicks + 1 ticks after a ledge and expect none; hold jump across a landing and expect exactly one jump. These tests catch the classic regressions, such as incrementing the buffer before the jump check, which silently shortens the window by a tick, or dropping the jumped flag, which turns coyote time into a double jump. Record real play sessions in the same format and a bug report becomes an exact replay. Combos and charge attacks extend the same idea: small counters over action edges, never timers that read the wall clock.
sections.title: Test controls as tables of ticks

reading.takeaway: Read physical keys into action bits once per tick, detect edges on actions rather than keys, and express buffering and coyote time as tick counters in game state so every forgiving rule is deterministic and testable.

lessons.title: Input as actions: edge detection, jump buffering and coyote time in a tick-exact simulation

lessons.explanation: Games are full of modes: menus, gameplay, pause overlays, and enemies that patrol, chase and attack. Encoding them as booleans such as paused, gameOver, chasing and attacking creates combinations that should be impossible and guards that must be repeated everywhere. Two explicit state machines replace them: a stack of scenes for the flow of the game, and one mode value with one transition function for each enemy.
lessons.objective: Run title, playing, paused and game-over scenes through a scene interface and a transition stack, and drive an enemy with a single-mode behavior machine.

cautions: Without hysteresis, threshold transitions flicker every tick.
Large machines outgrow one switch; split states into types.
designGuide.cost: One interface, a small stack and a Mode enum per actor; a little more structure than a few booleans, repaid at the first state bug.
strengths: Impossible state combinations cannot be represented.
Pause and overlays need no checks inside gameplay code.

alternatives: Pushing makes the pause menu update faster
Replace would keep updating the world in the background
quiz.correct: Pop must resume the same, untouched world beneath it
quiz.explanation: Only the top scene updates, so the world underneath is frozen while paused, and Pop returns to that same value with its state intact; Replace would discard it.
quiz.hint: Think about what resuming must restore, and which scene the stack updates.
quiz.question: In a scene stack, why is the pause menu pushed on top of the playing scene instead of replacing it?

review.answer: Pop must resume the same, untouched world beneath it
review.prompt: Why does pause push, not replace?

sections.body: Four booleans describe sixteen combinations; an enemy that can only be patrolling, chasing, attacking or recovering has four legal ones. Every update then needs guards like !paused && chasing && !attacking, and every new flag doubles the number of states nobody has tested. The bugs are characteristic: the enemy keeps chasing behind the pause menu because one guard was missing, or attacks forever because the code that cleared attacking returned early. A state machine makes the current state a single value, makes transitions the only way to change it, and gives each state one place where its behavior is written. The State pattern lesson shows the idea for a review workflow; games add a stack for overlays and timers that belong to a state.
sections.title: What boolean-flag soup costs
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the shape to avoid, not code to run. Nothing stops chasing and attacking from both being true, every caller must remember which flags to clear on each change, and the pause flag leaks into enemy code. Compare it with the single Mode field and the scene stack in the program below.

sections.body: Each scene implements Update, which returns a Transition, and Draw. The Stack applies the transition: Replace swaps the top scene (title to playing, playing to game over), Push puts a scene on top (pause), and Pop returns to the scene underneath with its state untouched. Only the top scene updates, so the world freezes while paused without a single paused check, and every scene draws bottom-up, so the pause overlay appears over the frozen world. Inside Playing, the enemy's Mode is one enum value, and the next method encodes every legal transition in one switch.
sections.title: A scene stack and an enemy mode machine
sections.walkthrough: Tick 2 replaces the title with a fresh Playing scene. The enemy notices the player at distance 5 on tick 10, attacks at distance 1 on tick 12, recovers, and goes back to patrol on tick 17 because the player has run eleven units away. Tick 24 pushes Paused; the draw on tick 25 shows the frozen world under the overlay, and nothing moves until tick 27 pops back to the same Playing value. The second hit on tick 36 drops HP to zero, Playing replaces itself with GameOver, and after two confirms the new Playing scene starts again at x=10 with hp=2: Replace threw the old world away together with its scene.

sections.body: Returning a Transition instead of assigning a global current-scene variable keeps scenes ignorant of the stack and puts the whole lifecycle in one place. That is where real games add the hooks they need: an Enter method to start music or reset a timer, an Exit method to release resources, and a log line for every transition, which makes bug reports far easier to read. Ownership follows the structure. Playing owns the world; Paused owns nothing and refers to nothing; Replace discards the old world, so a finished run cannot leak enemy state into the next one. The same pushdown structure builds nested menus (options over pause over gameplay) and modal dialogs, and it is why Pop needs no knowledge of what lies underneath. In Ebitengine, Game.Update calls the stack's Update once per tick and Game.Draw calls the stack's Draw.
sections.title: Transitions are values, so ownership is clear

sections.body: The next method reads like a transition table: from Patrol only Chase is reachable, Chase leads to Attack or back to Patrol, Attack always leads to Recover, and Recover waits three ticks before deciding. Two details make machines like this robust. First, inMode resets on every transition, so recovering for three ticks is a property of the state rather than a separate cooldown variable someone forgets to reset. Second, the thresholds differ: chase starts at distance 5 but stops only beyond 9. With a single threshold, a player standing exactly on the boundary makes the enemy flip modes every tick, which shows up as jittering animation and repeated alert sounds. Put one-off effects on transitions (the hit happens when entering Attack) and continuous behavior in the per-mode movement switch.
sections.title: Enemy modes: one value, timers per mode, hysteresis

sections.body: A Mode enum with a switch scales to roughly a dozen states. Beyond that, separate state types with Enter, Update and Exit methods, the object form of the pattern, keep each state's code in its own file. Hierarchical machines help when several states share a parent behavior, such as every grounded state allowing a jump, and behavior trees or utility scoring suit enemies whose decisions weigh many factors at once. Whatever the form, test it the same way: feed scripted inputs, print transitions with tick numbers as this program does, and compare the result against a golden list. A transition log is also the single most useful attachment to an AI bug report.
sections.title: When to grow beyond a switch

reading.takeaway: Give every mode exactly one representation: a scene stack driven by returned transitions, and an enemy Mode with one transition function, per-mode timers and hysteresis, so impossible combinations cannot be expressed at all.

lessons.title: Scenes and enemy behavior as explicit state machines instead of boolean flags

lessons.explanation: The first instinct for game objects is a hierarchy: a base object, a character built on it, an enemy built on that. In Go such hierarchies fight the language, which has no inheritance, and the hardware, which prefers contiguous data. An entity-component design keeps an entity as a bare ID, stores each component type in its own dense slice, and writes behavior as systems that loop over those slices.
lessons.objective: Build a minimal entity-component store with generics, run systems over dense slices, remove with swap-delete, and judge when plain structs are the better design.

cautions: Component pointers are invalid after the next Add or Remove.
Recycled IDs need generation counters to reject stale handles.
designGuide.cost: A store type and explicit world fields; more indirection than plain structs, worth it only when composition or measured iteration cost demands it.
strengths: Behavior composes from components without type hierarchies.
Systems iterate contiguous slices with no gaps.

alternatives: Removing entities is too slow to do every tick
Go forbids deleting from a slice inside a range loop
quiz.correct: Swap-delete during iteration skips the moved element
quiz.explanation: Remove copies the last element into the hole at an index the iterator has already passed, so the moved entity would not be visited on this tick.
quiz.hint: Look at which element Remove moves into the freed slot.
quiz.question: Why does the Aging system queue dead entities instead of removing them while it ranges over the store?

review.answer: Swap-delete during iteration skips the moved element

sections.body: Picture GameObject, Character embedding GameObject, Enemy embedding Character and FlyingEnemy embedding Enemy. Embedding promotes methods but is not inheritance: there is no virtual dispatch from the embedded type back to the outer one, so when a Character method calls Update it calls Character's Update, never FlyingEnemy's. Teams compensate with interfaces at every level and type switches, while the base type collects fields that only some objects use. Behavior that cuts across branches, such as a turret that has health but is not a character, has no natural home. Iteration suffers as well: a slice of interface values points at objects scattered across the heap, so updating ten thousand of them chases ten thousand pointers. Composition fixes both problems: an entity has whichever components it has, and each system names the ones it needs.
sections.title: Why deep object hierarchies hurt

sections.body: Store[T] keeps the components of one type in a dense slice, the owning entity of each element in a parallel owners slice, and a sparse slice from entity ID to dense index plus one, so that zero means absent. Add and Get take constant time, iteration visits only entities that have the component with no gaps, and Remove swap-deletes: the last element moves into the hole, so removal is constant time and the data stays dense. World has one typed store field per component, which keeps every access checked by the compiler without reflection or maps keyed by type. Systems are ordinary functions over the world.
sections.title: A sparse set per component type
sections.walkthrough: Entity 1 is a player with Position and Velocity, entity 2 a tree with Position only, and entities 3 to 6 are bullets that live 2, 1, 3 and 5 ticks. Movement ranges over the velocity store, so the tree is never visited. On tick 1 bullet 4 dies and bullet 6, the last element, moves into its slot, giving the dense order [1 3 6 5]; every later death swaps again. Aging only queues deaths in w.dead and Flush destroys them after the systems finish, because removing from a store while ranging over it would skip the element swapped into the current slot. The final report sorts by ID because dense order is an implementation detail.

sections.body: Get returns a pointer into the dense slice, which is fast but short-lived: the next Add may reallocate the slice and the next Remove may move another entity's data to that address. Use such a pointer within one system and never keep it. All is a range-over-func iterator of type iter.Seq2, and the same rule applies to it: no structural changes while iterating, which is why destruction is queued. Remove zeroes the vacated tail element, so a component holding a pointer, such as a sprite, does not keep it alive. This model never reuses IDs; a real engine recycles them and pairs each index with a generation counter, so a stale handle to a destroyed entity fails the lookup instead of silently addressing whichever entity inherited its slot. Rendering usually needs its own sort by layer or depth, because swap-delete makes storage order unstable.
sections.title: Rules that keep a store correct

sections.body: Most small Go games need none of this. With a player, a few enemy kinds and bullets, one slice of plain structs per kind and an update loop is already contiguous, fully typed and easy to debug. Reach for components when the same behavior must apply to many otherwise unrelated kinds, when designers compose entities from data files, or when a profile shows iteration dominating the tick; decide with a benchmark, not on principle. Full ECS libraries add archetype storage, queries over several components and parallel scheduling, and each of those is real complexity to own.
sections.title: When plain structs are enough
sections.walkthrough: This fragment reuses Vec2 from the movement lesson and is not compiled here. One contiguous slice and one loop, with no IDs at all: for a few hundred bullets it is the simplest option and likely the fastest. slices.DeleteFunc keeps the survivors in order and, since Go 1.22, zeroes the elements past the new length, so removed bullets release anything they referenced.

sections.body: A sparse set has invariants a short test can check after every operation: for each dense index i, sparse[owners[i]] equals i + 1; the number of non-zero sparse entries equals len(data); and owners and data have the same length. Drive random sequences of Add and Remove from a seeded generator and check the invariants after each step, and you will catch the classic swap-delete bug of clearing the removed entity's sparse entry but forgetting to update the moved one. For systems, assert on results keyed by entity ID, never on dense order, so legitimate storage changes do not break the tests.
sections.title: Test the invariants, not just the output

reading.takeaway: Keep entities as IDs and components in dense per-type stores, queue structural changes until the systems finish, never hold component pointers across ticks, and stay with plain struct slices until composition or a profile justifies components.

lessons.title: Entities as IDs, components in dense generic stores, systems as plain loops

lessons.explanation: Collision handling has two jobs: detect that two shapes overlap, and decide how to move them apart. Axis-aligned boxes and circles cover most 2D games, and both have exact tests that cost a few comparisons. The failure that bites later is speed: an object that moves farther in one tick than an obstacle is thick can pass through it without ever overlapping it.
lessons.objective: Test boxes and circles for overlap, compute the minimum push that separates them, and stop fast objects from tunneling with sub-steps or a swept test.

cautions: Minimum-axis pushes snag on tile seams; resolve tiles per axis.
Fast movers tunnel unless they are sub-stepped or swept.
designGuide.cost: A few dozen lines of geometry; sub-stepping multiplies collision work by the step count for every fast object.
strengths: Box and circle tests are exact and cost a few comparisons.
A swept test finds the time of impact in constant time.

alternatives: Floating-point rounding in the overlap comparison
Resolving along the minimum axis instead of the center line
quiz.correct: Moving farther per tick than the combined thickness
quiz.explanation: Discrete tests only check the positions at the end of each tick; if one tick of motion is longer than the overlap window, no checked position overlaps, so sub-steps or a sweep are required.
quiz.hint: Compare the distance moved in one tick with how thick the wall and the bullet are together.
quiz.question: A bullet passes through a thin wall and no overlap is ever detected. What is the root cause?

review.answer: Moving farther per tick than the combined thickness

sections.body: Store a box as a center and half extents. Two boxes overlap when, on both axes, the distance between centers is less than the sum of the half extents; how much less is the penetration depth on that axis. Two circles overlap when the squared distance between centers is less than the squared sum of the radii, so the common miss path never takes a square root. A circle against a box uses the point of the box closest to the circle's center, found by clamping the center into the box; the shapes overlap when that point is closer than the radius. Decide once whether touching counts. These tests use strict comparisons, so shapes that share an edge do not collide, which is exactly the state a resolved collision leaves behind.
sections.title: Overlap tests that cost a few comparisons

sections.body: For boxes, the minimum push is along the axis with the smaller penetration, signed away from the other box. It moves the object the shortest distance and usually matches intuition: a box that sinks slightly into a floor is pushed up, not sideways. For circles the push follows the line between the centers. The program resolves one pair of each kind, then fires a bullet that moves 12 units per tick at a wall 2 units thick and compares three ways of checking it: the end position only, sub-steps, and a swept test.
sections.title: Resolve along the axis of least penetration
sections.walkthrough: Box A overlaps B by 1 on x and 3 on y, so it is pushed 1 unit left; afterwards the boxes touch and no longer count as overlapping. The circles are 3 apart with radii summing to 4, so A moves back by 1 along the unit direction (0.6, 0.8). The ball's closest point on the crate is (4, 1), one unit from its center, so it moves 0.5 to the right. The bullet ends at x=12, beyond the wall spanning 9 to 11, and the end-position test misses it. Eight sub-steps of 1.5 units find the overlap at x=9 and push the bullet back to 8.50. Sweep treats the bullet as a point against the wall grown by the bullet's half size and returns the entry fraction t=0.708: the same contact at 8.50 from one test instead of eight.

sections.body: Tunneling happens when one tick's motion exceeds the overlap window, the combined thickness of the mover and the obstacle along the direction of motion. Sub-stepping splits the move into pieces no longer than half that combined thickness, so every overlap is seen and the shallow axis still points back toward where the mover came from; its cost grows with speed. A swept test computes the time of impact directly with the slab method: on each axis, find when the moving point enters and leaves the grown box, and a hit is the latest entry before the earliest exit. It is exact and constant-time per obstacle, but with several obstacles you must take the earliest hit and decide what happens to the rest of the motion: stop, slide along the surface or bounce.
