The cheapest fix is often design: cap speeds, or model bullets as rays.
sections.title: Tunneling and the two standard fixes

sections.body: Minimum-axis resolution has a known failure on tile maps. A player sliding along a floor made of separate tiles can reach a seam where the horizontal penetration into the next tile is momentarily smaller than the vertical one, and gets pushed sideways: the character snags on a flat floor. The standard fix for grid worlds is to move along x and resolve x against solid tiles using the sign of the motion, then move along y and resolve y. Each axis is pushed back the way it came, so seams never matter, and landing, ceiling bumps and wall stops fall out of which axis collided. Keep minimum-axis and circle resolution for free-moving objects such as pickups, debris and enemies bumping into each other.
sections.title: Platformers: move and resolve one axis at a time
sections.walkthrough: This fragment reuses AABB and Push from the program above and runs in your own project. The overlap test is the same, but the resolution ignores the shallow axis and snaps the box to the near face of the solid, chosen by the sign of dx. A matching moveY does the same vertically and reports a landing when dy is positive in screen coordinates, where y grows downward. Moves longer than a tile still need sub-steps.

sections.body: Collision bugs live at exact boundaries, so test them on purpose: shapes exactly touching (no hit), overlapping by a tiny amount, identical centers (the code must pick a fixed direction rather than divide by zero), a circle whose center is inside the box (the closest point equals the center, so the code falls back to the box rule), zero-length motion in Sweep, and motion parallel to a slab. Every case must give the same answer on every run, which is why these examples print fixed precision; compare floats in tests with a tolerance. Once many bodies interact, resolution order matters too: resolving pairs in a fixed order, such as the sorted pair list of the spatial hash lesson, keeps the outcome deterministic.
sections.title: Test collisions at the boundaries

reading.takeaway: Use strict overlap tests for boxes and circles, push along the shallow axis or the line between centers, resolve tile movement one axis at a time, and stop tunneling with sub-steps no longer than half the combined thickness or a swept time-of-impact test.

lessons.title: AABB and circle collisions: detect overlap, push out along the shallow axis, sweep fast movers

lessons.explanation: Checking every object against every other costs n(n-1)/2 tests: 124,750 for 500 objects, every tick, and almost all of those pairs are far apart. A broad phase discards distant pairs cheaply so the exact tests from the collision lesson run only on near candidates. A uniform grid stored in a hash map is the simplest broad phase that works well for most 2D games.
lessons.objective: Build a uniform-grid spatial hash, insert objects by bounding box, query neighbors with deduplication, and count pair checks against the naive all-pairs loop.

cautions: Map iteration order is random; never derive pair order from it.
Clustered scenes and poor cell sizes degrade toward naive cost.
designGuide.cost: A map or dense array rebuilt every tick plus a mark slice; memory grows with objects times cells touched.
strengths: Cuts pair checks from quadratic to near linear in spread-out scenes.
Simple to rebuild every tick and to verify against the naive loop.

alternatives: Lower-indexed objects were already removed from the grid
Objects with lower indices cannot overlap later ones
quiz.correct: So each unordered pair is checked once, not twice
quiz.explanation: Neighborhood queries are symmetric, so each pair appears from both objects; keeping only j > i checks it once and also drops the object itself, which every query returns.
quiz.hint: The pair (3, 8) is found when object 3 queries and again when object 8 queries.
quiz.question: In the grid pair search, every object queries its own bounds. Why does the loop skip candidates with j <= i?

review.answer: So each unordered pair is checked once, not twice
review.prompt: Why j > i in the pair loop?

sections.body: A spatial hash divides the plane into square cells of one size and maps each cell coordinate to the objects touching it. The key is the pair floor(x / size), floor(y / size). Floor matters: converting with int() truncates toward zero, so both -0.5 and 0.5 land in cell 0, the cell at the origin becomes twice as wide as the others, and collisions near negative coordinates start to misbehave in ways that are hard to reproduce. A struct of two ints is a perfectly good Go map key; packing the pair into a uint64 saves a little hashing at the cost of clarity. Choose the cell size from your objects: around the size of a typical object, and at least the largest diameter if every object should touch at most two cells per axis.
sections.title: Cells, keys and the truncation trap

sections.body: The program builds a seeded scene of 500 circles with radii between 2 and 8 in an 800 by 600 world. Insert files each object under every cell its bounding box touches. Query walks the cells under a box and returns each object found there exactly once: an object spanning two cells sits in both buckets, so the grid keeps a mark per object and a stamp that increases with every query, which deduplicates without allocating a set. Pair finding queries each object's own bounds and keeps only candidates with a higher index, so every unordered pair is checked once, from its lower-indexed object. The naive loop runs as well, and the two lists of overlapping pairs are compared.
sections.title: Insert by bounds, query with a stamp, count the work
sections.walkthrough: rand.NewPCG(2026, 11) fixes the scene, so the numbers repeat on every run with this toolchain. The naive loop makes 124,750 checks and finds 90 overlaps. The grid reads 2,254 bucket entries, counting duplicates and each object's own entry, and runs only 330 exact checks to find the same 90 pairs; slices.Equal confirms that the sorted lists match. The last query models an explosion of radius 40 at the center of the world: 7 objects are candidates and 4 of them actually intersect the blast.

sections.body: A broad phase produces two different duplicates. The first is one object found in several cells during a single query; the stamp removes it. The second is the pair (i, j) found once from i and again from j; the j > i rule removes it, and also drops the object itself, which every query returns. Miss either and overlaps are reported twice, so collision responses apply twice and objects bounce with double force. Ordering is the subtler issue. Iteration over a Go map is deliberately randomized, so a broad phase that produces pairs by ranging over the cell map yields a different pair order on every run; any resolution that moves objects then depends on that order, and the simulation stops being reproducible. This program never ranges over the map: it walks objects by index and reads cells by key, and it sorts the final list anyway before comparing.
sections.title: Two kinds of duplicates and one ordering trap

sections.body: Most games rebuild the grid every tick, because moving objects change cells and incremental updates add bookkeeping that rarely pays off. A fresh map every tick allocates; resetting each bucket to length zero keeps the backing arrays but also keeps keys for cells nobody occupies any more, so clear the map now and then. For a bounded world, a dense grid indexed by row*cols + col avoids hashing entirely and keeps memory predictable. Tune the cell size by measurement: too small and large objects touch many cells, too large and buckets fill until the grid degenerates toward the naive loop. Heavily clustered scenes, such as a crowd packed into one room, defeat any uniform grid; quadtrees or sort-and-sweep along one axis handle those better.
sections.title: Grids in production: rebuild, reuse, tune
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the bounded alternative to the map-based Grid and runs in your own project. Reset keeps each bucket's backing array, so after the first few ticks a rebuild allocates nothing. cell clamps coordinates into the world, which is a design decision: objects outside the bounds pile into the edge cells instead of disappearing, and the exact narrow-phase test still decides whether they collide.

sections.body: The strongest test for a broad phase is the one the program already runs: on seeded scenes, the set of overlapping pairs must equal the naive result exactly. Repeat it across several seeds, densities and cell sizes, including objects larger than a cell and objects at negative coordinates, and keep it in the test suite as the oracle for every later optimization. Then benchmark on realistic scenes and record pair checks next to nanoseconds, because the counts explain the timings. A broad phase that is fast but occasionally misses a pair is the kind of bug that surfaces as a bullet passing through an enemy once a week.
sections.title: Keep the naive loop as the oracle

reading.takeaway: Bucket objects into cells with floor-based keys, query only nearby cells, deduplicate with a per-query stamp and a lower-index pair rule, never derive pair order from map iteration, and keep the naive loop as the correctness oracle.

lessons.title: A spatial hash for the broad phase: bucket by cell, query neighbors, check each pair once

summary: Fixed timesteps, Ebitengine structure, vectors, input actions, state machines, components, collisions and spatial hashing.
title: Game loop, input and physics
translationNote: Runnable models are engine-free and deterministic. Build windowed games with Ebitengine in your own native environment; GopherForge does not run a graphics engine.

lessons.explanation: The previous unit gave every entity a world position and a fixed-timestep update. A tile map lays a grid over that world, and a camera decides which part of it reaches the screen. Both are small pieces of arithmetic, and most tile-map bugs are one of three mistakes in it: the wrong coordinate space, the wrong rounding or the wrong edge.
lessons.objective: Convert between tile, world and screen coordinates, keep a following camera inside the map and compute the exact range of tiles to draw.

cautions: int() truncation misplaces negative coordinates by one tile.
Rounding the camera inside the simulation makes smooth follow stutter.
designGuide.cost: Two small conversion functions and a range calculation per frame; the real cost is discipline about which space every value lives in.
strengths: Draw cost depends on the view size, not the map size.
One transform pair keeps drawing and picking consistent.

alternatives: Float division by 16 loses precision for negative values
The camera offset is applied twice for negative positions
quiz.correct: int() truncates toward zero, so -0.5 maps to tile 0
quiz.explanation: Go's float-to-int conversion discards the fraction, rounding toward zero, so negative positions land one tile too far right or down; math.Floor returns -1 and the bounds check rejects it.
quiz.hint: Compare how int() and math.Floor round -0.56.
quiz.question: A click lands at world x = -9, in the margin left of the map. Why does int(x / 16) report the wrong tile?

review.answer: int() truncates toward zero, so -0.5 maps to tile 0
review.prompt: Why floor, not int(), for tiles?

sections.body: Tile coordinates are integer column and row indexes into the map. World coordinates are continuous positions in world pixels: with 16-pixel tiles, tile (c, r) covers x from c*16 up to, but not including, (c+1)*16. Screen coordinates are what the window shows after the camera offset and zoom. The map owns the tile-to-world rule and the camera owns the world-to-screen rule; no other code should do either conversion by hand. Simulation, collision and pathfinding stay in world or tile space. Screen space appears only at the two boundaries where the player meets the game: drawing, and turning a mouse or touch position back into a world point. Store each cell as a small index into a shared tileset rather than as an object with its own image. That is the flyweight pattern: a 40x30 map becomes 1200 bytes instead of 1200 sprite objects, and the tileset is loaded once.
sections.title: Three coordinate spaces, owned by two types

sections.body: The program builds a 40x30 map of 16-pixel tiles and shows it through a 640x360 window at zoom 2, which is a 320x180 view in world pixels. It moves the target to the top-left corner, the middle and the bottom-right corner and prints where the camera settled and which tiles intersect the view. It then sends a click through the inverse transform, centers a room smaller than the view, and shows what integer conversion does to a click in the margin beside that room.
sections.title: Follow, clamp and cull with one camera value
sections.walkthrough: Follow first centers the target (target minus half the view) and then clamps each axis to the range from 0 to mapSize - viewSize, so the corner targets print camera (0,0) and (320,300) instead of showing empty space past the edge. When the map is smaller than the view the limit is negative, and clampAxis returns half of it, which centers the 192x128 room at (-64,-26). Visible floors the top-left corner, takes ceil(edge / tileSize) - 1 for the bottom-right corner and clamps both to the map. A camera at x=140 therefore draws columns 8 to 28: 21 columns, one more than an aligned view, because partial tiles show at both edges. ScreenToWorld divides by the zoom and adds the camera position; WorldToScreen undoes it exactly, which the click line proves by returning to (100,50). The last line is the bug the next section explains.

sections.body: Go's conversion from float to int truncates toward zero, so int(-9.0/16) is 0, not -1. A click in the margin left of a centered room becomes a click on tile (0,0), and an entity standing just west of a chunk boundary is filed under the wrong chunk. math.Floor returns -1, which the bounds check then rejects. The same off-by-one hides at the far edge: a 320-pixel view starting at x=8 touches 21 columns, not 20, and a range computed as start + view / tileSize leaves a strip of unpainted background on the right. Clamping the range to the map is what makes culling safe as well as cheap: the draw loop can index the tile slice directly, because Visible never returns a column outside 0 to Cols-1, whatever the camera does. Keep the camera position as float64 in the simulation so smooth follow and screen shake stay smooth, and round it only at draw time. Pixel art drawn at fractional offsets shimmers and opens one-pixel seams between tiles; snapping the camera, not each tile, keeps neighbors exactly one tile apart.
sections.title: Floor at the edges, and snap only when drawing

sections.body: In a real game the same Camera drives Draw. Ebitengine scales the logical screen size returned by Layout to the window, and each DrawImage call takes a GeoM matrix. Translate by the tile position minus the snapped camera, then scale by the zoom. GeoM applies operations in the order you call them, so this is exactly WorldToScreen from the program.
sections.title: Draw the visible range in Ebitengine
sections.walkthrough: This fragment needs github.com/hajimehoshi/ebiten/v2 and runs in your own native environment, not in the app. g.tiles holds sub-images cut once from a single tileset image with SubImage at load time, so consecutive draws share one source texture and Ebitengine can merge them into fewer GPU draw calls. One DrawImageOptions value is reset and reused for the whole loop instead of being allocated per tile; the frame-budget lesson measures why that matters. Flooring the camera to whole world pixels means that at zoom 2 every tile lands on an even screen pixel.

sections.body: A camera locked rigidly to the player feels twitchy. Common refinements are a dead zone (move the camera only when the target leaves a central rectangle), look-ahead (offset toward the facing or velocity direction) and smoothing (move a fraction of the remaining distance each tick, which the tweening lesson builds properly). Apply all of them before the clamp so no refinement can push the view past the map edge. Parallax background layers reuse the same camera with its position multiplied by a factor below 1. Large worlds split the map into chunks and cull chunks first, then tiles inside each visible chunk, with the same floor-based range math. Test the camera as a table: targets at all four corners and the center, a map smaller than the view on one axis only, zoom 1, 2 and a fractional zoom such as 1.5, and a property check that every screen pixel converts back to a world point inside the reported tile range.
sections.title: Camera behavior players notice, and how to test it

reading.takeaway: Keep the simulation in world space, convert through one camera type, floor (never truncate) from world to tile coordinates, clamp the camera before drawing and clamp the visible range so culling can never index outside the map.

lessons.title: A camera is a coordinate transform: follow the target, clamp to the map, draw only visible tiles

lessons.explanation: Chasing the player in a straight line works until the first wall. Breadth-first search finds a way around but ignores terrain cost; Dijkstra respects cost but explores every cell closer than the goal, in all directions. A* keeps Dijkstra's guarantee while steering the search with an estimate of the remaining distance. Its quality depends on three choices that are easy to get subtly wrong: the cost model, the heuristic and the tie-break.
lessons.objective: Implement grid A* with container/heap, choose a heuristic that matches the movement rules, make equal-cost choices deterministic and decide when a flow field beats per-unit searches.

cautions: Manhattan on an 8-way grid overestimates and loses optimality.
An unreachable goal explores every reachable cell; budget it.
designGuide.cost: A heap, two arrays sized to the map and a careful Less method; time grows with the cells expanded times the log of the open-set size.
strengths: Optimal paths with far fewer expansions than Dijkstra.
Integer costs and a total order make results replayable.

alternatives: container/heap keeps equal entries in insertion order
An admissible heuristic guarantees one unique path
quiz.correct: Equal-cost paths otherwise depend on incidental order
quiz.explanation: Admissibility guarantees an optimal cost, not a unique route, and a binary heap is not stable; only a total order such as f, then h, then push sequence fixes which equal-cost path wins.
quiz.hint: Consider what a binary heap promises about entries that compare equal.
quiz.question: Two routes to the goal have the same cost. What makes an A* implementation keep choosing the same one after a refactor?

review.answer: Equal-cost paths otherwise depend on incidental order

sections.body: For each cell A* tracks g, the cheapest known cost from the start, and h, an estimate of the cost from the cell to the goal. The open set is a priority queue ordered by f = g + h; the search repeatedly expands the lowest-f cell and relaxes its neighbors. If h never overestimates the true remaining cost, it is admissible, and the first time the goal leaves the queue its path is optimal. With h = 0, A* is Dijkstra; a larger admissible h expands fewer cells. The pathfinder should not own the map. It asks a walkability question per cell, so the same search can run against static walls, a door table or a temporary obstacle overlay. Use integer costs, 10 per straight step and 14 per diagonal, so sums are exact and comparisons cannot depend on floating-point rounding.
sections.title: What A* tracks and what it guarantees

sections.body: The program parses a small ASCII level, runs a 4-way search with the Manhattan heuristic and an 8-way search with the octile heuristic, and draws each path with asterisks. It then runs the 8-way search with a zero heuristic to compare the work done, and finally seals both gaps in the central wall to show what an unreachable goal costs.
sections.title: A* with container/heap and a total order
sections.walkthrough: openSet implements heap.Interface, and heap.Push and heap.Pop keep it ordered by Less, which compares f, then h, then a sequence number assigned at push time, so no two entries ever compare equal. Instead of a decrease-key operation, a cheaper route simply pushes a new entry; when the outdated entry surfaces later, its g no longer matches best and it is skipped. A diagonal step is allowed only when both orthogonal neighbors are open, so a path never squeezes between two diagonal walls. The 4-way path costs 200 over 20 steps; diagonals cut it to 182 over 17. The zero heuristic finds the same cost but expands 57 cells instead of 43. With both gaps sealed, the search exhausts all 37 reachable cells before it can report that no path exists.

sections.body: Manhattan distance, 10*(dx+dy), is exact on an empty 4-way grid and admissible with walls. On an 8-way grid it overestimates: one diagonal step costs 14, but Manhattan charges 20, so the search can return a path that is not the cheapest. Octile distance, 10*max(dx,dy) + 4*min(dx,dy), is exact on an empty 8-way grid. Euclidean distance is admissible for both but underestimates, so it expands more cells than octile for no benefit on a grid. If some terrain costs less than 10 per step, such as roads, scale the heuristic by the cheapest step cost or it stops being admissible. An inadmissible heuristic is sometimes a deliberate choice: multiplying an admissible h by 1.2 finds paths faster and guarantees a result at most 20 percent longer than optimal, a trade many games accept for background units. Make that a named weight, not an accident of mixing movement rules.
sections.title: The heuristic must match the movement rules

sections.body: On a grid many paths share the same cost, so the order of equal-f entries decides which path you get. A binary heap is not stable: entries that compare equal leave in whatever order the heap happens to hold them. The search is still repeatable for one fixed sequence of pushes, but a harmless-looking refactor, such as generating neighbors in another order, reusing a heap between searches or reading blocked cells from a map, silently changes the chosen route. That breaks golden tests, replays that rerun the simulation from recorded inputs, and any lockstep network model where peers must agree. A total order fixes it: lower f first; among equal f, lower h, which prefers entries closer to the goal and usually expands fewer cells; then the push sequence number. Keep the neighbor order in a fixed slice, never a map, and write the ordering rule in a comment, because the chosen path is now part of the contract.
sections.title: Tie-breaking is part of the result

sections.body: A* answers one start for one goal. Thirty units converging on a base would run thirty searches over nearly the same cells. A flow field inverts the problem: one breadth-first or Dijkstra pass outward from the goal records, for every reachable cell, the neighbor one step closer, so each unit just follows next[cell] each tick. Its cost scales with the map, not with the number of units, and units spawned anywhere are handled for free. Rebuild it when the goal moves or walls change. For a few long-lived units with different goals, cache A* results keyed by start, goal and a map version counter that increments on every wall change, and revalidate a cached path lazily when its next step becomes blocked. When a search is expensive, give it a budget of expansions per tick and resume it on the next tick rather than letting one search consume the frame.
sections.title: Many units, one goal: cache paths or build a flow field
sections.walkthrough: This fragment reuses Grid, Point and the steps slice from the program above; paste it below FindPath and call it from main to run it in your own native environment. It is a breadth-first search, so it assumes every step costs the same; weighted terrain needs the same loop driven by a heap, as in A*. dist doubles as the visited set and as the answer to whether a unit can reach the goal at all. That matters because the zero value of next would otherwise point every unreachable unit at cell (0,0). On the lesson level it reports a distance of 20 steps from S, matching the 4-way A* path.

sections.body: Keep golden ASCII fixtures like the ones printed above and compare the rendered path, its cost and the expansion count; a jump in expansions exposes a broken heuristic even when the path still looks right. Check that a start equal to the goal returns a one-cell path, that a goal inside a wall or behind a sealed wall returns no path, and that every returned path is contiguous, avoids walls and costs exactly the sum of its steps. For optimality, generate many seeded random maps and assert that the A* cost equals the zero-heuristic cost. Benchmark the worst case, an unreachable goal on the largest map, because that search explores everything; decide in game design whether units should even try, or should first check a cheap connectivity label for the two regions.
sections.title: Test the search, not the screenshot

reading.takeaway: Use an admissible heuristic that matches the movement rules, give the open set a total order so equal-cost choices are reproducible, and switch to one shared flow field when many units travel to the same goal.

lessons.title: A* on a grid: a heap, a heuristic that matches the moves, and tie-breaking you can replay

lessons.explanation: Procedural generation is only useful when the same seed builds the same world: a player shares a seed, a tester attaches one to a bug report, a replay regenerates the level instead of storing it. That property is not automatic. It depends on who owns each random generator, how many values each system draws and in what order, and whether any code path reaches for a generator nobody seeded.
lessons.objective: Generate a seeded cave with a math/rand/v2 PCG source, keep each system on its own derived stream and explain why global or shared randomness breaks replays.

cautions: Map iteration, goroutines or global rand silently break replays.
Floating-point results can differ across architectures through FMA.
designGuide.cost: A few generator constructors and a validation pass; the lasting cost is keeping old generator versions alive while saved seeds depend on them.
strengths: A 64-bit seed rebuilds the whole level anywhere.
Named streams let systems change without reshuffling others.

alternatives: Reseeding the global generator with the world seed first
Switching the source from PCG to ChaCha8
quiz.correct: Extra draws in one system cannot shift another's values
quiz.explanation: The cave reads the next values of whatever stream it uses; if loot draws from the same stream, every later value moves. A stream derived per system keeps each sequence private, and math/rand/v2 has no global Seed anyway.
quiz.hint: Ask which code shares the sequence of values the cave consumes.
quiz.question: A designer adds one loot roll at level start, and every seeded cave changes shape. Which design prevents this?

review.answer: Extra draws in one system cannot shift another's values
review.prompt: Why one RNG stream per system?

sections.body: A seeded generator is a pure function of its seed and of the sequence of calls made on it. Store a 64-bit seed and a generator version and you can rebuild a whole cave on load, on a server or on a teammate's machine. The contract breaks in three ways: a different seed, which is obvious; different code, such as a tuned constant or a new pass; or a different number or order of draws from the same stream, which is subtle and the usual bug. The last one is why each system needs its own generator. In math/rand/v2, rand.New(rand.NewPCG(seed1, seed2)) returns a *rand.Rand over a PCG source with 128 bits of state, and nothing else in the process can draw from it unless you hand it over.
sections.title: A seed replaces the content you did not store

sections.body: The program derives a terrain stream from a world seed and the name "terrain", fills a 36x12 grid with 45 percent walls and runs four smoothing passes in which a cell becomes wall when at least five of the nine cells in its 3x3 block are walls. It prints the cave, counts floor regions, regenerates with the same seed, tries the next seed, and then shows what a single extra loot roll does to a shared stream compared with separate streams.
sections.title: A cellular-automaton cave from a named stream
sections.walkthrough: stream hashes the system name with FNV-1a into seed2, so "terrain" and "loot" get unrelated sequences from one world seed and adding a system never requires renumbering the others. Cave draws exactly one IntN per cell in row-major order, then smooths into a second buffer and swaps the two. Reading and writing one grid would let already-updated cells bias their neighbors, and the result would depend on scan direction. Border cells are forced to wall so the cave is closed. Regions flood-fills floor cells with an explicit stack and finds 2 regions, the main cave and a sealed pocket on the left, which the last section deals with. The fingerprints are FNV hashes of the printed map, handy as golden values in tests. One IntN(6) before generation on a shared stream changes the whole map; on separate streams it changes nothing.

sections.body: The top-level functions in math/rand/v2, such as rand.IntN, draw from a process-wide source that is seeded randomly at startup and has no Seed function, so a map built with them can never be rebuilt. A seedable shared generator fails in the way the shared-stream line shows: any new call anywhere, from a particle effect, a library or a debug overlay, shifts every value drawn after it. Concurrency makes it worse. A *rand.Rand is not safe for concurrent use, and even behind a mutex, which goroutine draws next depends on the scheduler, so the world changes from run to run. The rule is ownership: each system or chunk gets its own *rand.Rand, passed explicitly as a parameter or held in a field and used by one goroutine. Name streams after what they generate, such as terrain, loot, enemies and weather, and derive them all from the single world seed the player sees.
sections.title: Why global and shared randomness break replays

sections.body: Draw the same number of values in the same order on every run: loop over slices and fixed coordinate ranges, never over a map, whose iteration order Go randomizes on purpose. For streamed or endless worlds, derive a stream per chunk from the world seed and the chunk coordinates, so chunk (12, -3) is identical whether the player reaches it first or last. Prefer integer rules like the automaton above. Floating-point noise is reproducible on one platform, but the Go specification allows fused multiply-add, which compilers use on architectures such as arm64, so an arm64 client and an amd64 server can differ in the last bits; when generation must match bit for bit, use integer or fixed-point math or force rounding with explicit float64 conversions. Store a generator version beside the seed and keep old generators while saves reference them. The PCG source implements MarshalBinary and UnmarshalBinary, so a mid-run generator state can go into a save file. Finally, PCG itself is a fixed algorithm, but helpers such as IntN are library code; golden fingerprints in tests tell you at upgrade time whether a toolchain change altered any world.
sections.title: Rules that keep generation reproducible

sections.body: A random fill does not promise a playable level. The cave printed above has two regions, and a player spawned in the small pocket is trapped. Make validation part of generation: flood-fill from the spawn point, fill unreachable pockets with wall or carve a tunnel to them, require a minimum floor area and confirm that the exit is reachable with the pathfinding code from the previous lesson. When a candidate fails, retry deterministically by deriving the next attempt from the seed and the attempt number, and cap the attempts so a pathological seed fails loudly instead of looping. Test with a few thousand seeds in CI: assert the invariants on each one, record the fingerprints of a handful as golden values, and keep every seed that ever produced a broken map as a permanent regression fixture.
sections.title: Validate the world before the player sees it

reading.takeaway: Give every generating system its own seeded *rand.Rand derived from the world seed, never draw from global or shared generators in generation code, and validate and fingerprint the result so a seed stays a reliable save format.

lessons.title: Reproducible worlds: one seed, one random stream per system, and no global rand

lessons.explanation: A panel slides in, a coin bounces, a character cycles through four walking frames. The tempting implementation reads time.Now in Draw and computes progress from it. That ties animation to the wall clock: it keeps running while the game is paused, it behaves differently at 60 Hz and 144 Hz, and a replay cannot reproduce it. The fixed-timestep loop from the previous unit already provides a better clock: the tick.
lessons.objective: Drive easing curves, chained and retargeted tweens and sprite animation clips from tick counts so motion is deterministic, pausable and free of jumps.

cautions: Wall-clock animation diverges from the simulation and replays.
Pointer targets outlive destroyed entities; use IDs.
designGuide.cost: A few small structs and pure easing functions; motion granularity is one tick unless Draw interpolates between ticks.
strengths: Pause, slow motion and replays work without special cases.
Values land exactly on the target; nothing drifts.

alternatives: Restart the close tween from the menu's fully open position
Finish the open tween instantly, then play the close tween
quiz.correct: Retarget: start a new tween from the current value
quiz.explanation: Starting from the current value means the first eased step moves only a fraction away from where the panel already is; both alternatives teleport it to an end point first, which is the 37.5 to 75.0 jump in the program.
quiz.hint: Look at the value shown on the tick right after the cancel.
quiz.question: A menu is closed while its opening animation is halfway done. Which approach avoids a visible jump?

review.answer: Retarget: start a new tween from the current value

sections.body: Model a tween as a value holding a start, an end, a duration in ticks, the elapsed tick count and an easing function. Update calls Step once per tick and Draw reads Value. Because Value is computed from elapsed / duration instead of adding a small delta every tick, it cannot accumulate rounding error, and the last tick lands exactly on the target. Pausing means not calling Step, slow motion means stepping every other tick, and a replay reproduces every intermediate value. An easing function maps linear progress t from 0 to 1 onto eased progress with f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 1. It changes when the motion happens, not where it ends. Some easings leave the 0 to 1 range on purpose: outBack overshoots to give a panel a small bounce before it settles.
sections.title: A tween is data: from, to, duration and elapsed ticks

sections.body: The program samples four easings over a 10-tick tween, plays a two-step chain, cancels a slide partway through and compares a naive restart with a retarget, and finally picks sprite frames for a looping walk clip and a one-shot attack clip at selected ticks. Every value prints with fixed precision, so the output is identical on every platform.
sections.title: Ease, chain, retarget and animate in one program
sections.walkthrough: The table shows the character of each curve: outCubic covers almost half the distance in the first fifth of the time, inOutQuad starts and ends slowly, and outBack peaks at 1.099 before settling at exactly 1.000. Chain advances the current tween and moves to the next one only after the current one reports Done, so 100.0 appears once and the second step starts from it: eight samples for 4 + 3 ticks. The cancelled slide is at 37.5 after three of eight ticks. Restarting a tween from the original end point jumps to 75.0 on the next tick, while Retarget starts from the current value and glides down to 0.0. Clip.Frame divides elapsed ticks by ticks per frame. The walk loop wraps with a modulo, so tick 24 shows frame 4 again; the one-shot attack clamps to its last frame and reports Finished at tick 24, which a state machine can use to leave the attack state.

sections.body: Interruptions are where tweens go wrong. When a menu closes while it is still opening, there are three policies: hold (stop where it is), complete (jump to the end) and retarget (start a new tween from the current value toward the new target). Retarget is almost always what players expect; jumping to an end point first is the visible snap the program prints. Make the policy explicit in the API instead of letting each caller overwrite fields. Chains need a rule for the boundary tick: show either the last value of one tween or the first value of the next, never both and never neither. Completion callbacks are convenient, but a callback that starts another tween on the same object while the chain is still iterating is a classic source of skipped steps; prefer reporting Done and letting the owner decide. Refer to tween targets by entity ID resolved each tick, not by pointer, so a tween whose entity was destroyed finds nothing and ends instead of writing into a recycled slot.
sections.title: Cancelling and chaining without visible jumps

sections.body: A clip is a list of sprite-sheet indexes and a ticks-per-frame rate. The current frame is computed from the ticks since the clip started, so an entity stores only the clip and its start tick, not a frame counter that must be incremented and reset correctly. Switching from walk to attack records a new start tick; switching to the clip that is already playing must not, or a held key restarts the walk cycle on every tick. Gameplay events tied to animation, such as the frame where a sword connects, belong in the simulation as tick offsets within the clip, not in Draw, so they happen on the same tick in a replay and on a server. In Ebitengine, Update runs at the tick rate (60 per second unless SetTPS changes it) while Draw can run at the display rate. That is the right split: step tweens and clips in Update, read them in Draw, and interpolate between the previous and current tick with the fixed-timestep alpha if motion looks steppy on fast displays.
sections.title: Sprite frames are a function of elapsed ticks

sections.body: Because every value is a function of the tick, tests need no timers and no sleeps. Assert f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 1 for each easing, compare curves at fixed ticks against golden values formatted to three decimals like the table above, and check monotonicity wherever a curve promises it. Cover the edges: a zero-duration tween reports its target immediately, stepping past the end stays at the end, a retarget never moves the value on the retarget tick itself, and a one-shot clip with a single frame finishes after exactly its ticks-per-frame. If designers tune durations in seconds, convert them to ticks once at load time with an explicit rounding rule and test that the conversion is stable for your tick rate.
sections.title: Test animation as a table of samples

reading.takeaway: Advance tweens and sprite clips by simulation ticks, compute values from elapsed ticks instead of accumulating deltas, retarget from the current value when interrupted, and keep animation-driven gameplay events in Update.

lessons.title: Tweens and sprite frames advance with the simulation tick, not the wall clock

lessons.explanation: A save file outlives the build that wrote it, sits in a folder the player can edit and gets shared on forums. A loader that unmarshals it straight into game state will eventually meet a save from an older version, a save from a newer version, a file truncated by a crash and a hand-edited file with 999 health. Each of those needs a deliberate answer, and none of them should be a panic.
lessons.objective: Design a versioned JSON save format, migrate v1 saves to v2, reject unknown fields and out-of-range values, and replace a save file without ever leaving it half-written.

cautions: os.Rename is not atomic on non-Unix platforms.
Checksums catch corruption, not deliberate tampering.
designGuide.cost: A struct and a migration function per format version, one fixture per release, and a few extra system calls on every save.
strengths: Old saves keep loading as the format evolves.
A crash during saving never destroys progress.

alternatives: It stops players from editing the save between sessions
os.WriteFile cannot replace a file that already exists
quiz.correct: A crash leaves the old or new file, never half of each
quiz.explanation: On POSIX file systems rename swaps the directory entry in one step, so readers see the complete old save or the complete synced new one; writing in place truncates first and can leave a torn file.
quiz.hint: Picture the file if power fails halfway through the write.
quiz.question: Why does the save code write to a temporary file in the same directory and then rename it over the old save?

review.answer: A crash leaves the old or new file, never half of each
review.prompt: Why temp file + rename for saves?

sections.body: Old files: a field was renamed or restructured, the new struct silently decodes it as zero, and a v1 player loads with 0 health. Newer files: a player downgrades or copies a save from a newer build, the old build drops fields it does not know and then overwrites the file with less data than it read. Torn files: the game crashes or the device loses power during a write, and the only save is part old and part new. Crafted files: someone sets an inventory count to a billion or adds an item that does not exist, and the game indexes past a slice or grants a debug item. The answers are a version field read first, pure migration functions, strict decoding followed by explicit validation, and an atomic replace when writing.
sections.title: Four ways a naive loader fails

sections.body: The program loads a v1 save (flat hp, a position array and a list of item names) and migrates it to v2 (structured health, a position object and item stacks). It loads a valid v2 save, then feeds the loader six bad files: an unknown field, impossible health, a position outside the map, an unknown item, a newer version and a file with a second JSON value appended. Finally it writes the last good save atomically into a fresh directory under os.TempDir, reloads it and confirms that no temporary file was left behind.
sections.title: Decode the version, migrate, then validate
sections.walkthrough: Load caps the input at 64 KiB with io.LimitReader before parsing anything. json.Unmarshal into a struct holding only the version reads the version and, because Unmarshal requires exactly one JSON value, also rejects the file with trailing data; a json.Decoder alone would stop after the first value and never notice it. The switch then decodes with a Decoder whose DisallowUnknownFields turns godMode into an error instead of silently ignoring it. migrateV1 is a pure function that groups items into stacks in first-seen order rather than through a map, so its output is stable. Validate checks every invariant the game relies on; the negated range test for position also rejects NaN produced by a buggy migration. WriteAtomic writes a temporary file in the destination directory, syncs it, closes it and renames it over the target, and the deferred cleanup removes the temporary file if any step fails.

sections.body: Each release that changes the format gets a new struct and one function from the previous version to the next. Loading a v1 file in a v4 build runs v1 to v2, v2 to v3 and v3 to v4, so each migration is written and tested once against its own fixtures and never needs to know about later versions. Migrations choose defaults explicitly: v1 had no maximum health, so the function writes 100 rather than letting a zero value slip through. Refuse versions newer than the build supports, because a downgraded game that loads a v3 file into v2 structs and saves it back destroys progress. Do not rewrite the original file on load; write the migrated save on the next normal save through the atomic path, and keep the previous file as a backup slot until the new one has loaded successfully once. Note that encoding/json matches field names case-insensitively and lets a repeated key overwrite the earlier one; the strict JSON lesson shows the encoding/json/v2 options that reject both when a format needs it.
sections.title: Migrate forward in small, pure steps

sections.body: Writing a save in place truncates the file first, so a crash mid-write leaves neither version. Writing a temporary file in the same directory and renaming it over the old one gives readers either the complete old file or the complete new one, because on POSIX file systems rename replaces the directory entry in one step. The temporary file must live in the same directory, since a rename across file systems fails. Call Sync before Close so the bytes are durable before the name points at them, and on Unix also sync the directory if the rename itself must survive a power cut. The os.Rename documentation states that on non-Unix platforms it is not atomic even within one directory, so a Windows build should keep a backup slot and verify the new file on load. Console and mobile platforms usually provide save APIs with their own guarantees; prefer them there.
sections.title: Atomic replace: what rename does and does not promise
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs at the end of a function like WriteAtomic, runs in your own native environment and applies to Unix systems. Opening the parent directory and calling Sync asks the file system to persist the directory entry that rename changed; without it, a power loss right after the rename can bring back the old name on some file systems. It does not replace the Sync on the file itself, which persists the contents.

sections.body: Decoding proves only that the bytes matched the struct shape. Validation proves the game can use the result: ranges for every number, existence for every reference such as item IDs or level names, limits on every collection, and cross-field rules such as current health at most maximum health. Decide per field whether to reject the save or repair it with a logged clamp; rejecting is safer for anything that indexes memory, repairing is kinder for cosmetic settings. A checksum detects accidental corruption but is not tamper protection, because any key shipped in the client can be extracted; competitive or economy data belongs on a server. Keep a fixture directory with one real save from every released version and load all of them in CI, then fuzz the loader with those fixtures as the seed corpus.
sections.title: Validate after decoding, and test the loader like a parser
sections.walkthrough: This test fragment lives in a _test.go file in your own module and runs with go test -fuzz=FuzzLoad on your machine; fixtureSaves is your helper that reads the fixture directory. The property is simple and strong: for any bytes, Load either returns an error or returns a save that passes Validate, and it never panics, hangs or allocates without bound. Crashing inputs found by the fuzzer are written under testdata/fuzz and become permanent regression cases.

reading.takeaway: Read the version first, migrate with pure per-version functions, decode strictly and validate every invariant, refuse newer formats, and replace saves by renaming a synced temporary file from the same directory.

lessons.title: Save files are untrusted input: version them, migrate forward, validate and write atomically

lessons.explanation: In a multiplayer game every client is a program you do not control. If clients report their own positions, a modified client can teleport, fly or walk through walls, and the server has no grounds to refuse. An authoritative server inverts that: clients send what the player wants to do, the server decides what happens, and everyone receives the server's version of the world. Goroutines and channels fit this shape well, provided exactly one goroutine owns the state.
lessons.objective: Build a server tick loop in which one goroutine owns all game state, clients send inputs over channels, movement is validated against speed and rate limits, and snapshots are copies in a deterministic order.

cautions: A blocking broadcast lets one slow client stall the tick.
Strict rules without tolerance punish lossy connections.
designGuide.cost: Server CPU for every player's simulation, a round trip of latency the client must hide, and a validation rule for every action.
strengths: A modified client cannot teleport or exceed the speed cap.
One owner goroutine removes locks from game logic.

alternatives: Directions are smaller to encode, which is the main reason
Directions let clients keep moving while the server is busy
quiz.correct: Inputs with sequence numbers; the server computes moves
quiz.explanation: With directions the server applies its own speed cap, collision and bounds, so a hacked client can at most choose where to walk; a reported position would let the client decide the outcome.
quiz.hint: Which side decides where a modified client ends up?
quiz.question: Why does the authoritative server accept movement directions from clients instead of positions?

review.answer: Inputs with sequence numbers; the server computes moves
review.prompt: What should a game client send?

sections.body: An input message carries a sequence number and a desired direction. It has no position, health or score field, so there is nothing to forge. The server tick applies inputs with its own speed, its own collision rules from the previous unit and its own map, then publishes a snapshot. Ownership is the other half of the design: the world lives in one goroutine. Network readers and timers talk to it through channels, and nothing outside that goroutine holds a pointer into the world. That removes locks from game logic, makes each tick a sequential function you can review and test, and gives every rule a single place to be enforced. The sender's identity comes from the connection, never from a field in the payload.
sections.title: Clients send intent; the server computes outcomes

sections.body: The program starts a server goroutine that owns three players, creates one Session per simulated client and runs four ticks. In each tick every client goroutine sends its inputs concurrently; the main goroutine waits for all sends, asks the server for a tick and prints the snapshot. Player 1 walks right, player 2 uses keyboard diagonals and then turns, and player 3 cheats with an oversized direction, three moves in one tick, a replayed sequence number, a NaN direction and a forged player ID.
sections.title: A tick loop with validation and deterministic order
sections.walkthrough: Inputs travel over an unbuffered channel, so each Send completes only when the server goroutine has received the value, and wg.Wait therefore proves that every input is in pending before the tick request is sent. Arrival order still depends on the scheduler, so step sorts by player and sequence before applying anything, and the output is identical on every run. apply drops a sequence at or below the last one seen, allows one move per player per tick, rejects non-finite directions and normalizes any direction longer than 1, logging only lengths that no real controller produces. Dropped extras still advance the ack so the client stops resending them. Positions are clamped to the arena, which is why player 3 stops at 100.0. Session overwrites Player, so player 3's attempt to send as player 1 just moves player 3. Snapshots copy values into PlayerState, so no client can alias server memory.

sections.body: Every rule needs a tolerance chosen with real networks in mind. Packets get duplicated and reordered, so an old sequence number is dropped quietly rather than treated as an attack. A burst of inputs after a lag spike is normal: a production server usually queues a few inputs per player and applies them over the next ticks, dropping only beyond that budget, whereas this program drops extras immediately to stay short. Normalizing direction vectors means a gamepad, a keyboard and a hacked client all move at the same maximum speed without the server guessing intent. Record violations with player, tick and sequence, and act on rates over time rather than on one event, because a single odd input is far more often a bug or a bad connection than a cheat. Never use a client-reported position even as a hint; if client and server disagree, the server is right and the client is corrected, which is the subject of the next lesson.
sections.title: Validation rules that do not punish honest players

sections.body: The program drives ticks by hand to stay deterministic. A real server replaces the tick request with a time.Ticker and broadcasts each snapshot to per-client channels. The broadcast must never wait for a slow client: a full channel means that client misses this snapshot and gets the next one, which is harmless when each snapshot carries complete state rather than a delta.
sections.title: The production loop: a ticker, one select and non-blocking fan-out
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs in your own native environment; its ticks come from the wall clock, so its output is not reproducible the way the program's is. Joins arrive as messages in the same select, so the clients slice is touched only by the owner goroutine, and leaves would work the same way. Each client has a small buffered snapshots channel drained by its own writer goroutine that encodes and sends; all writers read the same snapshot, so treat it as immutable once published. A time.Ticker drops ticks when the receiver falls behind instead of queueing them, so measure each tick's duration and alert when it approaches the interval.

sections.body: The tick loop does not care whether inputs come from an in-process Session, UDP datagrams or WebSocket messages. Fast-paced games usually prefer UDP because a lost packet should not hold newer inputs back the way in-order TCP delivery does. The reader goroutine does the untrusted-input work: size limits, decoding, mapping the sender to an authenticated session, and dropping instead of blocking when the server is busy.
sections.title: A real transport feeds the same channel
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment with a conn from net.ListenPacket("udp", ":7777"); Sessions, decodeInput and the handshake are yours to define. A source address alone is not authentication, because UDP source addresses can be spoofed, so Verify checks a per-session token or message authentication code agreed during an authenticated connect. Ignoring unknown senders without replying keeps the server from becoming a traffic amplifier. The buffer is reused across reads, which is safe because decodeInput copies values into an Input before the next ReadFrom. A WebSocket transport, which needs a third-party package because the standard library has none, would feed the same channel.

sections.body: Most server logic lives in step, a function of world state and a batch of inputs. Test it directly with tables of inputs and expected snapshots, including the cheats from the program, duplicated and reordered sequences, players joining and leaving between ticks, and inputs for unknown players. Run the goroutine wrapper under the race detector to prove nothing else touches the world, and fuzz decodeInput with arbitrary bytes. Then add a few integration tests over a loopback socket with injected latency and loss; they are slower and noisier, but they catch framing and shutdown bugs. This model runs in one process. A production server adds authentication, matchmaking, persistence, interest management so each client receives only nearby entities, and metrics for tick duration and per-client drops.
sections.title: Test the tick, not the network

reading.takeaway: Let one goroutine own the world, accept only intent with sequence numbers, take identity from the connection, validate direction, rate and order every tick, sort inputs before applying them, and publish copied snapshots without blocking on slow clients.

lessons.title: An authoritative server owns the world in one goroutine and accepts only validated intent

lessons.explanation: The authoritative server from the previous lesson is fair but feels slow. With 50 ms of latency each way, a player presses right and nothing moves for a tenth of a second. Client-side prediction runs the same movement rule locally so the press responds at once, reconciliation fixes the prediction when the server disagrees, and interpolation shows other players smoothly, slightly in the past. They solve three different problems with three different pieces of state.
lessons.objective: Hide round-trip latency by predicting local movement, reconcile with acknowledged server snapshots by replaying pending inputs, and draw remote players by interpolating a snapshot buffer.

cautions: Prediction needs identical movement code on both sides.
Remote players are shown in the past; hits need lag compensation.
designGuide.cost: A pending-input buffer, a snapshot buffer and replay work proportional to the round-trip time on every snapshot.
strengths: Local movement responds on the same tick as the input.
Corrections are limited to real server disagreement.

alternatives: Keep its prediction, since the snapshot is already old
Snap to the server position and discard inputs 4 to 8
quiz.correct: Reset to server state, replay inputs after the ack
quiz.explanation: Inputs 4 to 8 are still in flight and the server will apply them; replaying them on top of the authoritative state predicts where the server will be and corrects only real disagreements, such as the closed door.
quiz.hint: The server has not applied some of the inputs yet; which ones still matter?
quiz.question: A snapshot arrives with the server position and ack = 3 while the client has already sent inputs up to 8. What should the client do?

review.answer: Reset to server state, replay inputs after the ack

sections.body: Prediction needs the local player's predicted state and a buffer of inputs that were sent but not yet acknowledged. Reconciliation needs each snapshot to carry the server's state for this player plus the last input sequence the server applied, the ack. Interpolation needs a short buffer of snapshots of the remote entities, each tagged with its server tick. The local player is drawn at the predicted present; everyone else is drawn at a deliberate point in the past, where two real snapshots surround the render time. Mixing those up causes familiar bugs: predicting remote players makes them jitter and snap whenever they change direction, and interpolating your own character makes the controls feel delayed.
sections.title: Three techniques, three pieces of client state

sections.body: The program simulates both ends in one loop, with a one-way latency of 3 ticks and a snapshot every 2 ticks. The client presses right for ten ticks. At server tick 5 a door at x = 6 closes, which the client cannot predict. A second player runs right for five ticks and then turns back. Each snapshot arrival prints the reconciliation, and the remote lines show what the client draws for the other player next to what was true at that moment and what is true now.
sections.title: A deterministic network with fixed latency
sections.walkthrough: Predict appends the input to pending and moves immediately with the shared Move function. Reconcile resets to the snapshot's position and door state, keeps only inputs after the ack and replays them. Until the door closes the replay lands exactly on the prediction, so the correction is 0.0. At t=9 the snapshot from server tick 6 reports x=3.0, ack 3 and a closed door; replaying inputs 4 to 8 stops at the door, so the predicted 8.0 is corrected by 2.0 and later predictions stay at 6.0. The remote player is drawn at server time t - latency - interpDelay. At t=10 that is time 5, between the snapshots for ticks 4 and 6, which are both 18.0, so the true peak of 20.0 never appears: interpolation smooths over events that fall between snapshots. After the last ack, pending is empty and client and server agree.

sections.body: Snapping to the server position without a replay would discard every input still in flight and pull the character back by a full round trip on every snapshot. Replaying pending inputs on top of the authoritative state keeps corrections small: only the part the server actually disagreed with changes. That works only if client and server run the same movement code, which is easy in Go when both binaries import one simulation package. Bound the pending buffer to a few hundred milliseconds of inputs and treat overflow as a broken connection. Ignore any snapshot older than one already applied; this program never needs that check because its link never reorders. Keep the simulation state snapped to the corrected value, but let the rendered position chase it over a few frames, so a 2-unit correction looks like a slight drift rather than a teleport, and snap the rendered position too when the error is large, such as after a respawn.
sections.title: Reconcile by replaying, then smooth what the player sees

sections.body: The client never sees other players' inputs, so it cannot predict them well. Instead it draws them at a render time behind the newest snapshot and interpolates between the two snapshots that bracket it. The delay must cover the snapshot interval plus network jitter; many games use two intervals so that one lost packet does not empty the buffer, while this program uses one to keep the output short. When the buffer runs dry, hold the last position or extrapolate for a short, capped time, then hold. The delay has a visible cost: you see opponents where they were, so a shot aimed at them would miss on the server unless the server performs lag compensation, rewinding other players to the moment the shooter saw before testing the hit. That decision is a fairness trade-off between shooter and target, and it belongs on the server, never in the client.
sections.title: Remote players live in the past on purpose

sections.body: Prediction tolerates small divergence because reconciliation corrects it. Lockstep networking, where peers exchange only inputs, does not: it needs bit-identical simulation on every machine, which in Go means iterating slices instead of maps, avoiding goroutine-dependent order and remembering that floating-point fusion can differ between arm64 and amd64 builds. Test netcode the way this program runs: a simulated link with configurable latency, jitter, loss and reordering driven by a seeded generator, with no sockets and no sleeps. Assert convergence, meaning that after inputs stop and messages drain, client and server agree and pending is empty; assert zero corrections when no server-only event happens; and assert bounded corrections when one does. Then add adversarial schedules: a snapshot lost right before the door event, two snapshots arriving in one tick and a snapshot older than one already applied.
sections.title: How much determinism you need, and how to test it

reading.takeaway: Predict the local player with shared movement code, keep unacknowledged inputs, reconcile by resetting to the server state and replaying inputs after the ack, and draw remote players interpolated between buffered snapshots at a fixed delay.

lessons.title: Client prediction replays unacknowledged inputs; remote players are interpolated from the past

lessons.explanation: At 60 frames per second each frame has about 16.6 ms for input, simulation, drawing and whatever the runtime needs. Go's garbage collector runs concurrently, but its work is paid for by your program: the more a game allocates per frame, the more often a cycle starts and the more CPU the collector takes from the loop. The useful goal is not zero allocations ever; it is an update that allocates nothing in steady state, verified by a number a test can check.
lessons.objective: Turn refresh rates into frame budgets, count allocations per update with testing.AllocsPerRun, remove per-frame slices, maps, closures and strings, and profile a game loop with pprof and execution traces.

cautions: Non-zero allocation counts change between Go releases.
sync.Pool may drop pooled objects at any GC cycle.
designGuide.cost: Scratch fields on the world, capacity planning at level load, and code that is slightly less obvious than allocating fresh values.
strengths: A zero-allocation assertion catches regressions in CI.
Loop-owned buffers are deterministic and cache-friendly.

alternatives: As few as possible, with runtime.GC called every frame
Any amount, since Go's concurrent GC never slows the loop
quiz.correct: Zero in steady state, enforced by an AllocsPerRun test
quiz.explanation: Allocation rate drives how often GC cycles start and how much assist work the loop pays; an update that allocates nothing in steady state removes that pressure, and asserting exactly zero stays valid when releases change non-zero counts.
quiz.hint: Think about which number a test can assert reliably across Go releases.
quiz.question: What allocation target should a game's per-frame update have, and how do you keep it there?

review.answer: Zero in steady state, enforced by an AllocsPerRun test

sections.body: Divide one second by the refresh rate: about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz and 6.9 ms at 144 Hz. Ebitengine calls Update at the tick rate and Draw once per displayed frame, and both share that budget with the graphics driver and the operating system. A frame that misses its deadline is a visible hitch, and players notice a single 30 ms spike more than a steady 10 ms average. Allocation feeds that risk. The collector paces cycles by heap growth, so a loop that allocates a few megabytes per second starts cycles regularly; during a cycle, background workers take a share of the CPU and goroutines that keep allocating are charged assist work, which lands directly in your update. Reducing the allocation rate is therefore the first lever, and GOGC or GOMEMLIMIT tuning, covered by the GC budget lesson, comes after it.
sections.title: Where the 16.6 ms goes

sections.body: testing.AllocsPerRun runs a function once to warm up, counts heap allocations over the requested number of runs and returns the integer average, with GOMAXPROCS set to 1 during the measurement. It works outside tests too, so the program uses it on paired implementations: a visibility query written the obvious way and one that reuses storage, deferred hit effects as closures and as values, and HUD text rebuilt every update versus cached. The two versions in each pair produce the same result; only their allocation behavior differs.
sections.title: Count allocations per update with testing.AllocsPerRun
sections.walkthrough: time.Second / time.Duration(hz) prints exact budgets. VisibleFresh allocates 22 times per call: append growing a nil slice to 173 elements, the map growing as IDs are inserted, and sort.Slice, which receives the slice as an interface and builds a reflection-based swapper. VisibleReuse truncates a slice sized at level load, replaces the map with a stamp slice compared against a frame counter and sorts with slices.SortFunc; its comparison closure captures w but does not escape, so it lives on the stack and the count is 0. QueueClosures stores 32 capturing closures in a slice for later, so each one escapes to the heap: exactly 32. QueueValues queues the same hits as structs: 0. fmt.Sprintf allocates twice, once to box the int into its ...any parameter and once for the new string, while the HUD cache rebuilds only when the score changes. Results go into package-level variables so the compiler cannot discard the work. The counts are stable for one toolchain but can change between Go releases as escape analysis improves.

sections.body: Size scratch slices when a level loads and reuse them with s = s[:0], so append writes into existing capacity. Replace per-frame sets with data the world already owns: a stamp slice, a bit set, or a long-lived map emptied with clear(m), which keeps its storage. Queue effects as plain structs processed in one loop instead of closures that capture entities; values are also easier to log, replay and send over the network. Closures are not the problem by themselves, escaping closures are: a closure passed to a function that only calls it, like the SortFunc comparator, stays on the stack. Watch for hidden boxing, because passing an int or a struct as any to fmt, a logger or an interface-typed event bus can allocate, and so can converting []byte to string for text. Build HUD strings when the value changes, not every frame. To see why a line allocates, go build -gcflags=-m prints the compiler's escape decisions.
sections.title: Patterns that keep the steady state allocation-free

sections.body: sync.Pool helps when many goroutines need short-lived buffers, such as a server encoding snapshots for hundreds of clients in parallel. It is a poor fit for game entities. The pool may drop any object during garbage collection, keeping one victim generation so an idle object survives about one extra cycle at most; Get may return a fresh object; and every Get and Put adds ownership rules, which the pool ownership lesson covers. A single-threaded update loop has a simpler, deterministic option: a free list. Keep particles or projectiles in a slice, mark dead ones and push their indexes onto a free list that the next spawn pops. Nothing is allocated once capacity is reached, nothing disappears behind your back, and iterating a dense slice is friendly to the CPU cache.
sections.title: sync.Pool or a free list owned by the loop
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs to an update loop in your own game and runs in your native environment; Particle is your struct with an Alive flag that the update skips. Spawn reuses a dead slot before growing items, so once items and free reach their working capacity, spawning and killing allocate nothing. Kill must run once per particle, and other systems that hold an index can see a reused slot; a generation counter per slot, checked on every lookup, catches those stale indexes. Choose sync.Pool when objects cross goroutines and reuse is only an optimization, and a free list when the loop owns them.

sections.body: A number printed once is a curiosity; a test that fails when the hot path starts allocating is a guard. Assert exactly zero rather than a non-zero count, because zero stays valid when a Go release changes escape analysis. Pair it with a benchmark that reports time and allocations per update for a scripted scene with a fixed seed, so two runs are comparable.
sections.title: Turn the measurement into a test and a benchmark
sections.walkthrough: This fragment goes into a _test.go file beside your World type and runs with go test in your own module. The explicit warm-up call lets scratch slices reach their working capacity before measuring; AllocsPerRun also warms up once on its own. Passing the method value w.Update is fine here because it is created once, outside the measured runs. b.Loop, available since Go 1.24, runs the body the right number of times and keeps the setup above it out of the timing. Run the zero-allocation test without -race and without coverage, since instrumentation can change the counts.

sections.body: When the budget is blown, benchmarks and profiles answer where the time goes and which lines allocate, and traces show whether a slow frame overlapped a GC cycle. Use the same deterministic scene for every comparison.
sections.code:
# Time and allocations per update, five samples for comparison
go test -run '^$' -bench 'Update' -benchmem -count 5 ./game

# CPU and heap profiles from the same benchmark
go test -run '^$' -bench 'Update' -cpuprofile cpu.out -memprofile mem.out ./game
go tool pprof -top cpu.out
go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_objects -list 'World.Update' mem.out

# GC cycles while the real game runs, one line per cycle on stderr
GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./mygame 2> gc.log

# Execution trace: GC, goroutines and processor use on one timeline
go test -run '^$' -bench 'Update' -trace trace.out ./game
go tool trace trace.out
sections.title: Profile the loop you actually ship
sections.walkthrough: Run these commands in your own module; ./game and ./mygame stand for your package and binary. -run '^$' skips ordinary tests so only benchmarks run. The heap profile written by -memprofile records allocation sites, and -sample_index=alloc_objects ranks them by count, which matches what AllocsPerRun measures; -list prints source lines with their numbers. gctrace prints one line per GC cycle while the game runs, and the execution trace puts GC, goroutines and processors on one timeline. For spikes that appear only in long sessions, runtime/trace's FlightRecorder keeps the last few seconds in memory, so a debug build can write it to a file when a frame exceeds its budget.

reading.takeaway: Budget each frame from the refresh rate, measure allocations per update with testing.AllocsPerRun, reach zero in steady state by reusing storage the loop owns, and confirm with benchmarks, pprof and traces before tuning the GC.

lessons.title: A 16.6 ms frame budget: measure allocations per update and make the steady state allocate nothing

summary: Tilemaps and cameras, A* pathfinding, seeded generation, tweens, save files, authoritative servers, prediction and frame budgets.
title: Worlds, AI and multiplayer
translationNote: Headless simulations stand in for rendering and sockets. Real transports, assets and platform builds belong to your own native project.
